Press “Step” to submit one task at a time.
🔍

abort: once the queue is full, submission throws — the caller decides what to do, and execute stops being a "fire and forget". caller-runs: nothing is lost and nothing throws, but the overhead is repaid by the caller doing the work, so it cannot submit (or accept) while it is busy — backpressure all the way to the TCP layer. discard: the newest request vanishes silently and the pool runs smoothly through what it accepted — fast, and fine only if a lost request is acceptable. discard-oldest: the queue sheds its oldest waiting task to make room, which keeps the newest work and quietly drops guaranteed-accepted work instead.

§Patterns worth stealing

The eighteen listings above are the book's. These two put the chapter's tuning knobs together the way a service actually configures them.

1One executor factory, sized from the machine

PATTERN Pool sized from N_cpu and W/C, bounded queue, caller-runs, named threads 
public final class Pools {
    private static final int N_CPU =
            Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();

    /**
     * N_threads = N_cpu * U_cpu * (1 + W/C)
     *   U_cpu - target utilization, 0..1
     *   W/C   - ratio of wait time to compute time (profile it, don't guess)
     */
    public static int sizeFor(double targetUtil, double waitToCompute) {
        if (targetUtil <= 0 || targetUtil > 1 || waitToCompute < 0)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad sizing input");
        return Math.max(1,
                (int) Math.ceil(N_CPU * targetUtil * (1 + waitToCompute)));
    }

    /** CPU-bound work: N_cpu + 1 covers page faults and scheduling gaps. */
    public static ThreadPoolExecutor computePool(String name) {
        int n = N_CPU + 1;
        return new ThreadPoolExecutor(n, n, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
                new LinkedBlockingQueue<Runnable>(1000),   // bounded: no silent growth
                named(name),
                new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());  // backpressure, no loss
    }

    /** I/O-bound work: more threads, same discipline. */
    public static ThreadPoolExecutor ioPool(String name, int maxBacklog) {
        int n = sizeFor(0.9, 4.0);          // e.g. 4x wait-to-compute
        return new ThreadPoolExecutor(n, n, 60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
                new ArrayBlockingQueue<Runnable>(maxBacklog),
                named(name),
                new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());       // we handle overflow
    }

    /** Threads you can find in a thread dump, with deaths that get logged. */
    private static ThreadFactory named(final String prefix) {
        final AtomicInteger n = new AtomicInteger();
        return new ThreadFactory() {
            public Thread newThread(Runnable r) {
                Thread t = new Thread(r, prefix + "-" + n.incrementAndGet());
                t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) ->
                        System.err.println("uncaught in " + th.getName() + ": " + e));
                return t;                   // non-daemon: we own the lifecycle
            }
        };
    }
}

2A pool that reports itself

PATTERN Hooks for latency percentiles, plus the gauges that tell you the pool is clogged 
public class InstrumentedPool extends ThreadPoolExecutor {
    private final ThreadLocal<Long> started = new ThreadLocal<Long>();
    private final LongAdder count = new LongAdder();
    private final LongAdder totalNanos = new LongAdder();
    private final AtomicLong maxNanos = new AtomicLong();

    public InstrumentedPool(int core, int max, BlockingQueue<Runnable> q,
                            ThreadFactory tf, RejectedExecutionHandler h) {
        super(core, max, 60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS, q, tf, h);
        // Let core threads time out: an idle pool should shrink (Java 6+).
        allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true);
    }

    @Override protected void beforeExecute(Thread t, Runnable r) {
        super.beforeExecute(t, r);
        started.set(System.nanoTime());
    }

    @Override protected void afterExecute(Runnable r, Throwable failure) {
        try {
            Long begin = started.get();
            if (begin != null) {
                long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - begin;
                count.increment();
                totalNanos.add(elapsed);
                long seen;
                do {                              // max, without a lock or a reset
                    seen = maxNanos.get();
                } while (elapsed > seen && !maxNanos.compareAndSet(seen, elapsed));
                started.remove();                 // never leak into the next task
            }
            if (failure != null)      // non-null for Errors only: execute()
                System.err.println("task died: " + failure);  // reports Exceptions via UEH
        } finally {
            super.afterExecute(r, failure);
        }
    }

    @Override protected void terminated() {
        try {
            long n = count.sum();
            System.out.printf("pool done: %d tasks, avg %.1f ms, max %.1f ms%n",
                    n,
                    n == 0 ? 0.0 : totalNanos.sum() / 1e6 / n,
                    maxNanos.get() / 1e6);
        } finally {
            super.terminated();
        }
    }

    /** Queue depth is the leading indicator of a clogged pool. */
    public String health() {
        return String.format("active=%d queued=%d completed=%d poolSize=%d",
                getActiveCount(), getQueue().size(),
                getCompletedTaskCount(), getPoolSize());
    }
}

§Vocabulary introduced in Chapter 8

TermMeaning as used hereWhere it goes
Implicit couplingA task that only works under a particular execution policy, even though the API does not say so.Ch. 8.1
Thread starvation deadlockEvery pool thread blocked waiting for work that is itself waiting in the pool's queue.Ch. 8.1.1
Clogged poolA pool whose threads are all held by long or blocked tasks, so short tasks queue behind them.Ch. 8.1.2
Ncpu + 1The usual optimum for purely compute-bound work — the extra thread covers page faults and pauses.Ch. 8.2
W/C ratioWait time ÷ compute time; the factor that makes I/O-bound pools larger than CPU-bound ones.Ch. 8.2
Core pool sizeThe target size kept even when idle; the pool exceeds it only when the queue is full.Ch. 8.3.1
Maximum pool sizeThe ceiling on active threads.Ch. 8.3.1
Keep-alive timeHow long an above-core idle thread may live before it can be reaped.Ch. 8.3.1
Synchronous handoffA SynchronousQueue-based policy with no queue: task goes straight to a waiting worker, or is rejected.Ch. 8.3.2
Saturation policyWhat happens when the queue is full — and when tasks are submitted after shutdown.Ch. 8.3.3
Caller-runsRun the overflow task in the submitting thread; backpressure instead of loss or exceptions.Ch. 8.3.3
Thread factoryThe callback that creates pool threads — names, exception handlers, subclasses.Ch. 8.3.4
Unconfigurable executorA wrapper hiding the configuration setters so an execution policy cannot be changed by its clients.Ch. 8.3.5
Execution hooksbeforeExecute, afterExecute, terminated — the supported way to extend a pool.Ch. 8.4
Result-bearing latchA CountDownLatch plus a value that only the first setter wins (ValueLatch).Ch. 8.5.1
Work queue as call stackRecursive search whose frontier lives in the pool rather than the stack — deeper by memory, breadth-first by order.Ch. 8.5.1

✓Cheat sheet & self-check

SymptomLikely causeFix
Everything hangs with dependent tasksThread starvation deadlock — pool too small or bounded queueUnbounded pool, or caller-runs with SynchronousQueue, or restructure to avoid waiting
Pool works in test, dies in productionUnbounded queue absorbing load until memory runs outBounded queue + saturation policy
Throughput collapses under loadLong tasks clogging a small poolTimed waits, separate pools per workload class, bigger pool sized by W/C
CPU at 40% with a full queuePool too small, or a hidden resource bound (connections)Size from the real bottleneck, not from thread count
Thread dumps are unreadableDefault thread namesCustom ThreadFactory
Task failures vanishsubmit swallows exceptions into the FutureFuture.get, afterExecute, or an uncaught exception handler
JVM never exitsNon-daemon pool threads, pool never shut downshutdown + awaitTermination; or allowCoreThreadTimeOut
Pool behaviour changes after deploymentSomeone called a setter on a shared executorPublish it as an unconfigurableExecutorService
✅
Do

Size from Ncpu, utilization and W/C — or from the scarcest resource. Bound the queue and choose the saturation policy on purpose. Name your threads. Instrument with the hooks. Document every policy requirement next to the configuration.

🚫
Avoid

Submitting a task that waits on another task in the same bounded pool. Hard-coding pool sizes. core=0 with a queue that has capacity. Relying on ThreadLocal to pass state between tasks. DiscardOldestPolicy with a priority queue.

🧠
The one habit

Before tuning a pool, ask what its steady state is: how many tasks arrive per second, how long each holds a thread, and what else they hold while doing it. Those three numbers decide pool size, queue size and policy — everything else is guesswork.

Five questions the chapter leaves you with

  1. Do any of my tasks wait for another task — and if so, what guarantees the second one a thread?
  2. What is my pool's W/C ratio, and is the pool size derived from it or from folklore?
  3. Which scarce resource limits this pool in practice — CPU, memory, connections, or the queue itself?
  4. When the queue is full, do I lose work, throw, run it myself, or block the producer? Am I happy with that?
  5. If the pool were 90% clogged right now, which number in my metrics would tell me?

Notes carried over from the chapter

  1. The single-threaded requirement is not quite as strong as it sounds: it would be enough that tasks never execute concurrently and that enough synchronization exists for one task's memory effects to be visible to the next — which is precisely what newSingleThreadExecutor guarantees.
  2. Core threads are not started when a ThreadPoolExecutor is created; they start as tasks are submitted, unless you call prestartAllCoreThreads.
  3. Setting the core size to zero in the hope that threads get torn down produces strange behaviour with any queue that has capacity: if the pool is at core size, a new thread is created only when the queue is full, so tasks wait until the queue fills. In Java 6, allowCoreThreadTimeOut lets all pool threads time out — enable it with a zero core size if you want a bounded pool and bounded queue that still releases every thread when idle.
  4. Queues can smooth transient bursts, but sustained overload must be throttled — analogous to flow control in a communications network: you can buffer some data, but eventually the sender must be told to slow down, or the excess dropped.
  5. The throughput advantage of newCachedThreadPool comes from SynchronousQueue rather than LinkedBlockingQueue; SynchronousQueue was replaced in Java 6 with a non-blocking algorithm that improved Executor benchmark throughput by a factor of three over the Java 5.0 implementation (Scherer et al., 2006).
  6. An alternative configuration for tasks that submit other tasks and wait for their results is a bounded thread pool with a SynchronousQueue work queue and the caller-runs saturation policy.
  7. The sliding-block puzzles referenced in §8.5.1 are described at puzzleworld.org.

Summary of Java Concurrency in Practice, Chapter 8 (Applying Thread Pools), pp. 105–116. All code listings are the book's, with annotations added; diagrams are drawn for these notes.

Java Concurrency in Practice · Chapter 9

Chapter 9 — GUI Applications

Every swing you have ever made at a frozen window was a thread bug. GUI toolkits are single-threaded subsystems: all presentation state lives in one event dispatch thread, and thread confinement — not synchronization — is what keeps it consistent. That single decision gives you a simple programming model and one hard rule: never block the event thread. The rest of the chapter is about obeying that rule without losing the ability to cancel, report progress, and share data.

📖 pp. 117–126 🧩 5 sections · 8 listings · 2 figures ⏱️ ~22 min read 🏷️ Part II — Structuring Concurrent Applications

Chapter in one paragraph

TL;DR — the six things worth remembering

  1. GUI toolkits are single-threaded on purpose. Multithreaded GUI frameworks were tried repeatedly and abandoned: the two-way flow between input events and application callbacks makes inconsistent lock ordering inevitable (§9.1).
  2. The single-thread rule. Swing components and models may be created, modified, and queried only from the event dispatch thread. Safety comes from confinement, not from synchronized.
  3. The event thread is an Executor. Events are tasks, the event queue is a work queue, and invokeLater/invokeAndWait are execute/submit().get() — which is why GuiExecutor is nine lines long.
  4. Never block the event thread. A long task run there freezes the UI — the user cannot even press Cancel, because the cancel listener is itself an event waiting behind the task.
  5. Long tasks hop threads. Start in the event thread, run in a background pool, then hop back to the event thread to touch presentation objects. Cancellation and progress belong in a reusable helper, not in each listener.
  6. Shared data models need a plan. Either make the model thread-safe, or split it: presentation model confined to the event thread, shared model thread-safe, updates flowing as snapshots or increments.

9.1Why Are GUIs Single-threaded?

Not for lack of trying. Multithreaded GUI toolkits are one of the recurring "failed dreams" of computer science, and the reason is structural rather than accidental.

Old GUI applications processed events from a "main event loop". Modern frameworks are only slightly different: they create a dedicated event dispatch thread (EDT) that pulls events off a queue and dispatches them to application-defined handlers. Qt, NextStep, MacOS Cocoa, X Windows and Swing all converged on this design.

The reason is the direction in which work flows. User-initiated actions bubble up from the OS into the application: the OS detects a click, the toolkit turns it into a mouse event, and it arrives at a listener as a higher-level "button pressed" event. Application-initiated actions bubble down: changing a component's background colour starts in application code and is dispatched to a component class and onward to the OS for rendering.

The recipe for deadlock

Activities access the same GUI objects in opposite orders. Add a requirement that each object be thread-safe, and each thread must acquire the objects' locks — in whatever order its direction of travel implies. Inconsistent lock ordering, and therefore deadlock (Chapter 10), is the predictable result.

Model–view–controller makes it worse rather than better. Factoring a user interaction into cooperating model, view and controller objects simplifies the application, but the controller calls into the model, the model notifies the view, and the controller can also call into the view — which may call back into the model to query state. Three objects, two directions, no global order.

📎

Graham Hamilton, then a Sun VP, put it plainly on his weblog: a multithreaded GUI toolkit can be made to work if it is very carefully designed, exposes its locking methodology in gory detail, and if you are very smart, very careful, and hold the whole structure of the toolkit in your head. "If you get one of these things slightly wrong, things will mostly work, but you will get occasional hangs (due to deadlocks) or glitches (due to races)." That set of characteristics does not scale to widespread commercial use — which is why your toolkit is single-threaded.

Single-threaded GUI frameworks achieve thread safety through thread confinement: every GUI object, visual component and data model is accessed exclusively from the event thread. The burden is pushed back onto the application developer, who must make sure the confinement actually holds.

9.1.1Sequential event processing

GUI applications process fine-grained events — mouse clicks, key presses, timer expirations. Events are a kind of task, and the AWT/Swing event machinery is structurally an Executor with a single worker and an unbounded queue.

One thread means tasks run sequentially: one finishes before the next begins, and no two overlap. That simplifies task code considerably — you never have to reason about interference from another task. The price is that a slow task makes every other task wait. If those other tasks are what respond to user input or paint feedback, the application looks frozen: a long task in the event thread means the user cannot even click Cancel, because the cancel button's listener is an event queued behind the task that is running.

So: tasks that execute in the event thread must return control quickly. Anything long-running — spell-checking a document, walking the file system, fetching a resource over the network — must run in another thread, and any update to the UI (progress, completion) must come back to the event thread. That is the whole of §9.3 in one sentence, and it can get complicated quickly.

9.1.2Thread confinement in Swing

All Swing components (JButton, JTable, …) and data model objects (TableModel, TreeModel) are confined to the event thread. GUI objects are kept consistent not by synchronization but by confinement: tasks in the event thread need no synchronization to touch presentation objects, and code outside the event thread may not touch them at all.

📏

The Swing single-thread rule. Swing components and models should be created, modified, and queried only from the event-dispatching thread.

As with all rules there are exceptions, all of them documented as thread-safe in the Javadoc:

  • SwingUtilities.isEventDispatchThread — asks whether the current thread is the event thread;
  • SwingUtilities.invokeLater — schedules a Runnable on the event thread; callable from any thread;
  • SwingUtilities.invokeAndWait — schedules a task on the event thread and blocks the caller until it completes; callable only from a non-GUI thread;
  • methods that enqueue a repaint or revalidation request on the event queue — callable from any thread;
  • methods that add and remove listeners — callable from any thread, though listeners are always invoked in the event thread.

invokeLater and invokeAndWait behave a great deal like Executor.execute and ExecutorService.submit(...).get(). In fact the threading-related methods of SwingUtilities can be implemented with a single-threaded executor, as in Listing 9.1 — not how Swing is implemented, since it predates the Executor framework, but probably how it would be if written today.

BOOK Listing 9.1 · Implementing SwingUtilities using an Executor 
public class SwingUtilities {
    private static final ExecutorService exec =
        Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(new SwingThreadFactory());
    private static volatile Thread swingThread;

    private static class SwingThreadFactory implements ThreadFactory {
        public Thread newThread(Runnable r) {
            swingThread = new Thread(r);
            return swingThread;
        }
    }

    public static boolean isEventDispatchThread() {
        return Thread.currentThread() == swingThread;
    }

    public static void invokeLater(Runnable task) {
        exec.execute(task);
    }

    public static void invokeAndWait(Runnable task)
            throws InterruptedException, InvocationTargetException {
        Future f = exec.submit(task);
        try {
            f.get();
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            throw new InvocationTargetException(e);
        }
    }
}

Two details make this more than a curiosity. The event thread is a single-threaded Executor that processes tasks from the event queue — and, like a thread pool, it occasionally loses its worker thread and replaces it, which is invisible to tasks. (swingThread is volatile precisely because the factory writes it from the new thread while any thread may read it in isEventDispatchThread.)

Sequential single-threaded execution is the right execution policy when tasks are short-lived, when scheduling predictability does not matter, or when it is imperative that tasks not run concurrently. GUI event handling is all three. GuiExecutor (Listing 9.2) goes the other way and builds an Executor on top of SwingUtilities — one that runs a task inline if it is already on the event thread, and hands it to invokeLater otherwise. That inline case matters: a task that is already on the event thread must not queue itself behind the work it is currently doing.

BOOK Listing 9.2 · Executor built atop SwingUtilities 
public class GuiExecutor extends AbstractExecutorService {
    // Singletons have a private constructor and a public factory
    private static final GuiExecutor instance = new GuiExecutor();

    private GuiExecutor() { }

    public static GuiExecutor instance() { return instance; }

    public void execute(Runnable r) {
        if (SwingUtilities.isEventDispatchThread())
            r.run();
        else
            SwingUtilities.invokeLater(r);
    }

    // Plus trivial implementations of lifecycle methods
}

The same idea transfers to other toolkits: SWT offers Display.asyncExec, which is invokeLater under another name. What transfers everywhere is the shape — a single-threaded subsystem plus a hand-off primitive — not the class name.

9.2Short-running GUI Tasks

Most GUI code never has to think about threads. It is worth knowing exactly where that free ride ends.

Events originate in the event thread and bubble up to application listeners, which usually compute something that affects presentation objects. For simple, short-running tasks the entire action can stay in the event thread.

Listing 9.3 is the canonical example: a button that changes colour when pressed. The toolkit delivers an ActionEvent on the event thread to every registered listener; the listener picks a colour and sets the button's background. The event originates in the toolkit and is delivered to the application; the application modifies the GUI in response.

BOOK Listing 9.3 · Simple event listener 
final Random random = new Random();
final JButton button = new JButton("Change Color");
...
button.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        button.setBackground(new Color(random.nextInt()));
    }
});

That trivial example characterizes the majority of interactions between GUI applications and GUI toolkits. So long as tasks are short-lived and touch only GUI objects — or other thread-confined or thread-safe application objects — you can almost totally ignore threading and do everything from the event thread, and the right thing happens.

A slightly more complicated variant, shown in Figure 9.2, adds a formal data model such as a TableModel or TreeModel. Swing splits most visual components into a model (the data) and a view (the rules for displaying it). Models fire events when their data changes and views subscribe. So a listener that changes a table updates the model and calls one of the fireXxx methods; those invoke the view's table model listeners, which update the view.

⚠️

The fireXxx methods of Swing data models call the model's listeners directly rather than posting an event to the queue. That is efficient and keeps ordering obvious, but it means fireXxx may only be called from the event thread — calling it from a background thread runs the views' listeners on that background thread, breaking the single-thread rule in the least visible way possible.

9.3Long-running GUI Tasks

If every task were short, the whole application could live in the event thread and you would never think about threads. Spell checking, background compilation and remote fetches end that idyll.

Swing makes it easy to have a task run in the event thread but — prior to Java 6 — provided no mechanism for helping GUI tasks execute code in other threads. Swing doesn't need to help: you can create your own Executor for long-running tasks. A cached thread pool is a good choice here, because GUI applications rarely launch large numbers of long-running tasks, so there is little risk of the pool growing without bound. (Contrast Chapter 8: the same pool would be a poor choice for a server.)

Start with the simplest version — a task with no cancellation, no progress, and no completion update — and add the features one at a time. Listing 9.4 binds a long-running task to a button.

BOOK Listing 9.4 · Binding a long-running task to a visual component 
ExecutorService backgroundExec = Executors.newCachedThreadPool();
...
button.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        backgroundExec.execute(new Runnable() {
            public void run() { doBigComputation(); }
        });
}});

Regardless of the two layers of inner classes, this is fairly straightforward: the listener is called in the event thread and submits a Runnable to the pool. But it is "fire and forget", which is rarely what a user wants — there is usually visual feedback when a long task completes. And you cannot touch presentation objects from the background thread, so on completion the task must submit another task to run in the event thread.

Listing 9.5 does that the obvious way, and is starting to get complicated: three layers of inner classes. The listener dims the button and sets a label, then submits the background task; when that finishes it queues a third task on the event thread that re-enables the button and restores the label.

BOOK Listing 9.5 · Long-running task with user feedback 
button.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        button.setEnabled(false);
        label.setText("busy");
        backgroundExec.execute(new Runnable() {
            public void run() {
                try {
                    doBigComputation();
                } finally {
                    GuiExecutor.instance().execute(new Runnable() {
                        public void run() {
                            button.setEnabled(true);
                            label.setText("idle");
                        }
                    });
                }
            }
        });
    }
});

The task triggered by the button is really three sequential subtasks whose execution alternates between the event thread and the background thread: update the UI and start the background work; do the work; queue the UI update. This thread hopping is typical of GUI code. Note the finally — the interface must be restored even if the computation throws, or the button stays disabled forever.

9.3.1Cancellation

Any task long enough to need a background thread is long enough that the user may want to cancel it. You could implement cancellation with thread interruption directly, but Future was designed to manage cancellable tasks and is much easier to use.

Calling cancel(true) on a Future interrupts the thread executing the task if it is running. If the task is written to be responsive to interruption (Chapter 7), it can return early. Listing 9.6 polls the thread's interrupted status and bails out.

BOOK Listing 9.6 · Cancelling a long-running task 
Future<?>  runningTask = null;    // thread-confined
...
startButton.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        if (runningTask != null) {
            runningTask = backgroundExec.submit(new Runnable() {
                public void run() {
                   while (moreWork()) {
                       if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
                           cleanUpPartialWork();
                           break;
                       }
                       doSomeWork();
                   }
                }
            });
    };
}});

cancelButton.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent event) {
        if (runningTask != null)
            runningTask.cancel(true);
}});

Because runningTask is confined to the event thread, no synchronization is needed when setting or checking it, and the start listener ensures only one background task runs at a time. What is still missing is notification of completion — so that, for example, the Cancel button could be disabled again when there is nothing to cancel.

9.3.2Progress and completion indication

Future simplified cancellation; FutureTask also has a done hook that facilitates completion notification. done is called after the background Callable completes. By having done trigger a completion task in the event thread, we can build a BackgroundTask class with an onCompletion hook that always runs on the event thread (Listing 9.7).

BackgroundTask also supports progress: the compute method can call setProgress, which causes onProgress to be invoked in the event thread. To use it you implement compute, which runs in the background thread, and optionally override onCompletion and onProgress, which run in the event thread.

BOOK Listing 9.7 · Background task class supporting cancellation, completion notification, and progress notification 
abstract class BackgroundTask<V> implements Runnable, Future<V> {
    private final FutureTask<V> computation = new Computation();

    private class Computation extends FutureTask<V> {
        public Computation() {
            super(new Callable<V>() {
                public V call() throws Exception {
                    return BackgroundTask.this.compute() ;
                }
            });
        }
        protected final void done() {
            GuiExecutor.instance().execute(new Runnable() {
                public void run() {
                    V value = null;
                    Throwable thrown = null;
                    boolean cancelled = false;
                    try {
                        value = get();
                    } catch (ExecutionException e) {
                        thrown = e.getCause();
                    } catch (CancellationException e) {
                        cancelled = true;
                    } catch (InterruptedException consumed) {
                    } finally {
                        onCompletion(value, thrown, cancelled);
                    }
                };
            });
        }
    }
    protected void setProgress(final int current, final int max) {
        GuiExecutor.instance().execute(new Runnable() {
            public void run() { onProgress(current, max); }
        });
    }
    // Called in the background thread
    protected abstract V compute()  throws Exception;
    // Called in the event thread
    protected void onCompletion(V result, Throwable exception,
                                     boolean cancelled)  { }
    protected void  onProgress(int current, int max)  { }
    // Other Future methods forwarded to computation
}
🧵

The class is a decorator: it implements Future by forwarding every method to the private FutureTask, and owns exactly one extra behaviour — the hop back to the event thread in done. That is why it can be handed to backgroundExec.execute as a Runnable and cancelled as a Future with the same object.

Because BackgroundTask is a Future, cancellation gets simpler too: the compute method can call isCancelled() instead of polling the interrupted flag. Listing 9.8 recasts Listing 9.6.

BOOK Listing 9.8 · Initiating a long-running, cancellable task with BackgroundTask 
public void runInBackground(final Runnable task) {
    startButton.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {
        public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
            class CancelListener implements ActionListener {
                BackgroundTask<?> task;
                public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent event) {
                    if (task != null)
                        task.cancel(true);
                }
            }
            final CancelListener listener = new CancelListener();
            listener.task = new BackgroundTask<Void>() {
                public Void compute() {
                   while (moreWork() && !isCancelled())
                       doSomeWork();
                   return null;
                }
                public void onCompletion(boolean cancelled, String s,
                                       Throwable exception) {
                   cancelButton.removeActionListener(listener);
                   label.setText("done");
                }
            };
            cancelButton.addActionListener(listener);
            backgroundExec.execute(task);
        }
    });
}

9.3.3SwingWorker

The framework built above — FutureTask plus an Executor plus an event-thread hand-off — applies to any single-threaded GUI framework, not just Swing. In Swing, most of it ships in SwingWorker, which provides cancellation, completion notification and progress indication. Versions have been published in The Swing Connection and The Java Tutorial, and an updated version is included in Java 6. Prefer it in new code; know how it is built, because you will meet home-grown equivalents in every Swing codebase written before 2007.

9.4Shared Data Models

Everything so far assumed the data lives in the presentation objects. The moment a database, file system or remote service is behind the table, more than one thread touches the data and the single-thread rule starts to cost something.

Swing presentation objects — including data models such as TableModel and TreeModel — are confined to the event thread. In simple programs all mutable state is in the presentation objects and the only other thread is the main thread, so enforcing the rule is easy: don't touch the model from main. More complicated programs use other threads to move data to and from a persistent store so as not to compromise responsiveness.

In the simplest case the model's data is entered by the user or loaded once at startup, and no thread but the event thread ever touches it. But sometimes the presentation model is only a view onto another data source — a database, a file system, a remote service — and then several threads touch the data as it moves in and out of the application.

The example that motivates the whole section

A tree control displaying the contents of a remote file system. Enumerating the whole file system before showing the tree would take too much time and memory, so the tree is populated lazily as nodes are expanded. Enumerating even one directory on a remote volume can take a long time, so the enumeration belongs in a background task. When it completes, the data has to get into the tree model somehow: a thread-safe tree model, a invokeLater hand-off from the background task, or the event thread polling for availability.

9.4.1Thread-safe data models

As long as responsiveness is not unduly hurt by blocking, multiple threads can simply share a thread-safe data model. If the model supports fine-grained concurrency, the event thread and background threads share it without responsiveness problems — DelegatingVehicleTracker (Ch. 4, p. 65) uses a ConcurrentHashMap whose retrieval operations offer a high degree of concurrency.

The downside is that such a model does not offer a consistent snapshot of the data, which may or may not be a requirement. And a thread-safe model must still generate change events so that views update.

Sometimes thread safety, consistency and responsiveness are all achievable with a versioned data model such as CopyOnWriteArrayList. An iterator obtained from a copy-on-write collection traverses the collection as it existed when the iterator was created — a stable snapshot by construction. But copy-on-write performs well only when traversals greatly outnumber modifications, which is probably not true of, say, a vehicle-tracking application where every vehicle moves. More specialised versioned structures avoid the restriction, but building one that is both efficiently concurrent and does not retain old versions longer than needed is not easy; consider it only when other approaches are impractical.

9.4.2Split data models

From the GUI's point of view, TableModel and TreeModel are the official repository for data to be displayed. But these model objects are often themselves views of objects managed by the application. A program with both a presentation-domain and an application-domain model is said to have a split-model design (Fowler, 2005).

🖥️
Presentation model

Confined to the event thread, exactly like any other Swing model. It holds only what is on screen and needs no synchronization at all.

🗄️
Shared model

Thread-safe, touched by both the event thread and application threads. It holds the real domain state and publishes change notifications.

🔔
The wire between them

The presentation model registers listeners on the shared model; each update either carries a snapshot of the relevant state or tells the presentation model to re-read it.

The snapshot approach is simple and works well when the model is small, updates are infrequent, and the two models have a similar shape. When the data is large, updates are frequent, or one side holds information the other cannot see, it is more efficient to send incremental updates instead. That has the effect of serialising updates on the shared model and replaying them in the event thread against the presentation model — and finer-grained information about what changed improves perceived quality: if one vehicle moves, repaint the affected region, not the whole display.

🧭

Choose a split-model design when a data model must be shared by more than one thread and a thread-safe data model would be inadvisable because of blocking, consistency, or complexity. That is the decision rule the chapter gives, and it is the one to quote in a design review.

9.5Other Forms of Single-threaded Subsystems

Thread confinement is not a GUI technique. It is the general answer to "this thing is not thread-safe and never will be".

Thread confinement can be used whenever a facility is implemented as a single-threaded subsystem. Sometimes it is forced on you for reasons that have nothing to do with avoiding synchronization or deadlock: some native libraries require that all access — including System.loadLibrary — be made from the same thread.

Borrowing the approach taken by GUI frameworks, you can create a dedicated thread or single-threaded executor for accessing the library, and provide a proxy that intercepts calls to the thread-confined object and submits them as tasks to that thread. Future and newSingleThreadExecutor make this easy: the proxy submits the task and immediately calls Future.get to wait for the result. If the confined class implements an interface, dynamic proxies can automate the whole thing — every method becomes "submit a Callable, wait for the result".

The general pattern: confine, then hand off

  1. Pick the one thread that is allowed to touch the object.
  2. Give that thread a work queue — an Executor is the queue.
  3. Every caller submits a task and, if it needs an answer, waits on the returned Future.
  4. Never let the confined object's references escape to another thread; only tasks cross the boundary.

The event dispatch thread is exactly this pattern with a toolkit attached. That is why GuiExecutor could be written in nine lines — and why the same nine lines work for a native library, a document model, or any other "must be single-threaded" resource.

📖

The chapter's Summary. GUI frameworks are nearly always implemented as single-threaded subsystems in which all presentation-related code runs as tasks in an event thread. Because there is only a single event thread, long-running tasks can compromise responsiveness and so should be executed in background threads. Helper classes like SwingWorker — or the BackgroundTask class built here — which support cancellation, progress indication and completion indication, can simplify the development of long-running tasks that have both GUI and non-GUI components.

on the EDT: the click handler does the work itself, so every later click — including the one on Cancel — sits in the event queue until the computation ends. The window does not repaint, and the operating system eventually offers to kill it. fire & forget: the work moves to a background thread, the UI stays responsive, but nothing ever runs on completion, so the button stays disabled and the label stays on "busy" — the classic half-migrated Swing handler. thread hop: the completion task is handed back to the EDT, so responsiveness and correct state both hold. + cancel: a Future plus a cancellation-aware compute loop stops the work within one tick, and the same completion hook tidies up the UI.

§Patterns worth stealing

The eight listings above are the book's. These two turn them into the helpers a Swing codebase actually needs: a checked hand-off, and a cancellable task with progress that cannot forget to clean up.

1Assert the thread, don't hope for it

PATTERN On-EDT assertion, safe hand-off, and a synchronous call that refuses to deadlock 
public final class Edt {
    private Edt() { }

    /** Fail fast: a violated single-thread rule shows up at the call site. */
    public static void checkOnEdt() {
        if (!SwingUtilities.isEventDispatchThread())
            throw new IllegalStateException(
                    "must be called on the EDT, but was " +
                    Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }

    /** From any thread: run later on the EDT. Never blocks. */
    public static void later(Runnable task) {
        if (SwingUtilities.isEventDispatchThread())
            task.run();                 // already there: queueing would invert order
        else
            SwingUtilities.invokeLater(task);
    }

    /**
     * From a background thread only: run on the EDT and wait for the result.
     * Calling it ON the EDT would wait for an event that can never be
     * dispatched -- an instant, guaranteed deadlock.
     */
    public static <T> T call(Callable<T> body)
            throws Exception {
        if (SwingUtilities.isEventDispatchThread())
            throw new IllegalStateException("call() on the EDT deadlocks");
        FutureTask<T> f = new FutureTask<T>(body);
        SwingUtilities.invokeLater(f);
        try {
            return f.get();
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            Throwable cause = e.getCause();
            if (cause instanceof Exception) throw (Exception) cause;
            if (cause instanceof Error) throw (Error) cause;
            throw e;
        }
    }
}

2A background task that cannot leak its state

PATTERN Cancellable, progress-reporting task whose completion always lands on the EDT 
public abstract class GuiJob<V> implements Runnable {
    private final AtomicInteger progress = new AtomicInteger();
    private final FutureTask<V> task = new FutureTask<V>(
            new Callable<V>() {
                public V call() throws Exception { return compute(); }
            }) {
        @Override protected void done() {                 // runs on the pool thread
            Edt.later(new Runnable() {
                public void run() { finish(); }           // ... hop to the EDT
            });
        }
    };

    /** Background thread. Poll isCancelled() rather than the interrupt flag. */
    protected abstract V compute() throws Exception;

    /** EDT. Called exactly once, whatever happened -- success, failure, cancel. */
    protected abstract void onDone(V value, Throwable failure, boolean cancelled);

    protected void onProgress(int done, int total) { }

    /** Background thread; the UI update is marshalled, not performed here. */
    protected final void report(int done, int total) {
        if (progress.getAndSet(done) != done)
            Edt.later(new Runnable() {
                public void run() { onProgress(done, total); }
            });
    }

    public final boolean isCancelled() { return task.isCancelled(); }

    public final void cancel() { task.cancel(true); }      // interrupts compute()

    public final void run() { task.run(); }                // submit to backgroundExec

    private void finish() {
        V value = null;
        Throwable failure = null;
        boolean cancelled = false;
        try {
            value = task.get();
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            failure = e.getCause();
        } catch (CancellationException e) {
            cancelled = true;
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();            // must be on the EDT: never expected
            return;
        } finally {
            onDone(value, failure, cancelled);             // ordering preserved: onDone runs last
        }
    }
}
💡

The two patterns answer the two questions every Swing codebase eventually asks: "am I allowed to touch this here?" (checkOnEdt) and "did I remember to put the UI back?" (a single onDone that is called on success, failure and cancellation). Both failures are invisible in manual testing and obvious in a stack trace or a stuck button.

invokeAndWaitSchedule a task on the EDT and block for it — submit().get(). Illegal from the EDT: it would wait for itself.Ch. 9.1.2

✓Cheat sheet & self-check

SymptomLikely causeFix
Window goes grey / "not responding"A long task or a blocking call on the EDTMove it to a background executor; leave only the UI updates on the EDT
Cancel button does nothingIts listener is queued behind the task it should cancelThe task must not run on the EDT; cancel the Future, don't poll a flag
Progress bar never movesUpdates posted from the background thread, or posted too ofteninvokeLater (or setProgress) and coalesce updates
Button stays disabled after the job endsCompletion update never hopped back to the EDT — the Listing 9.4 mistakeRestore UI state in the done/onCompletion hook, in a finally
Occasional flicker, wrong rows, broken selectionA model touched from a background threadViolation of the single-thread rule: assert with checkOnEdt()
Deadlock the moment you call invokeAndWaitCalled from the EDTGuard it; use invokeLater when already on the EDT
Table shows stale data after a background reloadModel updated without firing change events, or events fired off-EDTfireXxx on the EDT after the model data is swapped
Unexplained hangs in a complex dialogTwo threads acquiring component/model locks in opposite directionsDon't lock GUI objects at all — confine them, and hop threads instead
✅
Do

Keep every EDT task short. Hand off with invokeLater (or GuiExecutor). Put cancellation, progress and completion in one helper. Confine presentation models and share only thread-safe ones. Assert the thread you think you are on.

🚫
Avoid

Blocking I/O, sleeps or Future.get on the EDT. Calling invokeAndWait from the EDT. Touching components from a background thread. Firing model events off the EDT. Doing the UI cleanup in three different places.

🧠
The one habit

For every listener, ask two questions: how long can this run? and which thread am I on when I touch the UI? A handler that answers "long" and "the EDT" is a bug report waiting for a user to file it.

Five questions the chapter leaves you with

  1. Which of my listeners can block — and what is the worst-case duration of each?
  2. When a background task ends, what exactly puts the UI back into a consistent state, on which thread?
  3. Can the user cancel the long operation, and does the code notice within a reasonable time?
  4. Is my table/tree model shared with any other thread, and if so, which of the three strategies (thread-safe, versioned, split) did I choose on purpose?
  5. If the EDT were frozen for ten seconds right now, would any of my logs tell me which handler did it?

Notes carried over from the chapter

  1. The weblog cited by the book is Graham Hamilton's, at weblogs.java.net/blog/kgh/archive/2004/10 — a Sun VP explaining why multithreaded GUI toolkits became one of computer science's recurring failed dreams.
  2. AWT originally tried to support a greater degree of multithreaded access; the decision to make Swing single-threaded was based largely on that experience.
  3. Swing predates the Executor framework, which is why SwingUtilities is not implemented with one — but the analogy is exact enough that the book uses it to explain both.
  4. invokeAndWait must never be called from the event thread: it would wait for a task that cannot be dispatched until the current one returns.
  5. Prior to Java 6, Swing offered no mechanism for helping GUI tasks execute code in other threads; the background executor in §9.3 is the workaround, and SwingWorker in Java 6 is the fix.
  6. DelegatingVehicleTracker is the thread-safe-model example from Chapter 4 (p. 65); its ConcurrentHashMap gives concurrent reads but no consistent snapshot.
  7. The split-model design is from Martin Fowler's Presentation Model material (2005), cited by the book for the presentation-domain vs. application-domain distinction.
  8. Versioned collections such as CopyOnWriteArrayList are referenced in the book via CPJ §2.2.3.3 (Lea, Concurrent Programming in Java).

Java Concurrency in Practice · Chapter 10

Chapter 10 — Avoiding Liveness Hazards

Locking buys safety and can cost liveness. A deadlocked Java program does not recover — no victim is chosen, no transaction is rolled back, nothing is logged unless you ask for a thread dump. That asymmetry is why the book devotes a chapter to designing deadlock out rather than debugging it out: one lock at a time if you can, a documented global order if you cannot, and open calls so that the places where you hold two locks are few enough to audit.

📖 pp. 127–136 🧩 3 sections · 7 listings · 1 figure ⏱️ ~20 min read 🏷️ Part III — Liveness, Performance, and Testing

Chapter in one paragraph

TL;DR — the six things worth remembering

  1. A deadlock is a cycle, and Java does not break it. The JVM has no victim-selection and no rollback: the threads involved are permanently out of commission, and the only fix is to restart the process (§10.1).
  2. Order the locks or die. A program is free of lock-ordering deadlock if every thread acquires the locks it needs in a fixed global order — and verifying that needs a global look, not a local one.
  3. Argument order is lock order. The classic transferMoney(from, to) bug happens because the lock order is decided by the caller. Induce an order with System.identityHashCode (or a unique key), plus a tie-breaking lock for hash collisions.
  4. Deadlock hides behind method calls. Two cooperating objects can each take one lock and still form a cycle; the warning sign is an alien method called with a lock held.
  5. Open calls are the design fix. Call out to other objects with no locks held. Shrinking the synchronized block may cost atomicity — decide deliberately whether that matters.
  6. Liveness has other failure modes. Resource deadlock, thread-starvation deadlock, starvation from thread priorities, poor responsiveness from long lock holds, and livelock — where threads run but nothing progresses.

10.1Deadlock

Five philosophers, five chopsticks, and the oldest bug in concurrent programming.

Dining philosophers: five people at a round table, one chopstick between each pair, and each diner needs two chopsticks to eat. Some chopstick protocols let everyone eat eventually — grab both adjacent sticks, or put down the one you hold and retry after a pause. Some do not: each philosopher grabs the stick on his left and then waits for the one on his right, without ever releasing the left. That second protocol is deadlock: each holds a resource another needs and waits for one another holds.

The definition, and the graph

When thread A holds lock L and tries to acquire M, while thread B holds M and tries to acquire L, both wait forever. This is the simplest case of deadlock (or deadly embrace): multiple threads waiting forever because of a cyclic locking dependency.

Draw the threads as nodes of a directed graph, with an edge "A is waiting for a resource held by B". If that graph contains a cycle, you have a deadlock. Every technique in this chapter is really a way of keeping that graph acyclic — and every diagnostic tool is a way of finding the cycle after the fact.

Databases attack this head-on: a transaction may hold many locks until commit, so deadlocks are ordinary there. The server searches the is-waiting-for graph for cycles, picks a victim, and aborts that transaction — releasing its locks, letting the others proceed, and letting the application retry the victim.

The JVM is not nearly as helpful. When Java threads deadlock, that is the end of the game: those threads are permanently out of commission. Depending on what they were doing, the application may stall completely, a subsystem may stall, or throughput may merely sag. The only cure is to abort and restart — and hope it does not happen again.

⏳

Deadlocks rarely manifest immediately. A class having a potential deadlock does not mean it ever will, only that it can — and when it does, it is usually at the worst moment: under heavy production load, when the timing window is finally hit.

10.1.1Lock-ordering deadlocks

Listing 10.1 is the canonical case. leftRight takes left then right; rightLeft takes them the other way round. Two threads, one calling each, and the unlucky interleaving of Figure 10.1 completes a cycle.

DON'T Listing 10.1 · Simple lock-ordering deadlock 
// Warning: deadlock-prone!
public class LeftRightDeadlock {
    private final Object left = new Object();
    private final Object right = new Object();

    public void leftRight() {
        synchronized (left) {
            synchronized (right) {
                doSomething();
            }
        }
    }

    public void rightLeft() {
        synchronized (right) {
            synchronized (left) {
                doSomethingElse();
            }
        }
    }
}

The fix is ordering, and the important word is global: a program is free of lock-ordering deadlocks if all threads acquire the locks they need in a fixed global order. It is not sufficient to inspect each path that acquires multiple locks — leftRight and rightLeft are both "reasonable" ways to acquire those two locks, they are simply not compatible. When it comes to locking, the left hand needs to know what the right hand is doing.

10.1.2Dynamic lock-order deadlocks

Listing 10.2 looks harmless: it locks both accounts before transferring, so balances stay atomic and the "no negative balance" invariant holds. How can it deadlock? Because the lock order depends on the argument order, and the arguments come from outside:

DON'T Listing 10.2 · Dynamic lock-ordering deadlock 
// Warning: deadlock-prone!
public void transferMoney(Account fromAccount,
                          Account toAccount,
                          DollarAmount amount)
        throws InsufficientFundsException {
    synchronized (fromAccount) {
        synchronized (toAccount) {
            if (fromAccount.getBalance().compareTo(amount) < 0)
                throw new InsufficientFundsException();
            else {
                fromAccount.debit(amount);
                toAccount.credit(amount);
            }
        }
    }
}
CALLERS Two callers, opposite directions — the lock order is the argument order 
A: transferMoney(myAccount, yourAccount, 10);
B: transferMoney(yourAccount, myAccount, 20);

With unlucky timing, A holds myAccount and waits for yourAccount while B holds yourAccount and waits for myAccount. The deadlock is still visible as nested lock acquisitions; the difference is that you cannot fix it locally, because you do not control the call order. You must induce an ordering on the locks and use it everywhere.

One way is System.identityHashCode, which returns the value Object.hashCode would return (and, unlike a class's own hashCode, cannot be overridden to something unstable). Listing 10.3 orders the two accounts by that value. If the hashes are equal — vanishingly rare — a third tie-breaking lock ensures only one thread at a time takes the two locks in an arbitrary order.

FIX Listing 10.3 · Inducing a lock ordering to avoid deadlock 
private static final Object tieLock = new Object();

public void transferMoney(final Account fromAcct,
                          final Account toAcct,
                          final DollarAmount amount)
        throws InsufficientFundsException {
    class Helper {
        public void transfer() throws InsufficientFundsException {
            if (fromAcct.getBalance().compareTo(amount) < 0)
                throw new InsufficientFundsException();
            else {
                fromAcct.debit(amount);
                toAcct.credit(amount);
            }
        }
    }
    int fromHash = System.identityHashCode(fromAcct);
    int toHash = System.identityHashCode(toAcct);

    if (fromHash < toHash) {
        synchronized (fromAcct) {
            synchronized (toAcct) {
                new Helper().transfer();
            }
        }
    } else if (fromHash > toHash) {
        synchronized (toAcct) {
            synchronized (fromAcct) {
                new Helper().transfer();
            }
        }
    } else {
        synchronized (tieLock) {
            synchronized (fromAcct) {
                synchronized (toAcct) {
                   new Helper().transfer();
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

If Account has a unique, immutable, comparable key — an account number — the ordering is easier still: order the objects by their key, and the tie-breaking lock disappears. If collisions were common the tie lock would become a bottleneck (as a single program-wide lock would), but identity hash collisions are rare enough that this buys the last bit of safety cheaply.

🎯

"Locks are held only briefly, so the risk is small" is the wrong intuition. A production application may perform billions of lock acquire-release cycles per day; only one needs to be timed just wrong. And holding locks briefly — exactly what you are told to do for throughput — makes latent deadlocks less likely to show up in testing. DemonstrateDeadlock (Listing 10.4) is included precisely because it deadlocks quickly on most machines, so you can see what one looks like.

BOOK Listing 10.4 · Driver loop that induces deadlock under typical conditions 
public class DemonstrateDeadlock {
    private static final int NUM_THREADS = 20;
    private static final int NUM_ACCOUNTS = 5;
    private static final int NUM_ITERATIONS = 1000000;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        final Random rnd = new Random();
        final Account[] accounts = new Account[NUM_ACCOUNTS];

        for (int i = 0; i < accounts.length; i++)
            accounts[i] = new Account();

        class TransferThread extends Thread {
            public void run() {
                for (int i=0; i<NUM_ITERATIONS; i++) {
                    int fromAcct = rnd.nextInt(NUM_ACCOUNTS);
                    int toAcct = rnd.nextInt(NUM_ACCOUNTS);
                    DollarAmount amount =
                        new DollarAmount(rnd.nextInt(1000));
                    transferMoney(accounts[fromAcct],
                                  accounts[toAcct], amount);
                }
            }
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++)
            new TransferThread().start();
    }
}

10.1.3Deadlocks between cooperating objects

Multiple lock acquisition is not always as visible as in LeftRightDeadlock or transferMoney: the two locks need not be acquired by the same method. Listing 10.5 is a taxicab dispatcher — Taxi holds a location and a destination, Dispatcher holds the fleet — and no single method takes two locks.

Yet a thread calling setLocation acquires the Taxi lock and then, inside it, calls dispatcher.notifyAvailable, which needs the Dispatcher lock: Taxi → Dispatcher. A thread calling Dispatcher.getImage acquires the Dispatcher lock and then, for each taxi, calls t.getLocation(), which needs that Taxi's lock: Dispatcher → Taxi. Two locks, two threads, opposite orders — the same cycle as before, just spread across two classes.

DON'T Listing 10.5 · Lock-ordering deadlock between cooperating objects 
// Warning: deadlock-prone!
class Taxi {
    @GuardedBy("this") private Point location, destination;
    private final Dispatcher dispatcher;

    public Taxi(Dispatcher dispatcher) {
        this.dispatcher = dispatcher;
    }

    public synchronized Point getLocation() {
        return location;
    }

    public synchronized void setLocation(Point location) {
        this.location = location;
        if (location.equals(destination))
            dispatcher.notifyAvailable(this);
    }
}

class Dispatcher {
    @GuardedBy("this") private final Set<Taxi> taxis;
    @GuardedBy("this") private final Set<Taxi> availableTaxis;

    public Dispatcher() {
        taxis = new HashSet<Taxi>();
        availableTaxis = new HashSet<Taxi>();
    }

    public synchronized void notifyAvailable(Taxi taxi) {
        availableTaxis.add(taxi);
    }

    public synchronized Image getImage() {
        Image image = new Image();
        for (Taxi t : taxis)
            image.drawMarker(t.getLocation());
        return image;
    }
}

The warning sign is subtler than "this method takes two locks": it is an alien method (Ch. 4, p. 40) being called while a lock is held. Here Taxi.setLocation calls into another object — Dispatcher — with its own lock held, and Dispatcher.getImage calls back into a Taxi with its lock held. Invoking an alien method with a lock held is asking for liveness trouble: the alien method may take other locks (risking deadlock) or block for a long time (stalling everyone who needs the lock you hold).

10.1.4Open calls

Taxi and Dispatcher had no idea they were two halves of a deadlock, and they should not have to: a method call is an abstraction barrier meant to hide what happens on the other side. But precisely because you cannot see the other side, calling an alien method with a lock held is hard to analyze.

A call made with no locks held is an open call. Classes that rely on open calls are better behaved and more composable than classes that call out with locks held — the same relationship that encapsulation has with thread safety. The liveness analysis of a program that uses only open calls is far easier, because the places where multiple locks are held are few and visible.

FIX Listing 10.6 · Using open calls to avoid deadlock between cooperating objects 
@ThreadSafe
class Taxi {
    @GuardedBy("this") private Point location, destination;
    private final Dispatcher dispatcher;
    ...
    public synchronized Point getLocation() {
        return location;
    }

    public synchronized void setLocation(Point location) {
        boolean reachedDestination;
        synchronized  (this) {
            this.location = location;
            reachedDestination = location.equals(destination);
        }
        if (reachedDestination)
            dispatcher.notifyAvailable(this);
    }
}

@ThreadSafe
class Dispatcher {
    @GuardedBy("this") private final Set<Taxi> taxis;
    @GuardedBy("this") private final Set<Taxi> availableTaxis;
    ...
    public synchronized void notifyAvailable(Taxi taxi) {
        availableTaxis.add(taxi);
    }

    public Image getImage() {
        Set<Taxi> copy;
        synchronized  (this) {
            copy = new HashSet<Taxi>(taxis);
        }
        Image image = new Image();
        for (Taxi t : copy)
            image.drawMarker(t.getLocation());
        return image;
    }
}

The refactoring is mechanical: shrink the synchronized blocks so they guard only operations on shared state, compute the decision inside the lock, and make the call after leaving it. Very often the cause of trouble like Listing 10.5 is simply that synchronized was put on whole methods for compactness, not because the whole method needed guarding. (Bonus: smaller synchronized blocks usually improve scalability — see §11.4.1.)

⚖️

Open calls have a price: an operation that was atomic becomes non-atomic. Often that is fine — updating a taxi's location and telling the dispatcher needn't be one atomic step. Sometimes it is visible but acceptable — the deadlock-prone getImage produced a perfect snapshot of the fleet, the fixed one samples each taxi at a slightly different instant. Occasionally it is unacceptable, and then you need a different technique: use the lock to flip state so that other threads choose not to try. Shutting a service down is the canonical example — set the state to "shutting down" under the lock, release it, then wait for in-flight work, knowing no new work can start. That replaces "keep other threads out of a critical section" with "construct a protocol so they don't want in".

10.1.5Resource deadlocks

Threads can deadlock waiting for resources just as they can waiting for locks. Two connection pools, one task needing a connection to each, and no global order on acquiring them: thread A holds D1 and waits for D2 while thread B holds D2 and waits for D1. Resource pools are usually semaphores (§5.5.3), so the waiting is ordinary blocking. (Bigger pools make it rarer — with N connections per pool, deadlock needs N sets of cyclically waiting threads and a lot of bad luck — not impossible.)

The other resource deadlock is the one from Chapter 8: thread starvation deadlock. A task in a single-threaded executor that submits a task and waits for its result waits forever, stalling the executor and every task behind it. Tasks that wait for the results of other tasks are the primary source of this hazard, which is why bounded pools and interdependent tasks do not mix.

10.2Avoiding and Diagnosing Deadlocks

Prevention is a design property; diagnosis is a two-part audit plus a thread dump.

A program that never acquires more than one lock at a time cannot experience lock-ordering deadlock. That is not always practical, but if you can get away with it, it is a lot less work. If you must acquire multiple locks, lock ordering has to be part of the design: minimise the number of possible locking interactions, and follow and document a lock-ordering protocol for locks that may be acquired together.

The two-part audit for fine-grained locking

  1. Identify where multiple locks can be acquired. Try to make that a small set; a code review, or automated bytecode/source analysis, can find them if the program uses only open calls.
  2. Analyse those places globally. Confirm that lock ordering is consistent across the entire program — not just within each class.

10.2.1Timed lock attempts

A different tactic is to detect and recover rather than prevent: use the timed tryLock of the explicit Lock classes (Chapter 13) instead of intrinsic locking. Where synchronized waits forever, an explicit lock lets you specify a timeout after which tryLock reports failure. Choose a timeout far longer than you expect acquisition to take, and you regain control when something unexpected happens.

A failed timed attempt is not a diagnosis — maybe it was a deadlock, maybe a thread is in an infinite loop holding the lock, maybe something is just slow. But at least you can log what you were trying to do and fail one operation gracefully instead of killing the process. Used for pairs of locks, timed acquisition works even if the rest of the program uses plain synchronized: on timeout you release what you hold, back off, and retry. (It does not work when locks are nested through method calls, since you cannot release an outer lock you do not own the shape of.)

10.2.2Deadlock analysis with thread dumps

Prevention is your problem, but the JVM will help you identify a deadlock after the fact. A thread dump contains a stack trace for every running thread plus locking information: which locks each thread holds, in which stack frame it acquired them, and which lock a blocked thread is waiting for. Before emitting the dump the JVM searches the is-waiting-for graph for cycles and, if it finds one, prints the deadlock explicitly.

Trigger one with SIGQUIT (kill -3) on Unix, Ctrl+\ on Unix or Ctrl+Break on Windows, or from most IDEs. Periodic dumps are worth taking even when nothing is wrong — they show you how your program actually locks.

🧷

Explicit locks are harder to diagnose. Java 5.0 cannot associate Lock information with a thread dump at all — explicit locks simply do not appear. Java 6 adds thread-dump support and deadlock detection for them, but the information is less precise: an intrinsic lock is associated with the stack frame that acquired it, whereas an explicit Lock is associated only with the thread holding it.

Listing 10.7 is a real dump from a production J2EE application. The deadlock involved three components — the application, the container, and a JDBC driver — each from a different vendor, all extensively tested. Each had a bug that was harmless alone; together they were fatal.

BOOK Listing 10.7 · Portion of thread dump after deadlock 
Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"ApplicationServerThread":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x080f0cdc (a MumbleDBConnection),
  which is held by "ApplicationServerThread"
"ApplicationServerThread":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x080f0ed4 (a MumbleDBCallableStatement),
  which is held by "ApplicationServerThread"

Java stack information for the threads listed above:
"ApplicationServerThread":
        at MumbleDBConnection.remove_statement
        - waiting to lock <0x650f7f30> (a MumbleDBConnection)
        at MumbleDBStatement.close
        - locked <0x6024ffb0> (a MumbleDBCallableStatement)
     ...

"ApplicationServerThread":
        at MumbleDBCallableStatement.sendBatch
        - waiting to lock <0x6024ffb0> (a MumbleDBCallableStatement)
        at MumbleDBConnection.commit
        - locked <0x650f7f30> (a MumbleDBConnection)
     ...

Read it as a cycle: one thread holds the MumbleDBConnection and wants the MumbleDBCallableStatement; the other holds the statement and wants the connection. The driver has a lock-ordering bug — different call chains acquire several JDBC objects in different orders. But that bug was latent until a second bug exposed it: multiple threads were using the same JDBC Connection concurrently, which the application was never supposed to do. Nothing in the JDBC specification requires a Connection to be thread-safe; confining it to one thread, as intended here, is the normal design. The vendor had tried to deliver a thread-safe driver and synchronized on several objects without ordering them. Neither bug was fatal on its own, so both survived extensive testing.

10.3Other Liveness Hazards

Deadlock is the famous one. Starvation, poor responsiveness and livelock are the ones that get filed as "the app is slow" and never diagnosed.

HazardWhat is happeningThe tellThe fix
DeadlockA cycle of threads each waiting for a lock or resource another holdsThread dump; nothing progresses at allLock ordering, open calls, one lock at a time, timed tryLock
StarvationA thread is perpetually denied the resource (usually CPU) it needsOne thread's throughput collapses while others run fineDrop the priority tweaking; avoid unbounded work under a lock
Poor responsivenessLocks or CPU held long enough that interactive work waitsUI stutters while background jobs runSmaller synchronized blocks; lower priority for true background work
LivelockThreads are running, not blocked, and still never progressCPU is busy, throughput is zero, retries in the logsRandomised back-off; treat unrecoverable errors as unrecoverable

10.3.1Starvation

Starvation is a thread perpetually denied access to the resources it needs to make progress; the resource is usually CPU cycles. In Java it can come from inappropriate use of thread priorities, or from executing non-terminating constructs — infinite loops, waits that never end — while holding a lock, so that everyone who needs that lock is starved too.

Priorities are only scheduling hints. The Thread API defines ten levels that the JVM maps to OS priorities as it sees fit, and the mapping is platform-specific: two Java priorities may collapse to one OS priority on a system with fewer levels. Operating systems already go to great lengths for fairness beyond what the language requires, and most applications run every thread at NORM_PRIORITY anyway. Boosting a thread may do nothing at all, or may reliably starve another.

🚩

You can often spot a program that has been fighting priority problems by the Thread.sleep and Thread.yield calls in odd places — someone trying to give lower-priority threads a turn. It does not work: the semantics of Thread.yield and Thread.sleep(0) are undefined [JLS 17.9]; a JVM may implement them as no-ops or as hints, and is not required to reproduce Unix sleep(0) behaviour (put the current thread at the end of its priority's run queue).

10.3.2Poor responsiveness

One step removed from starvation. Chapter 9 built a framework for pushing long tasks onto background threads so the UI stays responsive — but a CPU-intensive background task still competes for cycles with the event thread, so the UI can still stutter. This is one of the few places where priorities do make sense: if the work really is background work, lowering its priority makes foreground tasks more responsive.

Poor responsiveness also comes from poor lock management: a thread that holds a lock while iterating a large collection and doing substantial work per element makes everyone who needs that collection wait.

10.3.3Livelock

Livelock is a liveness failure in which a thread is not blocked but still cannot make progress, because it keeps retrying an operation that always fails. The canonical form is the poison message in transactional messaging: a message that the handler cannot process is rolled back and returned to the head of the queue, then dequeued and handed to the same broken handler, forever. The thread is busy the whole time. This variety usually comes from over-eager error recovery that treats an unrecoverable error as a recoverable one.

The other form is cooperative: threads keep changing state in response to each other so that nobody can proceed — two people stepping aside for each other in a corridor, repeatedly. The fix is to introduce randomness into the retry. Two Ethernet stations that retry a collision after exactly one second collide forever; retry after a random delay (with exponential back-off for repeated collisions) and the problem disappears. Randomised waits and back-off are just as effective in concurrent applications.

📖

The chapter's Summary. Liveness failures are serious because there is no recovery short of aborting the application. The most common form is lock-ordering deadlock, and avoiding it starts at design time: ensure that when threads acquire multiple locks they do so in a consistent order. The best way to do that is to use open calls throughout the program, which greatly reduces the number of places where multiple locks are held at once and makes it more obvious where those places are.
