Press “Step”. Both threads try to take the first lock in their plan.
🔍

from→to: the plan is [fromAccount, toAccount], so A takes X then wants Y while B takes Y then wants X — a cycle, and both wait forever. This is Listing 10.2. ordered: both plans are sorted by identity hash, so both threads want the same lock first; one gets it, the other waits, and there is no cycle. tie lock: a forced hash collision makes both threads take the tie-breaking lock first, which serialises them completely — safe, but the two transfers no longer overlap. back off: the pair is acquired with timed tryLock, and on failure the thread releases what it holds and retries after a random delay, so the cycle is broken by randomness rather than by ordering.

§Patterns worth stealing

The seven listings above are the book's. These two turn deadlock avoidance into something you can put in a shared utility class: a lock-order comparator, and a tryLock-with-backoff pair.

1Order any two objects, deterministically

PATTERN Lock ordering by identity hash, a stable key, or a tie-breaking lock 
public final class LockOrder {
    private final Object tieLock = new Object();

    /** Stable order for any two objects: consistent for every caller, forever. */
    public static int compare(Object a, Object b) {
        if (a == b) return 0;
        int ha = System.identityHashCode(a);
        int hb = System.identityHashCode(b);
        if (ha < hb) return -1;
        if (ha > hb) return 1;
        // Hashes collide: fall back to a deterministic total order on the
        // objects themselves, or serialise through a tie lock below.
        return Integer.compare(System.identityHashCode(a.toString()),
                               System.identityHashCode(b.toString()));
    }

    /**
     * Run body with both objects locked, in a global order.
     * Deadlock-free however the two accounts are passed in.
     */
    public void withBoth(final Object a, final Object b, Runnable body) {
        int c = compare(a, b);
        if (c == 0) {                      // a == b: reentrant, lock once
            synchronized (a) { body.run(); }
            return;
        }
        if (System.identityHashCode(a) != System.identityHashCode(b)) {
            Object first = c < 0 ? a : b;
            Object second = c < 0 ? b : a;
            synchronized (first) {
                synchronized (second) { body.run(); }
            }
        } else {                           // true hash collision: serialise
            synchronized (tieLock) {       // rare, and only around the pair
                synchronized (a) {
                    synchronized (b) { body.run(); }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

2Acquire both or take neither

PATTERN Timed tryLock with random back-off: probabilistic deadlock avoidance 
/**
 * Avoids deadlock without a global order: never hold one lock while
 * blocking indefinitely for the other. Use when you cannot impose an
 * order (third-party callbacks, user-supplied comparators) and when a
 * retry is cheap.
 */
public final class LockPair {
    private static final Random RND = new Random();
    private static final long TIMEOUT_MS = 50;      // far above the real hold time
    private static final int MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5;

    public static void withBoth(Lock a, Lock b, Runnable body) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
            if (attempt > MAX_ATTEMPTS)
                throw new IllegalStateException("could not acquire both locks");
            boolean haveA = false, haveB = false;
            try {
                haveA = a.tryLock(TIMEOUT_MS, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
                if (!haveA) continue;
                haveB = b.tryLock(TIMEOUT_MS, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
                if (!haveB) continue;               // finally releases a
                body.run();
                return;
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // restore, then give up
                throw e;
            } finally {
                if (haveB) b.unlock();
                if (haveA) a.unlock();
            }
            // unreachable: the loop always continues or returns
        }
    }

    /** Randomised back-off, so two threads do not collide the same way twice. */
    private static void pause(int attempt) throws InterruptedException {
        long base = 1L << Math.min(attempt, 6);        // 2, 4, 8 ... 64 ms
        Thread.sleep(base + RND.nextInt(50));
    }
}
💡

Prefer the first pattern; keep the second as a fallback. Ordering is a design fix — provable, cheap and analysable. Back-off is a recovery fix: it costs retries, it cannot bound the worst case, and it needs the caller to accept that an operation may fail. The one thing you must never do is neither: acquire two locks in caller-controlled order and hope.

§Vocabulary introduced in Chapter 10

TermMeaning as used hereWhere it goes
LivenessThe property that something good eventually happens: threads keep making progress. Its failure modes all look like "it stopped".Ch. 10 intro
DeadlockMultiple threads waiting forever because of a cyclic dependency — on locks, on resources, or on other tasks.Ch. 10.1
Deadly embraceThe two-thread, two-lock case: A holds L and wants M, B holds M and wants L.Ch. 10.1
Is-waiting-for graphThreads as nodes, "A waits for something B holds" as edges. A cycle in this graph is the deadlock — the graph databases search and thread dumps print.Ch. 10.1
Lock-ordering deadlockDeadlock caused by two code paths acquiring the same locks in different orders.Ch. 10.1.1
Global lock orderA single, documented order in which every thread acquires any two locks it needs. The design-time cure.Ch. 10.1.1
Dynamic lock orderLock order determined at run time by arguments or data — the transferMoney(from, to) bug.Ch. 10.1.2
Tie-breaking lockA third lock taken before an arbitrarily ordered pair, used only when their identity hashes collide.Ch. 10.1.2
Alien methodA method belonging to another object (Ch. 4, p. 40). Calling one while holding a lock is the warning sign for hidden lock orders.Ch. 10.1.3
Open callA method call made with no locks held. Programs built from open calls are analysable; programs that call out under locks are not.Ch. 10.1.4
Resource deadlockA cycle over pooled resources rather than locks — two connection pools taken in different orders, for example.Ch. 10.1.5
Thread-starvation deadlockA pool task that waits for a task that can never get a thread; the executor version of the same cycle (Ch. 8.1.1).Ch. 10.1.5
Timed lock attempttryLock(timeout): give up instead of waiting forever, then release, back off, retry or report.Ch. 10.2.1
Thread dumpEvery thread's stack plus its held and awaited locks; the JVM also reports deadlock cycles it finds.Ch. 10.2.2
StarvationA thread perpetually denied the resource it needs — usually CPU, usually because of thread priorities.Ch. 10.3.1
LivelockThreads that are running, not blocked, and still never make progress — the poison message, the corridor shuffle.Ch. 10.3.3
Poison messageA message that always fails, is rolled back, and returns to the head of the queue to fail again.Ch. 10.3.3

✓Cheat sheet & self-check

SymptomLikely causeFix
Server stops serving; threads all BLOCKEDLock-ordering deadlockThread dump to confirm the cycle, then impose and document a global lock order
Deadlock only under load, never in testsA narrow interleaving; brief lock holds make it rarer to reproduceStatic audit for nested lock acquisition; DemonstrateDeadlock-style stress runs
Deadlock in a transfer/banking style APILock order taken from argument orderSort the pair by identity hash or a unique key; tie-breaking lock for collisions
Two classes deadlock, neither takes two locksAlien method invoked under a lock (callbacks, listeners, toString)Make it an open call: compute under the lock, notify outside it
Pool hangs with dependent tasksThread-starvation deadlockUnbounded pool, caller-runs, or restructure so tasks do not wait on tasks
Two pools exhausted at onceResource deadlock over pooled connectionsAcquire resources in a fixed order, or use one pool / one resource per task
One thread never gets CPUThread priorities, or unbounded work under a lockStop tuning priorities; bound the work done while holding locks

✅
Do

Keep the number of locks held at once at one, if you can. If not, order them globally and write the order down. Prefer open calls. Audit nested acquisition globally. Take a thread dump before you guess.

🚫
Avoid

Locking in the order arguments arrive. Calling alien methods under a lock. Public synchronized methods that call out. Tuning thread priorities. Sleeping or yielding to "fix" scheduling. Retrying a forever-failing operation unchanged.

🧠
The one habit

Whenever you write a second synchronized block inside a first, ask: what order does every other thread in this program take these two locks in? If the answer is not immediate, the code is not yet finished.

Five questions the chapter leaves you with

  1. Does any code path in this program hold two locks at once — and can I name the order it uses?
  2. Which of my synchronized methods call into another object while holding the lock?
  3. If this process deadlocked tonight, would anyone be able to produce a thread dump, and would they recognise the cycle?
  4. Do any of my tasks wait for other tasks in a bounded pool or a bounded resource pool?
  5. Which of my retry loops could run forever without making progress, and what randomisation or poison-message handling stops them?

Notes carried over from the chapter

  1. Ironically, holding locks for short periods — what you are supposed to do to reduce contention — increases the likelihood that testing will not disclose a latent deadlock.
  2. DemonstrateDeadlock ignores the question of negative account balances, for simplicity.
  3. The need to rely on open calls and careful lock ordering reflects the fundamental messiness of composing synchronized objects rather than synchronizing composed objects.
  4. Thread-dump locking information is useful even without a deadlock: periodically triggering dumps lets you observe your program's locking behaviour.
  5. The semantics of Thread.yield and Thread.sleep(0) are undefined [JLS 17.9]; a JVM may implement them as no-ops or as hints, and is not required to reproduce Unix sleep(0) semantics (placing the current thread at the end of the run queue for its priority), though some JVMs do.
  6. Missed signals, the remaining liveness hazard mentioned in §10.3, are covered in §14.2.3 of the book.
  7. transferMoney can also be written with polled tryLock and retries for probabilistic deadlock avoidance — the book's Listing 13.3, p. 280.

Java Concurrency in Practice · Chapter 11

Chapter 11 — Performance and Scalability

Threads are supposed to make programs faster, and badly used they make them slower — and less scalable than the sequential version. The organising idea is serialization: any part of the work that cannot be done in parallel caps the benefit of every extra processor. Amdahl's law turns that into arithmetic, and the rest of the chapter is a checklist for finding the serial parts — chiefly the exclusive lock — and shrinking them.

📖 pp. 137–152 🧩 6 sections · 8 listings · 3 figures ⏱️ ~26 min read 🏷️ Part III — Liveness, Performance, and Testing

Chapter in one paragraph

TL;DR — the six things worth remembering

  1. Performance and scalability are different questions. "How fast" is service time and latency; "how much" is throughput and capacity. Most optimizations help one and hurt the other — and many single-threaded tricks are actively bad for scalability.
  2. Safety first. First make it right, then make it fast — and only if measurements and requirements say it needs to be faster. The quest for performance is the single greatest source of concurrency bugs.
  3. Amdahl's law is the ceiling. Speedup ≤ 1/(F + (1−F)/N), so with 10% serialization you can never exceed 10×, and at 100 processors you top out at 9.2×.
  4. Find the serialization. Shared queues, shared result structures, and shared log files serialize work that looks parallel. Even the dequeue step counts as part of task processing time.
  5. Contention is frequency × duration. Three levers: hold locks less time (narrow the scope), request them less often (split and stripe), or stop using exclusive locks (concurrent collections, read–write locks, atomics, immutability).
  6. Context switches are the other tax. 5,000–10,000 cycles each; contended locks cause them. Move blocking I/O out of request threads and the whole system gets cheaper.

11.1Thinking about Performance

Improving performance means doing more work with fewer resources — and knowing which resource is actually scarce.

Some resource is usually in shortest supply: CPU cycles, memory, network bandwidth, I/O bandwidth, database requests, disk space. When an activity is limited by a particular resource it is bound by it — CPU-bound, database-bound, and so on. Threads never remove that bound; they can only help you use the bound resource more fully.

Using multiple threads always adds cost over the single-threaded approach: coordination (locking, signalling, memory synchronization), more context switches, thread creation and teardown, scheduling overhead. When threading is used effectively these are more than repaid by throughput, responsiveness or capacity. When it is not, a concurrent application can perform worse than the sequential one.

🪣

The book's cautionary anecdote: a colleague tested an expensive application with a tunable thread pool and found the optimal pool size was 1. Obvious in hindsight — a single-CPU machine and an almost entirely CPU-bound workload. If your program cannot keep the processors you already have busy, adding more processors will not help.

11.1.1Performance versus scalability

Performance can be measured many ways: service time, latency, throughput, efficiency, scalability, capacity. Some are measures of how fast a unit of work is processed (service time, latency); others of how much work can be done with given resources (throughput, capacity). Scalability is the ability to improve throughput or capacity when resources are added.

Tuning for performanceTuning for scalability
QuestionHow fast is one unit of work?How much more work with more resources?
Typical movesCache results, replace an O(n²) algorithm with O(n log n), avoid redundant workParallelize, partition, remove serialization
Who cares mostInteractive applications (latency)Server applications (throughput, capacity)
Can hurt the otherYes — many single-threaded tricks are bad for scalabilityYes — pipelining adds per-task work to gain parallelism

The classic illustration is the three-tier application: a monolith that fuses presentation, business logic and persistence will beat a well-factored multi-tier implementation on the first unit of work — no network hops, no queuing, no data copying at layer boundaries. But when the monolith reaches capacity, adding capacity may be prohibitively difficult. So we accept longer service times per unit of work in exchange for the ability to scale out.

11.1.2Evaluating performance tradeoffs

Nearly every engineering decision is a tradeoff. Thicker steel makes a bridge stronger and more expensive. Software tradeoffs are harder because we usually have less information: quicksort beats bubble sort on large data sets and loses on small ones, so "implement an efficient sort" is not a specification — and that is precisely why most optimizations are premature.

Optimizations also cost things that never appear in a benchmark: readability, maintainability, encapsulation, and the risk of error (faster algorithms are usually more complicated). If you cannot name the costs and risks, you have not thought it through enough to proceed. Before declaring one approach faster than another, ask:

  • What do you mean by "faster"?
  • Under what conditions will this be faster — light or heavy load, large or small data sets? Can you support that with measurements?
  • How often do those conditions arise in your situation? Measurements again?
  • Will this code be used in other situations where the conditions differ?
  • What hidden costs — development risk, maintenance risk — are you trading for the improvement?

Why a concurrency book is conservative about optimization

The quest for performance is probably the single greatest source of concurrency bugs. The belief that synchronization was "too slow" produced clever-looking but dangerous idioms (double-checked locking, §16.2.4) and is routinely cited as an excuse for skipping the rules. Concurrency bugs are among the hardest to track down, so anything that risks introducing one has to be undertaken very carefully — and when you trade safety for performance you may end up with neither. Two rules follow: measure, don't guess, and have concrete performance requirements so you know both when to start tuning and when to stop.

11.2Amdahl's Law

Some work parallelizes; some is farming's "wait for the crops to grow". Amdahl's law tells you which one you are stuck with.

If F is the fraction of the calculation that must be executed serially, then on a machine with N processors the speedup is at most:

Speedup ≤ 1 / (F + (1 − F) / N)

As N → ∞ the speedup converges to 1/F, no matter how many processors you buy.

Serial fraction FCeiling (1/F)Speedup at N = 10Speedup at N = 100Utilization at N = 100
0%unbounded10×100×100%
1%100×9.2×50×50%
5%20×7.5×17×17%
10%10×5.3×9.2×9%
30%3.3×2.7×3.2×3%

A program with fifty percent serial work can be sped up only by a factor of two, however many processors are available; ten percent serial caps you at ten. It also quantifies the efficiency cost: with ten processors, a program with 10% serialization achieves at most 5.3× (53% utilization), and with a hundred processors at most 9.2× (9% utilization). It takes a lot of idle CPUs to never reach that factor of ten.

Chapter 6 covered finding logical task boundaries. To predict the speedup of running on a multiprocessor you also need to find the sources of serialization inside those tasks.

BOOK Listing 11.1 · Serialized access to a task queue 
public class WorkerThread extends Thread {
    private final BlockingQueue<Runnable> queue;

    public WorkerThread(BlockingQueue<Runnable> queue) {
        this.queue = queue;
    }

    public void run() {
        while (true) {
            try {
                Runnable task = queue.take();
                task.run();
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                break;  /*  Allow thread to exit  */
            }
        }
    }
}

N threads pulling tasks from a shared work queue looks completely parallelizable — the tasks do not wait for each other. But fetching the task is part of processing it. The queue is shared and needs synchronization to stay consistent, so while one thread dequeues, others that need their next task must wait. That wait is the serial component. A LinkedBlockingQueue blocks less than a synchronized LinkedList because its algorithm is more scalable, but any shared data structure fundamentally introduces serialization.

The same applies to result handling. Every useful computation produces a result or side effect — otherwise it is dead code. Runnables have no return value, so results go somewhere shared: a log file, a result container, a counter. Each of those is a serialization point. Give each thread its own result structure and the final merge is a serialization point instead. All concurrent applications have some sources of serialization; if you think yours has none, look again.

11.2.1Serialization hidden in frameworks

Figure 11.2 compares two implementations of the same shared-queue workload — a LinkedList wrapped in synchronizedList, and a ConcurrentLinkedQueue — on an 8-way Sparc V880 running Solaris.

Each run does the same amount of "work", so the gap is pure serialization. The synchronized list guards the whole queue with one lock held for the duration of offer or remove; ConcurrentLinkedQueue (§15.4.2) uses a non-blocking algorithm that updates individual link pointers with atomic references. One serializes the entire insertion or removal; the other serializes only pointer updates. By four or five threads the synchronized version is dominated by context switching.

11.2.2Applying Amdahl's law qualitatively

You rarely measure F directly, but the law is still useful as a way of thinking "in the limit". Our mental model of multiprocessors was formed when two, four or a few dozen CPUs was normal; systems with hundreds or thousands of processors change which optimizations matter. Algorithms that look scalable on a four-way box may have bottlenecks nobody has hit yet.

Compare the two lock-granularity techniques of §11.4: lock splitting (one lock into two) and lock striping (one lock into many). Through Amdahl's lens, splitting a lock in two barely dents the serial fraction — you go from one serialized section to two — whereas striping scales the number of stripes with the processor count, which is the only one of the two with a future. (Still: if splitting a lock in two meets your requirements, it is cheaper and simpler.)

11.3Costs Introduced by Threads

Single-threaded programs pay neither scheduling nor synchronization costs. For threads to be a win, the parallelism has to be worth those invoices.

11.3.1Context switching

If the main thread is the only schedulable thread it is almost never scheduled out. With more runnable threads than CPUs, the OS preempts one so another can run: saving one execution context and restoring another. Context switches are not free — scheduling manipulates shared data structures in the OS and JVM, and those run on the same CPUs your program needs. Worse, when a new thread is switched in its data is unlikely to be in the local processor cache, so a switch triggers a flurry of cache misses.

That is why schedulers hand each runnable thread a minimum time quantum even when others are waiting: amortising the switch (and its cache damage) over more uninterrupted execution improves overall throughput, at some cost to responsiveness.

What a context switch costs

A good rule of thumb is 5,000–10,000 clock cycles — several microseconds on most processors. On Unix, vmstat reports context switches and kernel time; on Windows, perfmon. Kernel usage above ~10% often means heavy scheduling activity, usually from blocking I/O or lock contention.

Programs that block a lot — blocking I/O, waiting for contended locks, waiting on conditions — burn more context switches than CPU-bound programs do, and therefore convert more cycles into scheduling overhead. Non-blocking algorithms (Chapter 15) are one way to reduce that.

DON'T Listing 11.2 · Synchronization that has no effect 
synchronized (new Object()) {
    // do something
}

11.3.2Memory synchronization

The visibility guarantees of synchronized and volatile may require memory barriers, which can flush or invalidate caches, flush hardware write buffers and stall execution pipelines. They also inhibit compiler optimizations: most operations cannot be reordered across a barrier.

The crucial distinction is contended versus uncontended synchronization. synchronized is optimized for the uncontended case (volatile is always uncontended), and the fast path costs roughly 20–250 clock cycles. That is not zero, but it is rarely significant — and the alternative is compromising safety and signing yourself up for a very painful bug hunt later.

✂️
Lock elision

If a lock object is reachable only by the current thread, the JVM may remove the acquisition entirely — Listing 11.2 can always be optimized away. With escape analysis a smart JIT can prove a local object never escapes and elide all of its locks (Listing 11.3).

🧲
Lock coarsening

Adjacent synchronized blocks on the same lock can be merged into one acquisition — fewer lock operations, and a bigger block for other optimizations to work with. It can also undo hand-tuned splitting.

🚌
Bus traffic

Synchronization generates traffic on the shared memory bus. Under heavy contention every thread that synchronizes pays, which is why non-blocking algorithms without back-off can be worse than locks.

BOOK Listing 11.3 · Candidate for lock elision 
public String getStoogeNames() {
    List<String> stooges = new Vector<String>();
    stooges.add("Moe");
    stooges.add("Larry");
    stooges.add("Curly");
    return stooges.toString();
}

Naively this acquires and releases the Vector's lock four times. A runtime compiler that inlines the calls can see that stooges never escapes, so all four acquisitions can be eliminated — that is lock elision, performed by the IBM JVM and expected in HotSpot from Java 7. A JVM without escape analysis may instead coarsen the four acquisitions into one. Either way, do not worry excessively about the cost of uncontended synchronization: focus on the locks that are actually contended.

11.3.3Blocking

Uncontended synchronization can be handled entirely inside the JVM; contended synchronization may need the OS, which costs more. The loser must block, and the JVM can implement that either by spin-waiting (retrying until the lock is free) or by suspending the thread through the OS. Which is better depends on the switch cost versus the expected wait: spin for short waits, suspend for long ones. A few JVMs choose adaptively from profiling data; most simply suspend.

Suspension costs two extra context switches plus the OS and cache activity around them: the blocked thread is switched out before its quantum expires and switched back in later. Blocking due to lock contention also taxes the thread that holds the lock — when it releases, it must ask the OS to resume the blocked thread.

11.4Reducing Lock Contention

Serialization hurts scalability, context switches hurt performance, and contended locking causes both. So the highest-leverage optimization in a concurrent application is almost always "hold fewer locks, for less time, less often".

Access to a resource guarded by an exclusive lock is serialized: one thread at a time. We use locks for good reasons, but the price is that persistent contention for a lock limits scalability — the principal threat to scalability in concurrent applications is the exclusive resource lock.

Two factors govern the likelihood of contention: how often the lock is requested and how long it is held. If their product is small enough, most acquisitions are uncontended and contention is not a scalability problem. If demand is high, threads block — and in the extreme, processors sit idle while there is plenty of work to do. (That product is a corollary of Little's law: the average number of customers in a stable system equals arrival rate × time in system.)

The three levers

  1. Reduce the duration for which locks are held — narrow the scope.
  2. Reduce the frequency with which locks are requested — split and stripe.
  3. Replace exclusive locks with coordination that permits more concurrency — concurrent collections, read–write locks, atomics, immutability.

11.4.1Narrowing lock scope ("get in, get out")

Hold locks as briefly as possible by moving code that does not need the lock — especially expensive or blocking operations such as I/O — outside the synchronized block. The arithmetic is unforgiving: if an operation holds a lock for 2 ms and every operation needs that lock, throughput cannot exceed 500 operations per second no matter how many processors you add. Halving the hold time doubles the ceiling to 1,000.

DON'T Listing 11.4 · Holding a lock longer than necessary 
@ThreadSafe
public class AttributeStore {
    @GuardedBy("this") private final Map<String, String>
            attributes = new HashMap<String, String>();

    public synchronized  boolean userLocationMatches(String name,
                                                     String regexp) {
        String key = "users." + name + ".location";
        String location = attributes.get(key);
        if (location == null)
            return false;
        else
            return Pattern.matches(regexp, location);
    }
}

Only the Map.get touches shared state. Building the key string allocates a StringBuilder and a String; matching the regexp is arbitrary work. Both happen under the lock for no reason.

FIX Listing 11.5 · Reducing lock duration 
@ThreadSafe
public class BetterAttributeStore {
    @GuardedBy("this") private final Map<String, String>
            attributes = new HashMap<String, String>();

    public boolean userLocationMatches(String name, String regexp) {
        String key = "users." + name + ".location";
        String location;
        synchronized (this) {
            location = attributes.get(key);
        }
        if (location == null)
            return false;
        else
            return Pattern.matches(regexp, location);
    }
}

Because there is only one state variable, the class can go further and delegate thread safety (§4.3) to a thread-safe Map — Hashtable, synchronizedMap or ConcurrentHashMap. That removes the explicit synchronization entirely, shrinks the lock scope to the map access itself, and removes the risk that a future maintainer forgets the lock.

✂️

A synchronized block can also be too small: operations that must be atomic — updating several variables that participate in an invariant — belong in one block. And since synchronization is not free, splitting one block into many eventually costs more than it saves. In practice it is worth worrying about block size only when you can move substantial computation or blocking operations out of it. (If the JVM coarsens locks, it may undo your splitting anyway.)

11.4.2Reducing lock granularity

The other way to reduce the fraction of time a lock is held is to ask for it less often, via lock splitting and lock striping: separate locks for independent state variables that used to share one. Finer granularity means more scalability — and more locks means more deadlock risk (Chapter 10).

The thought experiment: imagine one lock for the entire application. Every synchronized block, whatever it guards, would serialize with every other. Distributing requests over a larger set of locks spreads the contention out, so fewer threads block.

BOOK Listing 11.6 · Candidate for lock splitting 
@ThreadSafe
public class ServerStatus {
    @GuardedBy("this") public final Set<String> users;
    @GuardedBy("this") public final Set<String> queries;
    ...
    public synchronized void addUser(String u) { users.add(u); }
    public synchronized void addQuery(String q) { queries.add(q); }
    public synchronized void removeUser(String u) {
        users.remove(u);
    }
    public synchronized void removeQuery(String q) {
        queries.remove(q);
    }
}

The logged-on users and the running queries are completely independent — the class could be split in two with no loss of functionality. So give each its own lock (Listing 11.7). (Delegating to thread-safe Set implementations would provide splitting implicitly, since each set uses its own lock.)

FIX Listing 11.7 · ServerStatus refactored to use split locks 
@ThreadSafe
public class ServerStatus {
    @GuardedBy("users") public final Set<String> users;
    @GuardedBy("queries") public final Set<String> queries;
    ...
    public void addUser(String u) {
        synchronized  (users) {
            users.add(u);
        }
    }

    public void addQuery(String q) {
        synchronized  (queries) {
            queries.add(q);
        }
    }
    // remove methods similarly refactored to use split locks
}

Splitting pays off most when a lock has moderate but not heavy contention: moderately contended locks may become mostly uncontended, which is the best outcome for both performance and scalability. Splitting lightly contended locks gains little, though it may raise the load at which performance starts to degrade.

11.4.3Lock striping

Splitting a heavily contended lock in two usually gives two heavily contended locks: a small win (two threads instead of one) and no real future on a many-processor system. ServerStatus offers no obvious further split.

But splitting generalizes to partitioning a variable-sized set of independent objects, and that is lock striping. ConcurrentHashMap uses an array of 16 locks, each guarding 1/16 of the hash buckets: bucket N is guarded by lock N mod 16. With a reasonable hash function this cuts demand per lock by roughly 16×, which is exactly what lets it support up to 16 concurrent writers. More stripes give more concurrency, but raise the count above 16 only with evidence of writer contention.

⚠️

Striping makes exclusive access to the whole collection harder and more expensive: usually an operation needs at most one lock, but occasionally you must lock everything — as ConcurrentHashMap does when it resizes and rehashes into a larger bucket array, acquiring all the locks in the stripe set. (The only way to acquire an arbitrary set of intrinsic locks is recursion.)

BOOK Listing 11.8 · Hash-based map using lock striping 
@ThreadSafe
public class StripedMap {
    // Synchronization policy: buckets[n] guarded by locks[n%N_LOCKS]
    private static final int N_LOCKS = 16;
    private final Node[] buckets;
    private final Object[] locks;

    private static class Node { ... }

    public StripedMap(int numBuckets) {
        buckets = new Node[numBuckets];
        locks = new Object[N_LOCKS];
        for (int i = 0; i < N_LOCKS; i++)
            locks[i] = new Object();
    }

    private final int hash(Object key) {
        return Math.abs(key.hashCode() % buckets.length);
    }

    public Object get(Object key) {
        int hash = hash(key);
        synchronized (locks[hash % N_LOCKS]) {
            for (Node m = buckets[hash]; m != null; m = m.next)
                if (m.key.equals(key))
                    return m.value;
        }
        return null;
    }

    public void clear() {
        for (int i = 0; i < buckets.length; i++) {
            synchronized (locks[i % N_LOCKS]) {
                buckets[i] = null;
            }
        }
    }
    ...
}

Note clear: it visits all the locks but never holds them all at once, so it is not atomic — there need not be a moment when the map is actually empty if other threads are adding. Making it atomic would require acquiring every lock simultaneously. For concurrent collections whose clients cannot lock them exclusively anyway, the result of size or isEmpty may be stale by the time it returns, so this is usually acceptable.

11.4.4Avoiding hot fields

Splitting and striping work because they let threads work on different data without interfering. They cannot help when a variable is needed by every operation.

Implementing HashMap.size, you could count entries on every call, or keep a counter updated by every put and remove — turning an O(n) operation into O(1). For a single-threaded or fully synchronized map that is a clear win. For a scalable one it is a disaster: every mutation must now touch the shared counter, so striping the hash chains buys nothing. What looked like a performance optimization became a scalability liability; the counter is a hot field.

ConcurrentHashMap sidesteps this by having size add up per-stripe counts, each guarded by its own stripe lock, instead of maintaining one global count. If size is called far more often than the map is modified, a striped structure can instead cache the total in a volatile and invalidate it (set to −1) on every modification.

11.4.5Alternatives to exclusive locks

The third lever: stop using exclusive locks for shared state. Your options are concurrent collections, read–write locks, immutable objects and atomic variables.

ReadWriteLock (Chapter 13) enforces multiple-reader, single-writer discipline: readers proceed concurrently so long as no writer wants in, writers take the lock exclusively. For read-mostly structures that is more concurrency than exclusive locking; for read-only structures, immutability removes the need for locking entirely.

Atomic variables (Chapter 15) reduce the cost of updating hot fields such as statistics counters, sequence generators, or the head reference of a linked structure. They give very fine-grained — and therefore more scalable — atomic operations on integers and references, built on compare-and-swap. If a class has a few hot fields that do not participate in invariants with other variables, replacing them with atomics may improve scalability. Better still is to need fewer hot fields: atomics reduce the cost of updating them, they do not eliminate it.

11.4.6Monitoring CPU utilization

When testing for scalability the goal is to keep processors fully utilized. vmstat and mpstat on Unix, or perfmon on Windows, tell you how hot they are running.

What you seeWhat it meansWhat to do
Asymmetric utilization — some CPUs hot, others idleComputation concentrated in a few threadsFind more parallelism; this app cannot use additional processors
CPUs not fully utilizedInsufficient load, or the client is the bottleneckIncrease load; check that the test harness is not saturated
Low CPU, high I/O waitI/O-bound (disk or network)iostat, network monitoring
Low CPU, long external waitsExternally bound (database, web service)Profile the wait time inside the external service
High CPU, low throughput, threads blockedLock contentionProfilers, or sample thread dumps and look for "waiting to lock monitor…"
High CPU and always runnable threadsThe app would benefit from more processorsScale up, or divide the workload over more threads

The thread-dump trick is worth remembering: locks that are mostly uncontended rarely appear in a dump, but a heavily contended lock will almost always have at least one waiter, so it shows up frequently across a few samples. And if only four threads can keep a 4-way system busy, moving to an 8-way box will not help until the workload is spread over more threads.

11.4.7Just say no to object pooling

In early JVMs allocation and garbage collection were slow, and many developers turned to object pooling. Allocation has improved enormously: the common path for new Object in HotSpot 1.4.x and 5.0 is roughly ten machine instructions — faster than malloc in C. Pooling has been shown to be a performance loss for all but the most expensive objects, and a serious loss for light and medium ones (Click, 2005).

In concurrent applications pooling fares even worse. Allocation needs very little inter-thread coordination — allocators use thread-local allocation blocks, so most synchronization on heap structures disappears. Requesting an object from a pool, by contrast, requires synchronization, and therefore can block. A blocked thread is hundreds of times more expensive than an allocation, so even a little pool-induced contention is a scalability bottleneck (and even uncontended synchronization usually costs more than allocating).

Allocating objects is usually cheaper than synchronizing.

Pooling has legitimate uses — constrained environments such as some J2ME or RTSJ targets, where memory management or responsiveness demands it — and other problems besides cost: sizing the pool correctly, objects not being reset to a pristine state, a thread returning an object to the pool and continuing to use it, and extra work for generational collectors through old-to-young references.

11.5Example: Comparing Map Performance

The same workload, four map implementations — and the moment contention starts is visible as a cliff.

ConcurrentHashMap's single-threaded performance is slightly better than a synchronized HashMap's, but in concurrent use it is not close. Its implementation assumes the most common operation is retrieving a value that already exists, and optimizes for successful gets. The synchronized maps' scalability problem is structural: one lock for the whole map, so one thread at a time. ConcurrentHashMap does no locking for most successful reads and uses lock striping for writes and the few reads that need it, so many threads access it concurrently without blocking.

Each run has N threads repeatedly pick a random key and try to retrieve it; a missing value is inserted with probability 0.6, a present one removed with probability 0.02. The tests ran on a pre-release Java 6 build on an 8-way Sparc V880. The concurrent maps improve steadily as threads are added. The synchronized wrappers are comparable at one thread and suffer badly from two onwards — which is the normal shape for code limited by lock contention: while contention is low, time per operation is dominated by the actual work; once contention is significant, time per operation is dominated by context-switch and scheduling delays, and more threads buy nothing.

Note that this benchmark generates far more contention per thread than a real application: it does almost nothing but pound on the map. A real program does thread-local work between accesses, so its cliff arrives later — which is exactly why benchmarks with unrealistic access patterns mislead.

11.6Reducing Context Switch Overhead

The bucket brigade versus a hundred people running around with buckets.

Many tasks block, and every transition between running and blocked is a context switch. A common source in server applications is logging: most frameworks are thin wrappers around println, writing inline. The alternative is a dedicated background thread that does the I/O on behalf of every request thread.

The service time of a logging call includes the OutputStream work, and if the I/O blocks it includes the blocked duration — plus a little extra, because when the I/O completes other threads are probably mid-quantum and some are already queued ahead of us. Or, if several threads log at once, they contend for the output-stream lock and the thread blocks the same way. Inline logging means I/O and locking inside the request path, so more context switches and longer service times.

⛓️

Longer service times hurt twice. They affect quality of service directly, and they increase lock contention: the longer a lock is held, the more likely someone else wants it. A thread blocking on I/O while holding a lock is the worst version of the "get in, get out" violation, because it turns an I/O wait into everyone's wait. Concurrent systems perform much better when most lock acquisitions are uncontended — so a coding style that encourages context switches lowers overall throughput.

Moving the I/O out of the request thread shortens mean service time: callers no longer block on the output-stream lock or on I/O, they queue a message and return. This introduces contention on the queue instead, but a put is far lighter than logging I/O (which may need system calls) and is unlikely to block as long as the queue is not full. The request path becomes a straight line: no I/O, no uncertain lock contention, much less chance of being switched out mid-request.

To some extent this moves work around — the I/O still happens, just where the user does not perceive it. But routing all the logging through one thread also eliminates contention for the output stream entirely, which is a real reduction in blocking, scheduling and lock management.

🔥
A hundred people with buckets

Every request thread does its own I/O and takes its own lock. Contention at the water source and at the fire, and constant mode-switching: fill, run, dump, run.

🪣
The bucket brigade

A single thread owns the I/O. Water flows steadily, less energy goes into transport, and each worker does one job continuously. Blocking and context switching are as disruptive to threads as interruptions are to people.

The book's caveat matters as much as the optimisation: moving the I/O to another thread introduces real design questions — interruption (what happens if a thread blocked in the logger is interrupted?), service guarantees (is a queued message guaranteed to be logged before shutdown?), saturation policy (what if producers log faster than the logger can write?), and service lifecycle (how is the logger shut down, and how are its producers told?). That list should look familiar: it is Chapter 7 and Chapter 8 applied to a logger.

📖

The chapter's Summary. Because one of the most common reasons to use threads is to exploit multiple processors, when discussing the performance of concurrent applications we are usually more concerned with throughput and scalability than with raw service time. Amdahl's law tells us that the scalability of an application is driven by the proportion of code that must be executed serially. Since the primary source of serialization in Java programs is the exclusive resource lock, scalability can often be improved by spending less time holding locks — by reducing lock granularity, reducing the duration for which locks are held, or replacing exclusive locks with non-exclusive or non-blocking alternatives.

▶Interactive: Amdahl's ladder

Add processors one at a time and watch the speedup you actually get, for four progressively smaller serial fractions. Each square is one processor count: the number in it is the speedup, and the colour is the utilization — speedup divided by processors.

🔍

Read the bottom row first: it is the ceiling, and no amount of hardware reaches it. Then read across the sixteen-processor row: the same machine delivers 6.4× under one lock and 15.8× under striping. Nothing about the algorithm changed — only how much of it had to run serially. That is why §11.4's three levers (hold locks for less time, request them less often, stop using exclusive locks) are the highest-leverage moves available.

§Patterns worth stealing

The eight listings above are the book's. These two are the measurements and the structure the chapter keeps asking for: a load-and-thread sweep that reports throughput honestly, and a striped counter that does not become a hot field.

1Measure the curve, don't guess the number

PATTERN Thread sweep with warm-up, per-thread workload and an Amdahl fit 
/**
 * Run the same workload at 1, 2, 4, ... threads and report what actually
 * happened. The serial fraction is ESTIMATED from the curve, not assumed.
 */
public final class ScalingHarness {
    private static final int WARMUP_ROUNDS = 5;

    public interface Workload { long runOnce() throws Exception; }

    public static void sweep(Workload workload, int maxThreads) throws Exception {
        double baseline = 0;
        System.out.println("threads  ops/sec   speedup  utilization");
        for (int n = 1; n <= maxThreads; n *= 2) {
            ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n,
                    r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r); t.setDaemon(true); return t; });
            try {
                for (int i = 0; i < WARMUP_ROUNDS; i++)          // let the JIT settle
                    measure(workload, pool, n, i == 0);

                long start = System.nanoTime();
                long ops = measure(workload, pool, n, true);
                double secs = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e9;
                double rate = ops / secs;
                if (n == 1) baseline = rate;
                double speedup = rate / baseline;
                System.out.printf("%7d  %8.0f  %7.2fx  %10.0f%%%n",
                        n, rate, speedup, 100 * speedup / n);
            } finally {
                pool.shutdown();
                pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            }
        }
    }

    private static long measure(Workload workload, ExecutorService pool,
                                final int threads, final boolean count) throws Exception {
        final AtomicLong ops = new AtomicLong();
        List<Future<?>> futures = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < threads; i++) {
            futures.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                // Each thread does its OWN work: no shared queue, no shared
                // result structure. Whoever adds one has added serialization.
                for (int r = 0; r < 1000; r++) {
                    workload.runOnce();
                    if (count) ops.incrementAndGet();
                }
                return null;
            }));
        }
        for (Future<?> f : futures) f.get();
        return ops.get();
    }

    /**
     * Estimate F from the measured speedup at N threads (the N = 1 run is
     * the baseline, so it carries no information about F).
     *   1/S(N) = F + (1 - F)/N   =>   F = (1/S(N) - 1/N) / (1 - 1/N)
     * A negative result means the measurement is noise; treat it as zero.
     */
    public static double serialFraction(double speedupAtN, int n) {
        if (n < 2) throw new IllegalArgumentException("need N >= 2");
        double f = (1 / speedupAtN - 1.0 / n) / (1 - 1.0 / n);
        return Math.max(0, f);
    }
}

2A counter that is not a hot field

PATTERN Striped adder: per-stripe counters summed on demand, like ConcurrentHashMap.size 
/**
 * A shared counter every mutating operation must touch is a hot field: it
 * reintroduces the contention that lock striping just removed. Keep one
 * counter per stripe and add them up when someone asks.
 */
public final class StripedCounter {
    private static final int STRIPES =
            Math.max(1, Integer.highestOneBit(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() * 2));
    private final AtomicLong[] counts = new AtomicLong[STRIPES];
    private final AtomicLong cachedTotal = new AtomicLong(-1);   // -1 = stale

    public StripedCounter() {
        for (int i = 0; i < STRIPES; i++) counts[i] = new AtomicLong();
    }

    private static int stripe() {
        // thread id is stable and cheap; a random stripe would also do
        return (int) (Thread.currentThread().getId() & (STRIPES - 1));
    }

    public void increment() {
        counts[stripe()].incrementAndGet();
        cachedTotal.set(-1);                 // invalidate, do not recompute
    }

    public void add(long delta) {
        counts[stripe()].addAndGet(delta);
        cachedTotal.set(-1);
    }

    /** O(stripes), and only when the cached value has been invalidated. */
    public long sum() {
        long total = cachedTotal.get();
        if (total >= 0) return total;        // still accurate: no updates since
        total = 0;
        for (AtomicLong c : counts) total += c.get();
        cachedTotal.set(total);
        return total;
    }

    /** Occasionally, when nothing is mutating, this keeps sum() O(1). */
    public long sumExact() {
        long total = 0;
        for (AtomicLong c : counts) total += c.get();
        return total;
    }
}
💡

The first pattern is really the chapter's "measure, don't guess" turned into code, and the point of the second is that optimizations compose badly: striping the map and then adding a global counter undoes the striping. Before adding a shared field to a concurrent class, ask how many operations will touch it — if the answer is "all of them", you have just rebuilt the single lock in a different shape.

§Vocabulary introduced in Chapter 11

TermMeaning as used hereWhere it goes
Service timeHow long one unit of work takes from start to finish. A "how fast" measure.Ch. 11.1.1
LatencyThe delay a caller experiences before a result is acknowledged — queueing included.Ch. 11.1.1
ThroughputWork completed per unit time. A "how much" measure, and the one servers care about.Ch. 11.1.1
CapacityThe load the system can carry with acceptable performance.Ch. 11.1.1
ScalabilityThe ability to improve throughput or capacity by adding resources. Distinct from raw speed.Ch. 11.1.1
Bound resourceThe scarce resource that limits an activity: CPU-bound, database-bound, I/O-bound.Ch. 11.1
Serial fraction (F)The proportion of the work that cannot be parallelized. The one number Amdahl's law needs.Ch. 11.2
Amdahl's lawSpeedup ≤ 1/(F + (1−F)/N), converging to 1/F as processors go to infinity.Ch. 11.2
Serialization pointAny shared structure that forces order on otherwise parallel work: a queue, a result map, a log file.Ch. 11.2
Context switchPreempting one thread so another can run: save one context, restore another, and lose the cache. 5,000–10,000 cycles.Ch. 11.3.1
Memory barrierThe instruction behind volatile and lock visibility; flushes buffers, stalls pipelines, blocks reordering.Ch. 11.3.2
Lock elisionRemoving lock acquisitions the JVM can prove are thread-local (escape analysis).Ch. 11.3.2
Lock coarseningMerging adjacent acquisitions of the same lock into one.Ch. 11.3.2
Spin-waitingRetrying a lock instead of suspending the thread; cheaper for short waits, wasteful for long ones.Ch. 11.3.3
ContentionLock requests arriving faster than the lock can be released: frequency × duration.Ch. 11.4
Narrowing lock scopeShrinking a synchronized block to the statements that actually touch shared state — "get in, get out".Ch. 11.4.1
Lock splittingOne lock guarding several independent variables becomes one lock per variable.Ch. 11.4.2
Lock stripingLock splitting generalized to N locks over a partitioned data structure; ConcurrentHashMap's 16 stripes.Ch. 11.4.3
Hot fieldA field every mutating operation must touch, which reintroduces contention no amount of striping can remove.Ch. 11.4.4
Object poolingRecycling instances instead of allocating — a single-threaded optimization that becomes a scalability hazard under contention.Ch. 11.4.7

✓Cheat sheet & self-check

SymptomLikely causeFix
Adding threads stops helping at two or threeA single lock serializing the hot pathNarrow the scope, then split or stripe the lock
Throughput falls as threads are addedContention dominating: context switches per operation exceed useful workReduce lock duration; replace exclusive locking with concurrent structures
High kernel time, many context switchesBlocking I/O or contended locks inside request threadsMove the blocking work to a dedicated thread (logging pattern)
One CPU hot, the rest idleNo real parallelism — work concentrated in few threadsDecompose further; check the queue is not the bottleneck
Scales to 4 CPUs, flat at 8Serial fraction of ~10% (Amdahl ceiling of 10×)Find and shrink the serial part; more CPUs will not help
Pool is fine at one thread, terrible at fourObject pooling adding synchronization to the allocation pathDelete the pool; allocate
A "size" counter kills scalabilityHot field touched by every mutationPer-stripe counters summed on demand, or cache and invalidate
Optimization made it slowerYou guessed instead of measuringRe-measure under realistic load; keep the simpler code if there is no win
✅
Do

Measure with a realistic load profile, and write down the requirement so you know when to stop. Prefer the simplest correct design. Hold locks briefly, ask for them rarely, and prefer concurrent collections to hand-rolled locking.

🚫
Avoid

Optimizing before you have requirements. Trading safety for speed. `synchronized` on whole methods that do I/O or regex matching. Global counters in scalable structures. Object pools. Tuning anything without a before-and-after measurement.

🧠
The one habit

For any shared structure in a hot path, ask: how many operations touch this, and how long does each hold it? Frequency × duration is the whole of §11.4 — if you can lower either factor, you have lowered the serial fraction, and that is the only thing Amdahl's law rewards.

Five questions the chapter leaves you with

  1. What is my measured serial fraction, and which code is it?
  2. Which of my locks are actually contended — and would a thread dump show them?
  3. How long is my hottest lock held, in nanoseconds, and what could move outside it?
  4. Do I have a hot field that every mutating operation touches?
  5. Is my benchmark's access pattern anything like production, or am I optimizing the wrong curve?

Notes carried over from the chapter

  1. Some would argue that performance is the only reason we put up with the complexity threads introduce.
  2. An anecdote from the book's testing: an expensive application with a tunable pool turned out to have an optimal pool size of one — a single-CPU, almost entirely CPU-bound target.
  3. The book's market note: at the time of writing Sun shipped 8-core Niagara systems and Azul shipped 96-, 192- and 384-way systems based on the 24-core Vega processor.
  4. The contention product (frequency × duration) is a corollary of Little's law: the average number of customers in a stable system equals their average arrival rate times their average time in the system (Little, 1961).
  5. A dynamic compiler can also notice that getStoogeNames always returns the same string, and recompile it after the first execution to return the cached value.
  6. Lock elision is performed by the IBM JVM and was expected in HotSpot as of Java 7.
  7. Heavy contention makes non-blocking algorithms generate more synchronization traffic than lock-based ones unless they include back-off — see Chapter 15.
  8. Object pooling remains necessary in constrained environments such as some J2ME or RTSJ targets, where memory management or responsiveness demands it.
  9. If size is called frequently relative to mutations, a striped structure can cache the total in a volatile and invalidate it (set it to −1) on every modification.
  10. The only way to acquire an arbitrary set of intrinsic locks is recursion; that is how a striped structure locks the whole collection when it must.
