Java Concurrency in Practice · Chapter 12

Chapter 12 — Testing Concurrent Programs

Everything before this chapter assumed you could tell whether a program was correct. For concurrent code that assumption is the problem: the failures you care about are low-probability events that depend on timing, load and scheduling, and the act of testing can change the schedule enough to hide them. The chapter is therefore two things: a bag of techniques for making safety failures more likely to show up, and a warning list of the ways performance measurements lie to you.

📖 pp. 153–169 🧩 4 sections · 13 listings · 5 figures ⏱️ ~28 min read 🏷️ Part III — Liveness, Performance, and Testing

Chapter in one paragraph

TL;DR — the six things worth remembering

  1. Concurrent tests search a state space; they do not check a line. A sequential test asserts a post-condition. A concurrent test spins up threads that race through the same code hoping to hit an unlucky interleaving — so "it passed" means "I did not find it", never "it cannot happen".
  2. Test safety and liveness separately, and test them twice. Safety tests look for invariant violations under concurrent load (checksums); liveness tests look for things that never finish — which forces you to decide, up front, how long "never" is.
  3. Checksums must not add synchronization. A shadow list needs a lock and would distort the very schedule you are trying to perturb. A per-thread checksum combined at the end (addition, XOR) is free.
  4. Coordination is the test's own hazard. A CyclicBarrier makes all threads start together; Thread.yield sprinkles context switches through critical sections; both are ways of buying interleavings with time.
  5. Performance numbers are guilty until proven innocent. GC pauses, JIT compilation, unrealistic code paths, unrealistic contention and dead-code elimination can each move a measurement by an order of magnitude.
  6. Testing is one pillar, not the building. Code review and static analysis find races that no test will ever trip — the book's own answer to "test everything" is "review everything, too".

12.1Testing for Correctness

Concurrent classes are tested with the same tools as sequential ones. The difference is that a green test proves almost nothing — so the whole craft is in making failure probable.

Concurrent programs share the design principles of sequential programs, but they add a degree of non-determinism: the number of potential interactions and failure modes grows combinatorially, and the interesting ones are rare. Tests that disclose such failures have to be more extensive and run for longer than typical sequential tests.

Most tests fall into the two classic categories from Chapter 1. Safety — "nothing bad ever happens" — is tested as invariants: if a linked list caches its size, compare the cached count against the real count. Liveness — "something good eventually happens" — covers progress and non-progress, and is much harder to quantify, because distinguishing "blocking" from "slow" requires a timeout, and a timeout is a guess.

👻

The book's footnote names the enemy: bugs that disappear when you add debugging or test code are called Heisenbugs. Test code can introduce timing or synchronization artifacts that mask exactly the bug you were hunting — which is why the techniques below work so hard to add concurrency without adding coordination.

Related to liveness tests are performance tests, and the book fixes three metrics up front: throughput (the rate at which a set of concurrent tasks is completed), responsiveness or latency (the delay between a request and its completion) and scalability (the improvement in throughput as resources are added).

Developing unit tests starts with the same analysis as for a sequential class: identify invariants and post-conditions that are amenable to mechanical checking. If you are lucky they are in the specification; the rest of the time, writing tests is an exercise in iterative specification discovery. The running example is a bounded buffer built from two counting semaphores.

availableItems counts the elements that can be removed and starts at zero — the buffer is empty. availableSpaces counts the slots available for insertion and starts at the capacity. A take first acquires a permit from availableItems, which succeeds immediately if the buffer is non-empty and blocks otherwise; then it removes an element and releases a permit back to availableSpaces. put is the mirror image, so on exit from either method the sum of the two permit counts always equals the bound.

BOOK Listing 12.1 · Bounded buffer using Semaphore 
@ThreadSafe
public class BoundedBuffer<E> {
    private final Semaphore availableItems, availableSpaces;
    @GuardedBy("this") private final E[] items;
    @GuardedBy("this") private int putPosition = 0, takePosition = 0;

    public BoundedBuffer(int capacity) {
        availableItems = new Semaphore(0);
        availableSpaces = new Semaphore(capacity);
        items = (E[]) new Object[capacity];
    }
    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return availableItems.availablePermits() == 0;
    }
    public boolean isFull() {
        return availableSpaces.availablePermits() == 0;
    }

    public void put(E x) throws InterruptedException {
        availableSpaces.acquire();
        doInsert(x);
        availableItems.release();
    }
    public E take() throws InterruptedException {
        availableItems.acquire();
        E item = doExtract();
        availableSpaces.release();
        return item;
    }

    private synchronized void doInsert(E x) {
        int i = putPosition;
        items[i] = x;
        putPosition = (++i == items.length)? 0 : i;
    }
    private synchronized E doExtract() {
        int i = takePosition;
        E x = items[i];
        items[i] = null;
        takePosition = (++i == items.length)? 0 : i;
        return x;
    }
}

In practice, if you need a bounded buffer you should use ArrayBlockingQueue or LinkedBlockingQueue rather than rolling your own. The technique matters because the same shape — permits controlling insertion and removal — applies to other data structures too.

12.1.1Basic Unit Tests

The most basic tests for BoundedBuffer are sequential: create a buffer, call its methods, assert post-conditions. A freshly created buffer should report itself empty and not full. A slightly more interesting safety test inserts N elements into a capacity-N buffer (which must not block) and asserts that the buffer now reports full and not empty.

BOOK Listing 12.2 · Basic unit tests for BoundedBuffer 
class BoundedBufferTest extends TestCase {
    void testIsEmptyWhenConstructed() {
        BoundedBuffer<Integer> bb = new BoundedBuffer<Integer>(10);
        assertTrue(bb.isEmpty());
        assertFalse(bb.isFull());
    }

    void testIsFullAfterPuts() throws InterruptedException {
        BoundedBuffer<Integer> bb = new BoundedBuffer<Integer>(10);
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)
            bb.put(i);
        assertTrue(bb.isFull());
        assertFalse(bb.isEmpty());
    }
}

These methods are entirely sequential, and that is the point. Including a set of sequential tests is often helpful because they disclose when a problem is not related to concurrency, before you start looking for data races. Every debugging session should begin by eliminating the boring explanations.

12.1.2Testing Blocking Operations

Testing an essential concurrency property requires more than one thread, and most testing frameworks are not concurrency-friendly: they rarely create threads or monitor them, and if a helper thread discovers a failure the framework usually has no idea which test it belongs to. The JSR 166 Expert Group built a base class for the java.util.concurrent conformance tests that relays failures back to the main thread and reports them during tearDown, under the convention that every test waits for all threads it created to terminate. You may not need to go that far — but it must be clear whether the test passed, and failure information must be reported somewhere usable.

If a method is supposed to block, the test should succeed only if the thread does not proceed — the same logic as testing that a method throws an exception. The complication is the unblock: start the blocking activity in another thread, wait until it blocks, interrupt it, and assert that the operation completed by throwing InterruptedException.

"Wait until the thread blocks" is easier said than done. In practice you make an arbitrary decision about how long a few instructions could possibly take, and wait longer than that — and you should be prepared to increase the value when you see spurious failures.

BOOK Listing 12.3 · Testing blocking and responsiveness to interruption 
void testTakeBlocksWhenEmpty() {
    final BoundedBuffer<Integer> bb = new BoundedBuffer<Integer>(10);
    Thread taker = new Thread() {
        public void run() {
            try {
                int unused = bb.take();
                fail();  /*  if we get here, it's an error  */
            } catch (InterruptedException success) { }
        }};
    try {
        taker.start();
        Thread.sleep(LOCKUP_DETECT_TIMEOUT);
        taker.interrupt();
        taker.join(LOCKUP_DETECT_TIMEOUT);
        assertFalse(taker.isAlive());
    } catch (Exception unexpected) {
        fail();
    }
}

The timed join ensures the test completes even if take gets stuck in some unexpected way. The method tests several properties at once: that take blocks, and that when interrupted it throws InterruptedException. This is one of the few cases where subclassing Thread explicitly beats submitting a Runnable to a pool — you need the thread handle to join on. The same approach tests that a taker unblocks once the main thread puts an element in the queue.

⚠️

It is tempting to use Thread.getState to verify that a thread is really blocked on a condition wait. Do not. Nothing requires a blocked thread to enter WAITING or TIMED_WAITING — the JVM may implement blocking by spin-waiting — and spurious wakeups are permitted, so a waiting thread may bounce back to RUNNABLE while its condition is still false. It also takes time for a thread to settle into a blocking state. getState is debugging information, not a concurrency control, and of limited use in tests.

12.1.3Testing Safety

Listings 12.2 and 12.3 test real properties of the buffer, but they are unlikely to disclose an error that comes from a data race. To test correctness under unpredictable concurrent access you need many threads, and a way to tell whether anything went wrong.

Building tests that disclose safety errors is a chicken-and-egg problem: the test program is itself a concurrent program. Developing good concurrent tests can be harder than developing the classes they test. The challenge is to find easily checked properties that will, with high probability, fail if something goes wrong — while making sure the checking code does not limit concurrency artificially. The ideal is a check that needs no synchronization at all.

For producer–consumer classes like BoundedBuffer, the property to check is that everything put in comes out, and nothing else does. The naive implementation — a "shadow" list, inserted into on put and removed from on take, asserted empty at the end — distorts the schedule, because modifying the shadow list needs synchronization and may block. You would be measuring your own test.

The checksum trick

Instead of tracking the elements, compute an order-sensitive checksum of what goes in and what comes out, and compare. If they match, the test passes. With one producer and one consumer this checks not only that the right elements came out but that they came out in the right order.

Scaling to multiple producers and consumers requires a checksum insensitive to order — so that per-thread checksums can be combined afterwards. Any commutative operation works: addition or XOR. Otherwise, a shared checksum field becomes either a concurrency bottleneck or a distortion of the test's timing.

And the checksum must be unguessable. Consecutive integers as test data mean the result is always the same, and a smart compiler could precompute it. Test data should be generated randomly — but not with a general-purpose RNG: most RNG classes are thread-safe, so they add synchronization and couple your test to the RNG's own contention. Give each thread its own non-thread-safe RNG.

🎲

The book's footnote is one of its best one-liners: many benchmarks are, unbeknownst to their developers or users, simply tests of how great a concurrency bottleneck the RNG is.

Rather than a general-purpose RNG, use a simple pseudorandom function. You do not need high-quality randomness — only enough that the numbers change from run to run. The xor-shift function below (Marsaglia, 2003) is among the cheapest medium-quality generators; seeding it from hashCode and nanoTime makes the sums both unguessable and almost always different per run.

BOOK Listing 12.4 · Medium-quality random number generator suitable for testing 
static int xorShift(int y) {
    y ^= (y << 6);
    y ^= (y >>> 21);
    y ^= (y << 7);
    return y;
}

PutTakeTest starts N producer threads that generate elements and enqueue them, and N consumer threads that dequeue them. Each thread updates its own checksum as elements go in or out; the per-thread sums are combined at the end, so the test adds no more synchronization or contention than the buffer itself requires.

There is a subtlety in how the threads are started. Creating and starting a thread is moderately expensive, so if you start threads in a loop, the worst case is that they run sequentially — the first thread finishes before the last starts. Even in the not-quite-worst case the first thread gets a head start, so you see fewer interleavings than you expected. The fix from §5.5.1 was a pair of latches; here the same effect comes from a CyclicBarrier initialized with the number of worker threads plus one, which the workers and the test driver all wait on at the beginning and at the end of the run. That ensures every thread is up and running before any of them starts working.

The final trick is a deterministic termination criterion: the test starts exactly as many producers as consumers, and each puts or takes the same number of elements, so no inter-thread coordination is needed to know when the test is done.

BOOK Listing 12.5 · Producer–consumer test program for BoundedBuffer 
public class PutTakeTest {
    private static final ExecutorService pool
            = Executors.newCachedThreadPool();
    private final AtomicInteger putSum = new AtomicInteger(0);
    private final AtomicInteger takeSum = new AtomicInteger(0);
    private final CyclicBarrier barrier;
    private final BoundedBuffer<Integer> bb;
    private final int nTrials, nPairs;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new PutTakeTest(10, 10, 100000).test(); // sample parameters
        pool.shutdown();
    }

    PutTakeTest(int capacity, int npairs, int ntrials) {
        this.bb = new BoundedBuffer<Integer>(capacity);
        this.nTrials = ntrials;
        this.nPairs = npairs;
        this.barrier = new CyclicBarrier(npairs * 2 + 1);
    }

    void test() {
        try {
            for (int i = 0; i < nPairs; i++) {
                pool.execute(new Producer());
                pool.execute(new Consumer());
            }
            barrier.await(); // wait for all threads to be ready
            barrier.await(); // wait for all threads to finish
            assertEquals(putSum.get(), takeSum.get());
        } catch (Exception e) {
            throw new RuntimeException(e);
        }
    }

    class Producer implements Runnable {  /*  Listing 12.6  */ }

    class Consumer implements Runnable {  /*  Listing 12.6  */ }
}
BOOK Listing 12.6 · Producer and Consumer classes used in PutTakeTest 
/* inner classes of PutTakeTest (Listing 12.5) */
class Producer implements Runnable {
    public void run() {
        try {
            int seed = (this.hashCode() ^ (int)System.nanoTime());
            int sum = 0;
            barrier.await();
            for (int i = nTrials; i > 0; --i) {
                bb.put(seed);
                sum += seed;
                seed = xorShift(seed);
            }
            putSum.getAndAdd(sum);
            barrier.await();
        } catch (Exception e) {
            throw new RuntimeException(e);
        }
    }
}

class Consumer implements Runnable {
    public void run() {
        try {
            barrier.await();
            int sum = 0;
            for (int i = nTrials; i > 0; --i) {
                sum += bb.take();
            }
            takeSum.getAndAdd(sum);
            barrier.await();
        } catch (Exception e) {
            throw new RuntimeException(e);
        }
    }
}

Tests like PutTakeTest are good at finding safety violations. The book's example: a common error in semaphore-controlled buffers is forgetting that the code doing the insertion and extraction needs mutual exclusion. A version of BoundedBuffer that omits synchronized on doInsert and doExtract fails PutTakeTest fairly quickly. Running it with a few dozen threads, iterating a few million times, on buffers of various capacities, on various systems, increases confidence — it is not a proof.

Tests should run on multiprocessor systems for diversity of interleavings, but more than a few CPUs does not necessarily help. To maximise the chance of catching timing-sensitive races there should be more active threads than CPUs, so that at any moment some threads are running and some are switched out — which is precisely what destroys the predictability of the interactions.

⏳

In tests that run until they complete a fixed number of operations, a bug in the code under test can mean the test never finishes. The usual answer is for the framework to abort tests that exceed a time limit — but the limit has to be determined empirically, and each "failure" then has to be examined to see whether it was a real hang or just a limit set too low. This is not unique to concurrency: sequential tests must also distinguish long-running loops from infinite ones.

12.1.4Testing Resource Management

So far the tests check that the class does what it should. The other half of the contract is that it does not do what it should not — above all, that it does not hold on to what it no longer needs.

Any object that holds or manages other objects should not keep references longer than necessary. Such storage leaks prevent the garbage collector from reclaiming memory — or threads, file handles, sockets, database connections — and lead to exhaustion and failure.

Resource management matters especially for a class like BoundedBuffer, because the entire reason for bounding a buffer is to prevent failure when producers outrun consumers: bounding makes overly productive producers block instead of creating more and more work pending in memory.

Undesirable retention is easy to test with heap-inspection tools that force a collection and record heap size and usage. testLeak inserts several large objects and then removes them; memory at snapshot #2 should be approximately the same as at snapshot #1. If doExtract forgot items[i] = null, the two snapshots would clearly differ.

BOOK Listing 12.7 · Testing for resource leaks 
class Big { double[] data = new double[100000]; }

void testLeak() throws InterruptedException {
     BoundedBuffer<Big> bb = new BoundedBuffer<Big>(CAPACITY);
     int heapSize1 =  /* snapshot heap */ ;
     for (int i = 0; i < CAPACITY; i++)
         bb.put(new Big());
     for (int i = 0; i < CAPACITY; i++)
         bb.take();
     int heapSize2 =  /* snapshot heap */ ;
     assertTrue(Math.abs(heapSize1-heapSize2) < THRESHOLD);
}

This is one of the few places where explicit nulling is necessary. Most of the time it is either not helpful or actually harmful (Bloch, Effective Java, Item 5). Note also that you cannot truly force a collection — System.gc is a suggestion, and HotSpot can be told to ignore it with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC.

Testing a thread pool means testing elements of its execution policy: that threads are created when they should be and not when they should not be, that idle threads are reaped when they should be, and so on. A comprehensive suite is a major effort, but individual properties are easy to test in isolation. Thread creation can be instrumented with a custom ThreadFactory that counts the threads it creates.

BOOK Listing 12.8 · Thread factory for testing ThreadPoolExecutor 
class TestingThreadFactory implements ThreadFactory {
    public final AtomicInteger numCreated = new AtomicInteger();
    private final ThreadFactory factory
            = Executors.defaultThreadFactory();

    public Thread newThread(Runnable r) {
        numCreated.incrementAndGet();
        return factory.newThread(r);
    }
}

If the core pool size is smaller than the maximum, the pool should grow as demand increases. Submitting long-running tasks keeps the number of executing tasks constant long enough to make a few assertions — for example that the pool has expanded as expected. TestingThreadFactory could be extended to return a custom Thread that records its own termination, so tests could verify that threads are reaped according to the policy.

BOOK Listing 12.9 · Test method to verify thread pool expansion 
public void testPoolExpansion() throws InterruptedException {
    int MAX_SIZE = 10;
    ExecutorService exec = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(MAX_SIZE);

    for (int i = 0; i < 10 * MAX_SIZE; i++)
        exec.execute(new Runnable() {
            public void run() {
                try {
                    Thread.sleep(Long.MAX_VALUE);
                } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                }
            }
        });
    for (int i = 0;
         i < 20 && threadFactory.numCreated.get() < MAX_SIZE;
         i++)
        Thread.sleep(100);
    assertEquals(threadFactory.numCreated.get(), MAX_SIZE);
    exec.shutdownNow();
}
🔁

Read the retry loop as the honest part of this test. The assertion is not made immediately after submitting the tasks — the pool is allowed twenty 100 ms slices to grow, and only then is the count checked. Every assertion about a pool's state is really an assertion that it reaches a state within a bound.

12.1.5Using Callbacks

Client-supplied code runs at known points in an object's lifecycle — which makes those points the cheapest places to assert invariants.

Callbacks to client-provided code are helpful when constructing test cases, because libraries call them at exactly the moments worth checking. ThreadPoolExecutor calls the task Runnables and the ThreadFactory; a custom ThreadFactory or a wrapped Runnable can therefore observe creation, start and completion without touching the pool implementation.

The other reason callbacks matter in this chapter is the reverse: inserting a callback into production code is how you make a race more likely to be observed. A callback — or a yield, or a sleep — placed between two operations that must be atomic turns a rare interleaving into a common one.

12.1.6Generating More Interleavings

Testing for concurrency errors is a numbers game. You cannot enumerate the interleavings, but you can arrange for more of them to happen.

We have already met two levers: run on multiprocessors with more active threads than CPUs, and test on a variety of systems — different processor counts, operating systems and architectures — since a bug that needs a particular memory model will not show up on all of them.

A third lever is Thread.yield: sprinkle yields through operations that access shared state to encourage context switches. The effect is platform-specific, because the JVM is free to treat Thread.yield as a no-op [JLS 17.9]; a short but non-zero sleep is slower but more reliable. The method below transfers credits; between the two updates the invariant "the sum of all accounts is zero" does not hold, and by sometimes yielding in the middle of the operation you can activate timing-sensitive bugs in code that lacks adequate synchronization.

BOOK Listing 12.10 · Using Thread.yield to generate more interleavings 
public synchronized void transferCredits(Account from,
                                         Account to,
                                         int amount) {
    from.setBalance(from.getBalance() - amount);
    if (random.nextInt(1000) > THRESHOLD)
        Thread.yield();
    to.setBalance(to.getBalance() + amount);
}

The practical objection is that you have to add these calls for testing and remove them for production. The book's answer is aspect-oriented programming: weave the yields in for the test build and leave them out of the shipped one. §12.4.3 comes back to AOP.

12.2Testing for Performance

Performance tests are usually extended functionality tests — and they should always include the functionality checks, so that you are not measuring the performance of broken code.

The two kinds of test have different goals. Performance tests measure end-to-end metrics for representative use cases, and picking those scenarios is not always easy: ideally they reflect how the objects are actually used in your application. For a bounded buffer the scenario is obvious, because bounded buffers are nearly always part of a producer–consumer design — so measure the throughput of producers feeding consumers, by extending PutTakeTest.

A common secondary goal is to choose sizings empirically — numbers of threads, buffer capacities. These may be sensitive to platform characteristics enough to need dynamic configuration, but it is equally common that reasonable choices work well across a wide range of systems.

12.2.1Extending PutTakeTest to Add Timing

The primary extension is to measure the time a run takes. Rather than timing a single operation — which the timer's granularity would swamp — time the whole run and divide by the number of operations. The barrier is already coordinating start and stop, so use a barrier action that records the start and end times.

BOOK Listing 12.11 · Barrier-based timer 
this.timer = new BarrierTimer();
this.barrier = new CyclicBarrier(npairs * 2 + 1, timer);

public class BarrierTimer implements Runnable {
    private boolean started;
    private long startTime, endTime;

    public synchronized void run() {
        long t = System.nanoTime();
        if (!started) {
            started = true;
            startTime = t;
        } else
            endTime = t;
    }
    public synchronized void clear() {
        started = false;
    }
    public synchronized long getTime() {
        return endTime - startTime;
    }
}

The barrier action runs once per barrier trip, in the last thread to arrive, and it runs before the waiting threads are released — so the start time is taken before any worker begins its loop, and the end time after every worker has finished. The first trip starts the clock; the second stops it. clear() resets the timer so the same instance can be reused for the next run.

BOOK Listing 12.12 · Testing with a barrier-based timer 
public void test() {
    try {
        timer.clear();
        for (int i = 0; i < nPairs; i++) {
            pool.execute(new Producer());
            pool.execute(new Consumer());
        }
        barrier.await();
        barrier.await();
        long nsPerItem = timer.getTime() / (nPairs * (long)nTrials);
        System.out.print("Throughput: " + nsPerItem + " ns/item");
        assertEquals(putSum.get(), takeSum.get());
    } catch (Exception e) {
        throw new RuntimeException(e);
    }
}

Note what stayed: the correctness assertion is still there, after the measurement. A throughput test that does not check its own results is measuring an unknown program.

Running TimedPutTakeTest answers three questions: the throughput of the handoff for various parameter combinations, how the buffer scales with different numbers of threads, and how to choose the bound. Answering them needs a driver that sweeps the parameters.

BOOK Listing 12.13 · Driver program for TimedPutTakeTest 
public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
    int tpt = 100000;  /*  trials per thread  */
    for (int cap = 1; cap <= 1000; cap *= 10) {
        System.out.println("Capacity: " + cap);
        for (int pairs = 1; pairs <= 128; pairs *= 2) {
            TimedPutTakeTest t =
                new TimedPutTakeTest(cap, pairs, tpt);
            System.out.print("Pairs: " + pairs + "\t");
            t.test();
            System.out.print("\t");
            Thread.sleep(1000);
            t.test();
            System.out.println();
            Thread.sleep(1000);
        }
    }
    pool.shutdown();
}

Each configuration is run twice, with a one-second pause between runs. The first run is warm-up; the second is the reported one. The pauses also give the JVM's background threads a chance to catch up between trials.

A capacity of one gives very poor throughput, because each thread can make only a tiny bit of progress before blocking and waiting for another thread. Ten helps dramatically; past ten, diminishing returns.

It may be puzzling that adding a lot more threads degrades performance only slightly. The reason is easy to see on a CPU meter while the test runs: even with many threads, not much computation is going on — most of the time is spent blocking and unblocking threads. There is plenty of CPU slack for more threads to do the same thing.

🧪

Do not generalise that last paragraph. This test is artificial: producers do almost no work to generate the item, and consumers do almost no work with it. In a real producer–consumer application the workers do nontrivial work, the slack disappears, and the effect of too many threads can be very noticeable. What this test measures is the constraint that the handoff itself imposes on throughput — nothing more.

12.2.2Comparing Multiple Algorithms

BoundedBuffer is a solid implementation that performs reasonably — and it is no match for either ArrayBlockingQueue or LinkedBlockingQueue, which is why this algorithm was not chosen for the class library. Those algorithms were selected and tuned, in part, using tests just like these. The main reason BoundedBuffer fares poorly is structural: put and take each contain multiple operations that can contend — acquire a semaphore, acquire a lock, release a semaphore. Other approaches have fewer points at which two threads can collide.

That LinkedBlockingQueue scales better than ArrayBlockingQueue seems odd at first: a linked queue must allocate a node per insertion, so it appears to do more work. But even with the extra allocation and GC overhead, a linked queue permits more concurrent access by puts and takes, because the best linked-queue algorithms allow the head and tail to be updated independently. And because allocation is usually thread-local, algorithms that reduce contention by doing more allocation usually scale better. This is another case where intuition from traditional performance tuning runs counter to what scalability needs.

12.2.3Measuring Responsiveness

Throughput is usually the most important metric for concurrent programs, but sometimes what matters is how long an individual action takes — the variance of service time. Sometimes a longer average is a good trade for a smaller variance, because predictability is a performance characteristic too. Measuring variance lets you answer quality-of-service questions such as "what percentage of operations complete in under 100 ms?".

Histograms of task completion times are the best way to visualise variance. Measuring them is only slightly harder than measuring averages — keep per-task completion times alongside the aggregate. Because timer granularity can swamp a single short task, measure the run time of small batches of put and take operations instead.

The next two figures use a variant of TimedPutTakeTest with a buffer of 1000, in which each of 256 concurrent tasks iterates only 1000 items, comparing non-fair (default) and fair semaphores. (§13.3 explains fair versus non-fair queuing.)

It is possible to reduce the range by forcing more fairness in concurrency control — easy here, by initialising the semaphores in fair mode. That succeeds in greatly reducing variance, but also greatly reduces throughput. (A longer-running test with more typical tasks would probably show an even larger throughput reduction.) Note the absolute numbers: the fair run is roughly forty times slower in the mean, and that is the price of the predictability.

Where does the fairness cost come from? Mostly from blocking. Very small buffer sizes cause heavy context switching and poor throughput even in non-fair mode, because nearly every operation involves a context switch. Rerun with a buffer of one and non-fair semaphores perform comparably to fair ones — fairness does not make the average much worse, or the variance much better, when everyone is blocking anyway.

So, unless threads are continually blocking anyway because of tight synchronization requirements, non-fair semaphores give much better throughput and fair semaphores give lower variance. Because the results are so dramatically different, Semaphore forces its clients to choose which of the two to optimise for.

12.3Avoiding Performance Testing Pitfalls

In theory, performance testing is easy: find a typical usage scenario, run it many times, time it. In practice there are five ways the JVM quietly invalidates the number you just wrote down.

12.3.1Garbage Collection

Collection timing is unpredictable, so a collection may run during a measured trial. If N iterations trigger no collection but N + 1 would, a small change in the size of the run can have a big and entirely spurious effect on the measured time per iteration.

There are two strategies. One is to ensure collection does not run at all during the test — run the JVM with -verbose:gc to find out. The other is to make sure the collector runs several times during the run, so the measurement includes the real cost of ongoing allocation. The second is usually better: it needs a longer test, and it reflects real-world performance far more closely. Most producer–consumer applications allocate steadily — producers create objects that consumers use and discard — so running the buffer test long enough to incur multiple collections yields more accurate results.

12.3.2Dynamic Compilation

Benchmarking a dynamically compiled language is far harder than benchmarking C or C++. HotSpot interprets bytecode at first; when a method runs often enough, the dynamic compiler converts it to machine code and the JVM switches to direct execution. The timing of that switch is unpredictable, and it matters: there is no value in measuring interpreted code, since most programs run long enough that every frequently executed path is compiled.

Compilation biases a measured run in two ways: it consumes CPU, and the result is a meaningless blend of interpreted and compiled execution. Code can also be decompiled and recompiled — when a class load invalidates assumptions a prior compilation made, or when profiling data justifies different optimisations.

Two defences. Run for a long time — at least several minutes — so compilation and interpretation are a small fraction of the total. Or use an unmeasured warm-up run, executing the code enough to be fully compiled before timing begins; on HotSpot, -XX:+PrintCompilation prints a message when dynamic compilation runs, so you can verify it happened before, not during, the measured runs.

Running the same test several times in the same JVM also validates the methodology: discard the first group as warm-up, and treat inconsistent results in the remaining groups as a signal that the test needs explaining before its numbers can be trusted. And because the JVM runs background housekeeping threads, put explicit pauses between unrelated measured trials so the JVM can catch up with minimal interference. (Between runs of the same test, excluding those background tasks this way can produce unrealistically optimistic results.)

12.3.3Unrealistic Sampling of Code Paths

Runtime compilers use profiling information, so the same method may compile differently in two programs. The JVM may even optimise on assumptions that are only temporarily true and back them out later by invalidating the compiled code — for example, converting a virtual call into a direct call when no loaded class overrides the method, then undoing it if such a class is subsequently loaded.

So your tests must approximate not only the usage patterns of a real application but the set of code paths it takes. Otherwise a dynamic compiler can make special optimisations to a purely single-threaded test that could never apply in a real application containing at least occasional parallelism. Tests of multithreaded performance should therefore be mixed with single-threaded tests, even when single-threaded performance is all you want to measure. (This does not affect TimedPutTakeTest, whose smallest case already uses two threads.)

12.3.4Unrealistic Degrees of Contention

Concurrent applications interleave two very different kinds of work: accessing shared data — fetching the next task from a shared queue — and thread-local computation, executing the task. The proportion determines the contention level and hence the performance and scaling behaviour.

If N threads fetch compute-intensive, long-running tasks that seldom touch shared data, there is almost no contention and throughput is dominated by CPU availability. If the tasks are very short-lived, contention for the work queue dominates and throughput is dominated by the cost of synchronization. Neither measurement tells you anything about the other system.

To get realistic results, a concurrent performance test should approximate the thread-local computation of a typical application in addition to the coordination under study. Get the balance wrong and it is easy to draw unwarranted conclusions about where the bottleneck is. §11.5 made the point with the synchronized Map implementations: those tests do nothing but pound on the map, so even with two threads every access is contended — while an application doing significant thread-local work between accesses might see almost no contention at all. TimedPutTakeTest may be a poor model for some applications for the same reason: its workers do so little that coordination overhead dominates.

12.3.5Dead Code Elimination

Optimising compilers are good at spotting and eliminating code that has no effect on the outcome. Benchmarks often compute nothing, which makes them an easy target. If you are lucky the optimiser prunes the entire program and the bogus data is obvious; if you are unlucky, it speeds your program up by some plausible factor and you believe the number.

This is a problem in statically compiled languages too, but there you can look at the machine code and see what is missing. With dynamic compilation that information is not easily accessible. Many micro-benchmarks therefore perform much "better" with HotSpot's -server compiler than with -client — not only because the server compiler produces better code, but because it is more adept at eliminating dead code. That same elimination will not do quite so well on code that actually does something, so you should still prefer -server for production and testing on multiprocessor systems — you just have to write tests that cannot be optimised away.

The requirement: every computed result must be used somehow, in a way that needs neither synchronization nor substantial computation. In PutTakeTest the checksums are used, because the test needs them to verify correctness; but a value that is never used can still be optimised away. Printing it out guarantees the use — but do not do I/O while the test is running, or you distort the measurement.

A cheap trick for preventing a calculation from being optimised away without much overhead is to compute the hashCode of a derived object's field, compare it to an arbitrary value such as the current System.nanoTime, and print an ignorable message if they happen to match:

EXCERPT From the text · keeping a result alive 
if (foo.x.hashCode() == System.nanoTime())
    System.out.print(" ");

The comparison will rarely succeed, and if it does, the only effect is to insert a harmless space into the output — print buffers until println, so in the rare case that hashCode and nanoTime are equal no I/O is actually performed.

Not only should every computed result be used, it should also be unguessable — otherwise an optimising compiler is allowed to replace the computation with pre-computed results. PutTakeTest was built that way; any test program with static input data is vulnerable.

12.4Complementary Testing Approaches

"Find all the bugs" is not an achievable goal. The goal is confidence — and confidence is bought from several vendors, not just one.

NASA devotes more of its engineering resources to testing than any commercial entity could afford — an estimated twenty testers for every developer — and the code it produces still is not free of defects. In complex programs, no amount of testing finds all coding errors.

So the goal of testing is not so much to find errors as to increase confidence that the code works as expected. Given that you cannot find everything, a QA plan should achieve the greatest possible confidence with the resources available. Concurrent programs have more ways to go wrong than sequential ones, so they need more testing for the same confidence — and testing should be only one of the methodologies you employ. Different methodologies find different kinds of defect; code review and static analysis add confidence that no single approach can.

12.4.1Code Review

As effective as unit and stress tests are, they are no substitute for rigorous review by multiple people — and review is no substitute for testing either. Design tests to maximise the chance of discovering safety errors and run them frequently, but do not neglect to have concurrent code reviewed carefully by someone other than its author. Even concurrency experts make mistakes; expert concurrent programmers are better at finding subtle races than most test programs are. Platform issues — JVM implementation details, processor memory models — can also keep bugs from showing up on a particular hardware or software configuration, while a reviewer can spot them by reading.

Review has a second payoff: it usually improves the quality of the comments that describe implementation details, which lowers future maintenance cost and risk.

12.4.2Static Analysis Tools

Static analysis examines code without executing it. Tools such as the open-source FindBugs contain bug-pattern detectors for many common coding errors, several of which testing and review both tend to miss. They produce a list of warnings that must be examined by hand; historically tools like lint produced so many false alarms that developers stopped reading them, but FindBugs has been tuned to produce far fewer. The tools remain somewhat primitive, especially in their integration with development lifecycle, but are already effective enough to be a valuable addition.

🔒
Inconsistent synchronization

A field that is usually, but not always, accessed with the object's intrinsic lock held. Analysis tools must guess the synchronization policy, because Java classes have no formal concurrency specification — if @GuardedBy-style annotations were standardised, the guessing would stop and the analysis would get much better.

▶️
Invoking Thread.run

Thread implements Runnable, so it has a run method — but calling it directly instead of start runs the body on the caller's thread. Almost always a mistake.

🔓
Unreleased lock

Unlike intrinsic locks, an explicit Lock is not released when control leaves the scope where it was acquired. The idiom is finally; miss it and an exception leaves the lock held forever.

🕳️
Empty synchronized block

Empty blocks do have semantics under the memory model, but they are frequently used incorrectly, and there is usually a better solution to whatever the developer meant.

🪞
Double-checked locking

A broken idiom for cheap lazy initialisation: it reads a shared mutable field without appropriate synchronisation. §16.2.4 revisits it.

🏃
Starting a thread from a constructor

Introduces subclassing hazards and can let the this reference escape the constructor before the object is fully built.

📣
Notification errors

notify/notifyAll should only be called when the state behind the condition queue has changed. A synchronized block that signals but modifies nothing is probably a bug.

🔄
Condition wait errors

wait/await belongs in a loop, with the lock held, after testing a state predicate. Without the lock, without the loop, or without the predicate is almost certainly wrong.

🧩
Misusing Lock and Condition

Passing a Lock to a synchronized block is a typo; so is calling Condition.wait instead of await — though the latter announces itself with an IllegalMonitorStateException the first time it runs.

😴
Sleeping or waiting while holding a lock

Thread.sleep with a lock held can block everyone else for a long time — a serious liveness hazard. Waiting with two locks held is the same hazard with a bow on it.

🌀
Spin loops

Busy-waiting on a field wastes CPU and, if the field is not volatile, is not guaranteed to terminate. A latch or a condition wait is almost always better.

12.4.3Aspect-Oriented Testing Techniques

AOP has only limited applicability to concurrency so far, because most popular tools cannot place pointcuts at synchronization points. It can, however, be used to assert invariants or to check compliance with synchronization policies. Laddad (2003) shows an aspect that wraps every call to a non-thread-safe Swing method with an assertion that the call is happening on the event thread — requiring no code changes to production classes, and disclosing subtle publication and thread-confinement errors. The same weaving trick is what makes §12.1.6's Thread.yield calls practical: add them in the test build, omit them from the shipped one.

12.4.4Profilers and Monitoring Tools

Most commercial profilers have some thread support. Their feature sets vary, but they can show a timeline per thread with different colours for the thread states — runnable, blocked on a lock, blocked on I/O — which reveals how well the program uses the available CPUs, and where to look when it does not. Profilers are usually intrusive, though, and can substantially affect timing and behaviour; and the "which lock is contended" features are often a blunter instrument than the question requires.

The built-in JMX agent offers limited monitoring without an external tool. ThreadInfo includes the thread's current state and, if it is blocked, the lock or condition queue it is blocked on. If "thread contention monitoring" is enabled — it is off by default because of its performance cost — ThreadInfo also reports how many times the thread has blocked waiting for a lock or notification, and the cumulative time spent waiting.

Summary of the chapter

Testing concurrent programs for correctness can be extremely challenging because many of the possible failure modes are low-probability events sensitive to timing, load and other hard-to-reproduce conditions. Worse, the testing infrastructure itself can introduce synchronization or timing constraints that mask concurrency problems in the code being tested. Testing for performance is equally tricky: Java is harder to benchmark than C, because measurements are affected by dynamic compilation, garbage collection and adaptive optimisation. To have the best chance of finding latent bugs before they occur in production, combine traditional testing — carefully avoiding the pitfalls above — with code reviews and automated analysis tools. Each of these techniques finds problems the others are likely to miss.

▶Interactive: how many runs does a race need?

A concurrent bug that fires two percent of the time is, from your test suite's point of view, indistinguishable from a program that works. Step through test-suite runs for four different disclosure probabilities and watch the confidence climb — and the number of runs you would actually need.

test-suite runs →
run

verdictidle
A rare race (p = 2% per run): step through runs and watch how slowly confidence climbs.
Disclosure probability per runRuns for 95% confidenceConfidence after 10 runsConfidence after 40 runsWhat a green suite means
2% (rare race)14918.3%55.4%Almost nothing

📐

The arithmetic is just 1 − (1 − p)runs, but the conclusion is not: no failures observed is not no bugs present. A rare race at p = 2% survives forty green runs more than half the time, and forty runs is already far more than most teams ever give a test. This is precisely why §12.4 exists — review and static analysis do not need the bug to be probable, only present.

§Patterns worth stealing

The thirteen listings above are the book's. These two are the shape the chapter keeps reaching for: a concurrent harness with a checksum and real coordination, and a JUnit-friendly wrapper that turns "it hung" into a failure instead of a stuck build.

1A race-hunting harness in one class

PATTERN Bounded-buffer stress test: barrier start, per-thread checksum, deterministic finish 
/**
 * A test that hunts for races instead of checking a line. Run it with more
 * threads than CPUs and it will eventually trip an unsynchronized buffer.
 */
public final class BufferStress {
    private static final int PAIRS = 8;          // 16 workers + driver
    private static final int TRIALS = 100_000;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newCachedThreadPool();
        try {
            AtomicInteger checkSum = new AtomicInteger();
            CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(PAIRS * 2 + 1);
            BoundedBuffer<Integer> bb = new BoundedBuffer<>(10);

            for (int i = 0; i < PAIRS; i++) {
                pool.execute(() -> {                 // producer
                    try {
                        int seed = (int) System.nanoTime();
                        int sum = 0;
                        barrier.await();             // everyone starts together
                        for (int n = 0; n < TRIALS; n++) {
                            bb.put(seed);
                            sum += seed;
                            seed = xorShift(seed);   // unguessable: not precomputed
                        }
                        checkSum.addAndGet(sum);     // commutative combine
                        barrier.await();
                    } catch (Exception e) {
                        throw new RuntimeException(e);
                    }
                });
                pool.execute(() -> {                 // consumer
                    try {
                        int sum = 0;
                        barrier.await();
                        for (int n = 0; n < TRIALS; n++)
                            sum += bb.take();
                        checkSum.addAndGet(-sum);    // consumers subtract
                        barrier.await();
                    } catch (Exception e) {
                        throw new RuntimeException(e);
                    }
                });
            }

            barrier.await();                         // all ready
            long start = System.nanoTime();
            barrier.await();                         // all finished
            double secs = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e9;

            if (checkSum.get() != 0)                 // the whole point
                throw new AssertionError("put/take mismatch: " + checkSum.get());
            System.out.printf("ok: %d pairs, %.1f M ops/s%n",
                    PAIRS, (2.0 * PAIRS * TRIALS / secs) / 1e6);
        } finally {
            pool.shutdownNow();
        }
    }

    /* cheap per-thread PRNG; a thread-safe Random would add a second
       contention point and hide the one we are trying to expose */
    static int xorShift(int y) {
        y ^= (y << 6);
        y ^= (y >>> 21);
        y ^= (y << 7);
        return y;
    }
}

Three things make this a concurrency test rather than a benchmark: the barrier guarantees overlap, the checksum is order-insensitive so it costs nothing per operation, and the finish condition is deterministic — exactly PAIRS × TRIALS items go in, so no coordination decides when to stop. Delete synchronized from doInsert/doExtract and it fails within seconds.

2Make a hang a failure, not a stuck build

PATTERN JUnit rule: everything that blocks gets a deadline and a diagnostic 
/**
 * Wraps potentially-blocking work with a deadline and reports WHAT did not
 * finish instead of leaving the build hanging.
 */
public final class Deadline {
    public static <T> T call(String what, long millis,
                             Callable<T> body) throws Exception {
        ExecutorService one = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> {
            Thread t = new Thread(r, "test:" + what);
            t.setDaemon(true);                 // do not keep the JVM alive
            return t;
        });
        Future<T> f = one.submit(body);
        try {
            return f.get(millis, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        } catch (TimeoutException e) {
            // dump every thread: the stuck stack is the bug report
            Map<Thread, StackTraceElement[]> traces = Thread.getAllStackTraces();
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(what + " did not finish in "
                    + millis + "ms\n");
            traces.forEach((t, st) -> {
                sb.append("\n\"").append(t.getName()).append("\" ").append(t.getState());
                for (StackTraceElement el : st) sb.append("\n    at ").append(el);
            });
            throw new AssertionError(sb.toString(), e);
        } finally {
            one.shutdownNow();
        }
    }

    /* usage: a blocking take() must be interrupted, not merely slow */
    public static void assertBlocks(Callable<?> op, long millis) throws Exception {
        boolean finished;
        try {
            call("blocking op", millis, op);
            finished = true;
        } catch (TimeoutException expected) {
            finished = false;
        }
        if (finished)
            throw new AssertionError("operation returned; it should have blocked");
    }
}

The point of the wrapper is the stack dump on timeout. A test that fails with TimeoutException after four minutes tells you nothing; a test that fails with every thread's state and stack tells you which lock, which condition and which thread was holding what. That is the difference between §12.1.2's LOCKUP_DETECT_TIMEOUT as a guess and as a diagnostic.

§Vocabulary introduced in Chapter 12

TermMeaning as used hereWhere it goes
HeisenbugA bug that disappears when you add debugging or test code — the central hazard of testing concurrency.Ch. 12 intro
ThroughputThe rate at which a set of concurrent tasks is completed.Ch. 12 intro
Responsiveness / latencyThe delay between a request and the completion of the action.Ch. 12 intro
ScalabilityThe improvement in throughput as more CPUs are added.Ch. 12 intro
Safety testChecks that invariants hold under concurrent load: nothing bad happens.Ch. 12.1.3
Liveness testChecks progress or non-progress — always requires a timeout you had to guess.Ch. 12.1.2
Order-sensitive checksumProves single-producer order: what went in came out, in sequence.Ch. 12.1.3
Commutative checksumAddition or XOR, so per-thread sums combine without a shared field.Ch. 12.1.3
Shadow listThe naive alternative to checksums; needs a lock, so it distorts the schedule it is meant to test.Ch. 12.1.3
xor-shiftThree shifts and XORs: the cheapest medium-quality PRNG (Marsaglia, 2003).Ch. 12.1.3
Starting gateA latch or barrier that holds workers until everyone is ready, so they actually overlap.Ch. 12.1.3
Barrier actionCode that runs at each barrier trip, in the last arriving thread — the cheapest timer available.Ch. 12.2.1
Deterministic terminationA finish condition that needs no coordination: N producers × N trials = N consumers × N trials.Ch. 12.1.3
Storage leakA retained reference that prevents reclamation — the reason items[i] = null matters here.Ch. 12.1.4
TestingThreadFactoryA factory that counts threads, so pool policy can be asserted.Ch. 12.1.4
Warm-up runAn unmeasured execution that gets everything compiled before timing starts.Ch. 12.3.2
DecompilationReverting compiled code to interpreted execution when assumptions are invalidated.Ch. 12.3.2
Monomorphic call transformationTurning a virtual call into a direct call while no loaded class overrides it.Ch. 12.3.3
Dead code eliminationThe optimiser removing work whose result nobody reads — including your whole benchmark.Ch. 12.3.5
ThreadInfoJMX's per-thread view: state, blocking lock or condition, contention counts if enabled.Ch. 12.4.4

✓Cheat sheet & self-check

SymptomLikely causeFix
Test passes locally, fails in production under loadRare interleaving; your suite never reached itMore threads than CPUs, longer runs, barrier starts, Thread.yield in critical sections
Bug vanishes when you add loggingHeisenbug: the instrumentation changed the scheduleRemove the I/O; inject yields or use AOP so the perturbation is deliberate and uniform
A blocking test passes when it should failThe "wait until it blocks" sleep was too short — or the method never blockedInterrupt and assert InterruptedException + timed join; never assert on Thread.getState
Test hangs forever on a bugFixed-operation count with no deadlineFramework timeout plus a thread dump; make the failure diagnosable
Suspiciously good benchmark numbersDead code eliminatedUse every result; compare against System.nanoTime(); never use static input data
First run slow, later runs fastInterpreted then compiled executionWarm up; check with -XX:+PrintCompilation; discard the first group
Numbers vary wildly between runsGC landed inside the measurement window-verbose:gc; run long enough that collections are part of the average, not a surprise
Buffer test scales perfectly, application does notTest has no thread-local work, so contention is unrealisticAdd the compute the real consumers do; measure the mix, not the coordination alone
Fair semaphores look "better"You measured variance, not throughputDecide which you are optimising; fair mode traded ~40× the mean for a range of 13 ms
Pool grows past its core size in production but not in testsTasks finished before the expansion could be observedLong-running tasks plus a retry loop before the assertion
✅
Do

Write the sequential tests first. Use checksums, not shadow structures. Start every worker at a barrier so the run actually overlaps. Run with more threads than CPUs. Give every blocking test a deadline and a diagnostic. Warm up before you time anything.

🚫
Avoid

Asserting on Thread.getState. General-purpose RNGs in the hot path. Static input data. Printing inside a measured run. Concluding "correct" from "green". Trusting a single run of anything concurrent.

🧠
The one habit

Before you trust a concurrent test, ask what it would take for the bug to be likely in this run — and before you trust a performance number, ask what else the JVM was doing while you measured. Both questions are the same question: what changed the schedule?

Five questions the chapter leaves you with

  1. How many runs of my concurrency suite would it take to reach 95% confidence — and do I run that many?
  2. Which of my assertions would pass even if the class were completely unsynchronized?
  3. Does my safety check add synchronization to the code path it is checking?
  4. Is my benchmark measuring the handoff, or the work — and which one do I actually care about?
  5. When did a reviewer last read this code, as opposed to a test exercising it?

Notes carried over from the chapter

  1. Bugs that disappear when you add debugging or test code are playfully called Heisenbugs.
  2. In a counting semaphore, permits are not represented explicitly or associated with an owning thread; a release creates a permit and an acquire consumes one.
  3. The JSR 166 test base class: JSR166TestCase.java, from the conformance test suite for java.util.concurrent.
  4. Many benchmarks are, unbeknownst to their developers or users, simply tests of how great a concurrency bottleneck the RNG is.
  5. Technically it is impossible to force a garbage collection; System.gc only suggests it, and HotSpot can be told to ignore the call with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC.
  6. You might be able to outperform the library queues if you both are a concurrency expert and can give up some of the provided functionality.
  7. The JVM may perform compilation in the application thread or in a background thread; each can bias timing results in different ways.
  8. For example, the JVM can use monomorphic call transformation to convert a virtual method call to a direct call if no loaded class overrides that method — and invalidates the compiled code if one is later loaded.
  9. FindBugs: http://findbugs.sourceforge.net.
