Java Concurrency in Practice · Chapter 13

Chapter 13 — Explicit Locks

Java 5.0 added ReentrantLock, and a decade of blog posts promptly got it wrong: it is not a replacement for synchronized. It is an alternative that buys three things intrinsic locking cannot give you — an interruptible wait, a wait you can give up on, and a lock you can hold across block boundaries — at the price of doing the cleanup yourself. The chapter ends with the one place where relaxing mutual exclusion genuinely helps: read–write locks for read–mostly data.

📖 pp. 171–178 🧩 5 sections · 7 listings · 3 figures ⏱️ ~20 min read 🏷️ Part IV — Advanced Topics

Chapter in one paragraph

TL;DR — the six things worth remembering

  1. ReentrantLock is an alternative, not an upgrade. Same mutual exclusion, same memory semantics, same reentrancy as synchronized — plus four acquisition modes and a Condition factory. Take it when you need one of those; otherwise stay with synchronized.
  2. Release in finally, always. Intrinsic locks are released automatically on any exit from the block. An explicit Lock is not. Forget once and you have a lock that is never released — a time bomb whose origin leaves no trace.
  3. Polling and timing beat deadlock. tryLock lets you acquire what you can, back off, and return false instead of hanging forever. That is the only in-band recovery from lock-ordering deadlock the language offers.
  4. Interruptibility is a liveness feature. lockInterruptibly makes a lock wait cancellable — the piece §7.1.6 was missing when it listed lock acquisition as non-interruptible blocking.
  5. Fairness costs about two orders of magnitude. Fair locks queue everyone; non-fair locks let a thread barge when the holder has just released and the next waiter is still waking up. Statistical fairness is almost always enough.
  6. Read–write locks trade complexity for reader concurrency. Many readers or one writer, never both. On read–mostly data on multiprocessors this wins; otherwise it loses slightly to a plain lock. Measure.

13.1Lock and ReentrantLock

Before Java 5.0 the only tools for coordinating shared state were synchronized and volatile. The Lock interface adds a third, and its whole reason for existing is the shape of the operations rather than their semantics.

Lock offers a choice of unconditional, polled, timed and interruptible acquisition, and makes every lock and unlock explicit. Implementations must provide the same memory-visibility semantics as intrinsic locks, but may differ in scheduling algorithm, ordering guarantees and performance.

BOOK Listing 13.1 · Lock interface 
public interface Lock {
    void lock();
    void lockInterruptibly() throws InterruptedException;
    boolean tryLock();
    boolean tryLock(long timeout, TimeUnit unit)
        throws InterruptedException;
    void unlock();
    Condition newCondition();
}

ReentrantLock implements Lock, providing the same mutual exclusion and visibility guarantees as synchronized: acquiring it has the same memory semantics as entering a synchronized block, releasing it as exiting one, and it is reentrant in the same sense (§2.3.2).

Why create something so similar? Because intrinsic locking has functional limits. You cannot interrupt a thread waiting for an intrinsic lock. You cannot attempt to acquire one without being willing to wait forever. And an intrinsic lock must be released in the same block in which it was acquired — which simplifies coding and interacts nicely with exceptions, but makes non-block-structured locking impossible. None of that is a reason to abandon synchronized; it is a reason for a second tool.

BOOK Listing 13.2 · Guarding object state using ReentrantLock 
Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();
...
lock.lock();
try {
    // update object state
    // catch exceptions and restore invariants if necessary
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}

That finally is not stylistic. Without it, an exception in the guarded code leaves the lock held forever. And while using a lock you must also think about what happens if an exception escapes the try block: if the object could be left inconsistent, you may need an additional try–catch to restore invariants before releasing.

💣

Failing to use finally to release a Lock is a ticking time bomb. When it goes off you will have a hard time tracking down its origin, because there is no record of where or when the lock should have been released. This is the main reason not to use ReentrantLock as a blanket substitute for synchronized: it is more dangerous precisely because it does not clean up for you. FindBugs has an "unreleased lock" detector for exactly this.

13.1.1Polled and Timed Lock Acquisition

Timed and polled acquisition allow more sophisticated error recovery than unconditional acquisition. With intrinsic locks a deadlock is fatal: the only recovery is restarting the application, and the only defence is constructing the program so inconsistent lock ordering is impossible. Timed and polled locking add a third option: probabilistic deadlock avoidance.

tryLock lets you regain control if you cannot acquire all the required locks, release the ones you did acquire, and try again — or log the failure and do something else. The transfer below is the same dynamic-ordering problem from §10.1.2, solved by backing off instead of by ordering. The sleep has a fixed component and a random component, to reduce the chance of livelock; if the locks cannot be acquired within the specified time, transferMoney returns a failure status so the operation can fail gracefully.

BOOK Listing 13.3 · Avoiding lock-ordering deadlock using tryLock 
public boolean transferMoney(Account fromAcct,
                             Account toAcct,
                             DollarAmount amount,
                             long timeout,
                             TimeUnit unit)
        throws InsufficientFundsException, InterruptedException {
    long fixedDelay = getFixedDelayComponentNanos(timeout, unit);
    long randMod = getRandomDelayModulusNanos(timeout, unit);
    long stopTime = System.nanoTime() + unit.toNanos(timeout);

    while (true) {
        if (fromAcct.lock.tryLock()) {
            try {
                if (toAcct.lock.tryLock()) {
                    try {
                        if (fromAcct.getBalance().compareTo(amount)
                                < 0)
                            throw new InsufficientFundsException();
                        else {
                            fromAcct.debit(amount);
                            toAcct.credit(amount);
                            return true;
                        }
                    } finally {
                        toAcct.lock.unlock();
                    }
                }
            } finally {
                fromAcct.lock.unlock();
            }
        }
        if (System.nanoTime() < stopTime)
            return false;
        NANOSECONDS.sleep(fixedDelay + rnd.nextLong() % randMod);
    }
}

Note the nesting: two tryLock calls, two finally blocks, and the inner one unlocks before the outer. Read the failure path too — if the second lock is unavailable, the outer finally releases the first, the loop back offs, and the whole cycle repeats until the deadline. The lock ordering never had to be consistent, because no thread ever waits indefinitely.

Timed locks are also the tool for time budgets (§6.3.7). When an activity with a budget calls a blocking method, it can supply a timeout equal to the remaining budget, and terminate early if it cannot deliver in time. With intrinsic locks there is no way to cancel a lock acquisition once it has started — which puts time-budgeted activities at risk.

Concretely: the travel portal of Listing 6.17 creates a task per car-rental company, and soliciting a bid may need exclusive access to a scarce resource such as a dedicated communications line. A single-threaded executor (§9.5) is one way to serialise that access; an explicit lock is the other — and only the explicit lock can be given a deadline.

BOOK Listing 13.4 · Locking with a time budget 
public boolean trySendOnSharedLine(String message,
                                   long timeout, TimeUnit unit)
                                   throws InterruptedException {
    long nanosToLock = unit.toNanos(timeout)
                     - estimatedNanosToSend(message);
    if (!lock.tryLock(nanosToLock, NANOSECONDS))
        return false;
    try {
        return sendOnSharedLine(message);
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}

The subtraction is the whole idea: the lock may consume only the part of the budget that sending the message will not need. Asking for the full timeout would let a thread that eventually gets the lock blow the deadline anyway.

13.1.2Interruptible Lock Acquisition

Just as timed acquisition lets exclusive locking be used inside time-limited activities, interruptible acquisition lets it be used inside cancellable ones. §7.1.6 listed acquiring an intrinsic lock among the mechanisms that are not responsive to interruption, which complicates cancellable tasks. lockInterruptibly closes that gap and — just as importantly — avoids adding another category of non-interruptible blocking to the language.

BOOK Listing 13.5 · Interruptible lock acquisition 
public boolean sendOnSharedLine(String message)
        throws InterruptedException {
    lock.lockInterruptibly();
    try {
        return cancellableSendOnSharedLine(message);
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}

private boolean cancellableSendOnSharedLine(String message)
    throws InterruptedException { ... }

The canonical structure is slightly more complicated than ordinary acquisition, because two try blocks are needed — unless the interruptible acquisition itself can throw InterruptedException, in which case the standard try–finally idiom works unchanged, as here. The timed tryLock is also responsive to interruption, so it serves when you need both properties at once.

13.1.3Non-block-structured Locking

With intrinsic locks, acquire–release pairs are block-structured: a lock is always released in the same basic block in which it was acquired, however control leaves that block. Automatic release simplifies analysis and prevents a whole class of coding errors — and sometimes a more flexible discipline is exactly what the algorithm needs.

Chapter 11 showed that reducing lock granularity improves scalability; lock striping gives different hash chains different locks. The same principle applied to a linked list gives each node its own lock, so different threads can work on different portions of the list at once. A node's lock guards its link pointers and its data, so while traversing or modifying you must hold the lock on one node until you have acquired the lock on the next — and only then may you release the first. That technique is called hand-over-hand locking or lock coupling ([CPJ 2.5.1.4]), and it cannot be expressed with intrinsic locks at all.

🤝

Hand-over-hand locking is a good example of a technique that looks strictly better and often is not: acquiring a lock per node costs more than a single lock for the whole list unless the list is long and the contention heavy. It belongs in the toolkit as an option you reach for after measuring, not as a default.

13.2Performance Considerations

The reason ReentrantLock spread so fast in 2004 was a benchmark. That benchmark is now history — and the lesson in that is worth more than the number was.

When ReentrantLock arrived it offered far better contended performance than intrinsic locking. Contended performance is the key to scalability for synchronization primitives: if more resources are spent on lock management and scheduling, fewer are available for the application. A better lock implementation makes fewer system calls, forces fewer context switches, and initiates less memory-synchronization traffic on the shared memory bus — all operations that are time-consuming and divert computing resources from the program.

Java 6 uses an improved algorithm for managing intrinsic locks, similar to the one ReentrantLock uses, which closes the scalability gap considerably. The figure below is the same test as §11.5 — a HashMap guarded by an intrinsic lock versus one guarded by a ReentrantLock — on a four-way Opteron running Solaris. The curves are the "speedup" of ReentrantLock over intrinsic locking within a single JVM version.

On Java 5.0, intrinsic locking's performance drops dramatically going from one thread (no contention) to more than one; ReentrantLock drops far less, showing its better scalability. On Java 6 it is a different story — intrinsic locks no longer fall apart under contention and the two scale similarly.

📉

Graphs like Figure 13.1 remind us that statements of the form "X is faster than Y" are at best short-lived. Performance and scalability are sensitive to platform factors — CPU, processor count, cache size, JVM characteristics — all of which change over time. The book's own footnote is the best line in the chapter: when the authors started, ReentrantLock seemed the last word in lock scalability; less than a year later intrinsic locking gave it a good run for its money. Performance is not just a moving target, it can be a fast-moving target.

13.3Fairness

The ReentrantLock constructor offers two modes, and the default is the one with the worse-sounding name. There is a reason.

A fair lock grants acquisition in the order threads requested it. A non-fair lock permits barging: a thread requesting the lock can jump ahead of the queue if the lock happens to be available when it asks. (Semaphore offers the same choice.) Non-fair locks do not go out of their way to promote barging — they simply do not prevent it. With a fair lock, a requesting thread is queued if the lock is held or if threads are already queued; with a non-fair lock, it is queued only if the lock is currently held.

Wouldn't we want all locks to be fair? After all, fairness is good and unfairness is bad — just ask your kids. When it comes to locking, though, fairness has a significant performance cost, because of the overhead of suspending and resuming threads. In practice a statistical fairness guarantee — promising that a blocked thread will eventually acquire the lock — is often good enough, and far less expensive to deliver. Some algorithms rely on fair queuing for correctness, but those are unusual.

Why does barging perform so much better under heavy contention? Because there is a significant delay between a suspended thread being resumed and actually running. Thread A holds the lock, thread B asks and is suspended. When A releases, B is resumed — but meanwhile thread C requests the lock and there is a good chance C acquires it, uses it and releases it before B has even finished waking up. Everyone wins: B gets the lock no later than it otherwise would, C gets it much earlier, and throughput improves.

Fair locks therefore work best when they are held for a relatively long time, or when the mean time between requests is relatively long — in those cases the window in which barging helps (the lock is unheld but somebody is still waking up to claim it) is less likely to exist. Intrinsic locking offers no deterministic fairness either; the language specification does not require fair intrinsic locks and no production JVM implements them. ReentrantLock does not depress fairness to new lows — it only makes explicit something that was present all along.

🧾

One asymmetry worth filing away: the polled tryLock always barges, even on a fair lock. If your correctness argument depends on fair ordering, it has to survive that.

13.4Choosing Between Synchronized and ReentrantLock

Both give the same mutual exclusion and visibility. The honest way to choose is to ask what you need, not what is allegedly faster.

ReentrantLock provides the same locking and memory semantics as intrinsic locking plus additional features: timed lock waits, interruptible lock waits, fairness, and non-block-structured locking. Its performance dominates — slightly on Java 6, dramatically on Java 5.0. So why not deprecate synchronized? Some authors have suggested exactly that, treating synchronized as a legacy construct. That takes a good thing much too far.

✍️
Intrinsic locks are the better default

The notation is familiar and compact, existing code already uses it, and mixing the two inside one class is confusing and error-prone. ReentrantLock is genuinely the more dangerous tool: forget the finally once and the failure is silent until it hurts an innocent bystander.

🔧
Reach for it for a reason

Save ReentrantLock for when you need something it provides that intrinsic locking does not: timed, polled or interruptible acquisition, fair queuing, or non-block-structured locking. Otherwise prefer synchronized.

🔎
Debuggability favours the intrinsic lock

On Java 5.0, thread dumps show which call frames acquired which locks and can detect deadlocked threads. The JVM knows nothing about which threads hold ReentrantLocks. Java 6 addresses this with a management and monitoring interface that locks can register with — but the non-block-structured nature of ReentrantLock still means acquisitions cannot be tied to specific stack frames.

🚀
The future is optimised for synchronized

Because synchronized is built into the JVM, it can get optimisations a library cannot — lock elision for thread-confined objects, lock coarsening (§11.3.2). So unless you are deploying on Java 5.0 for the foreseeable future, choosing ReentrantLock for performance is a mistake.

⚖️

Locking information in thread dumps has saved many programmers from utter consternation. That is a real engineering property, not a stylistic one — a tool that helps you diagnose the failure you cannot reproduce locally is worth measurable performance, especially when the performance difference has since evaporated.

13.5Read–write Locks

Mutual exclusion is often a stronger discipline than the data needs. For read–mostly structures, readers do not conflict with each other — so why make them queue?

ReentrantLock allows at most one holder. But mutual exclusion prevents reader/reader overlap as well as writer/writer and writer/reader overlap. Many data structures are read–mostly: mutable, sometimes modified, but most accesses only read. Relaxing the requirement so multiple readers can be in at once is safe as long as each thread sees up-to-date data and no thread modifies while readers are viewing. That is what a read–write lock provides: multiple readers or a single writer, never both.

BOOK Listing 13.6 · ReadWriteLock interface 
public interface ReadWriteLock {
    Lock readLock();
    Lock writeLock();
}

The two locks are different views of one integrated read–write lock object, not two independent locks. Like Lock, ReadWriteLock admits multiple implementations varying in performance, scheduling guarantees, acquisition preference, fairness or locking semantics.

Read–write locks are a performance optimisation, not a correctness tool. They can improve throughput for frequently accessed read–mostly data on multiprocessors; under other conditions they perform slightly worse than exclusive locks because of their greater complexity. Whether they help is best determined by profiling — and because ReadWriteLock exposes each half as a Lock, swapping a read–write lock back for an exclusive one is a small, local change.

Implementation questionWhat it decidesThe trap
Release preferenceWhen a writer releases and both readers and writers are queued, who goes first — readers, writers, or whoever asked first?No answer is right for every workload; a writer-preferring lock starves readers and vice versa.
Reader bargingIf readers hold the lock and writers are waiting, may newly arriving readers enter immediately?Barging raises concurrency and risks writer starvation.
ReentrancyAre the read and write locks reentrant?Reentrant readers complicate fairness, as Java 5.0 discovered.
DowngradingMay a thread holding the write lock acquire the read lock without releasing? This is the safe direction — it lets a writer keep other writers out while it finishes reading.
UpgradingMay a read lock be upgraded to a write lock, ahead of other waiters?Deadlock-prone and therefore unsupported: two readers upgrading simultaneously both hold read locks and neither will release.

ReentrantReadWriteLock provides reentrant semantics for both locks and can be constructed non-fair (the default) or fair. With a fair lock, preference goes to the longest-waiting thread: if readers hold the lock and a thread requests the write lock, no further readers may acquire the read lock until that writer has been served and released. With a non-fair lock the order is unspecified. Downgrading from writer to reader is permitted; upgrading is not, and attempting it deadlocks.

As with ReentrantLock, the write lock has a unique owner and can be released only by the thread that acquired it. In Java 5.0 the read lock behaved more like a semaphore, tracking only the number of active readers and not their identities; Java 6 also tracks which threads hold the read lock. (One reason for the change: without that identity the implementation cannot tell a first request from a reentrant one, which would make fair read–write locks deadlock-prone.)

BOOK Listing 13.7 · Wrapping a Map with a read–write lock 
public class ReadWriteMap<K,V> {
    private final Map<K,V> map;
    private final ReadWriteLock lock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
    private final Lock r = lock.readLock();
    private final Lock w = lock.writeLock();

    public ReadWriteMap(Map<K,V> map) {
        this.map = map;
    }

    public V put(K key, V value) {
        w.lock();
        try {
            return map.put(key, value);
        } finally {
            w.unlock();
        }
    }
    // Do the same for remove(), putAll(), clear()

    public V get(Object key) {
        r.lock();
        try {
            return map.get(key);
        } finally {
            r.unlock();
        }
    }
    // Do the same for other read-only Map methods
}

ReadWriteMap does not implement Map, because implementing the view methods (entrySet, values) would be difficult and the "easy" methods are usually sufficient. And in reality ConcurrentHashMap is so good that you would use it for a concurrent hash-based map; the technique is worth having when you want to expose an alternate Map implementation such as LinkedHashMap concurrently.

Read–write locks improve concurrency when locks are typically held for a moderately long time and most operations do not modify the guarded resource. That is exactly the shape of the benchmark in the figure: many searches, a few modifications — which is why the read–write version keeps climbing while the exclusive one saturates at one process's worth of work.

Summary of the chapter

Explicit locks offer an extended feature set compared with intrinsic locking, including greater flexibility in dealing with lock unavailability and greater control over queuing behaviour. But ReentrantLock is not a blanket substitute for synchronized; use it only when you need features that synchronized lacks. Read–write locks let multiple readers access a guarded object concurrently, offering the potential for improved scalability when accessing read–mostly data structures.

▶Interactive: one lock, four ways to ask for it

Thread A holds the lock until tick 8. Thread B wants it from tick 1. Pick the acquisition method and step through the timeline: H is A holding, U is A unlocking, w is B waiting, L is B holding the lock, ✓ is B done and ✗ is B giving up.

🎛️

Only the middle two modes are about speed; the outer two are about control. lock() gives you no way to stop waiting, which is why a deadlock on intrinsic or unconditional locks is fatal and why §13.1.1 calls timed acquisition "probabilistic deadlock avoidance". tryLock() gives you no waiting at all, which is either exactly what you want (a back-off loop) or exactly what you do not (a hot spin).

§Patterns worth stealing

The seven listings above are the book's. These two are the shapes the chapter argues for in practice: a lock wrapper that cannot leak, and a back-off acquisition helper that returns a decision instead of throwing.

1A lock that cannot be forgotten

PATTERN try-with-lock: the finally block, written once 
/**
 * Acquire/release in one place, so no call site can forget the finally.
 * Bodies that throw still restore invariants: the catch runs before unlock.
 */
public final class With {
    private With() { }

    public interface Guarded<T> { T get(); }

    public static <T> T locked(Lock lock, Guarded<T> body) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            return body.get();
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();          // the whole pattern, right here
        }
    }

    /* interruptible variant: a cancellable task must not block uninterruptibly */
    public static <T> T lockedInterruptibly(Lock lock, Guarded<T> body)
            throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            return body.get();
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    /* timed variant: null instead of an unbounded wait */
    public static <T> T tryLocked(Lock lock, long timeout, TimeUnit unit,
                                  Guarded<T> body) throws InterruptedException {
        if (!lock.tryLock(timeout, unit))
            return null;                       // caller decides what "busy" means
        try {
            return body.get();
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
}

/* usage reads like the synchronized version it replaces */
Account snapshot = With.locked(account.lock, account::copyForStatement);

The value is not brevity. It is that every call site now has the same release path, and the one place where the unlock lives is small enough to review in a glance. The book's FindBugs "unreleased lock" detector is looking for exactly the mistake this shape makes impossible.

2Polled acquisition without livelock

PATTERN Two locks, deterministic deadline, randomised back-off 
/**
 * Try to hold both locks, or hold neither. Randomised back-off so two
 * polite threads do not keep retrying in lockstep (livelock).
 */
public boolean transfer(Account from, Account to, long amount,
                        long timeout, TimeUnit unit)
        throws InterruptedException {
    long deadline = System.nanoTime() + unit.toNanos(timeout);
    ThreadLocalRandom rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current();

    for (;;) {
        if (from.lock.tryLock()) {
            try {
                if (to.lock.tryLock()) {
                    try {
                        if (from.balance < amount)
                            return false;             // ordinary business failure
                        from.balance -= amount;
                        to.balance += amount;
                        return true;
                    } finally {
                        to.lock.unlock();
                    }
                }
            } finally {
                from.lock.unlock();                   // never hold one and wait
            }
        }
        long left = deadline - System.nanoTime();
        if (left <= 0)
            return false;                             // deadline, not deadlock
        TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.sleep(Math.min(left,
                TimeUnit.MICROSECONDS.toNanos(50 + rnd.nextInt(200))));
    }
}

Three properties make this safe and testable: the inner finally always releases before the outer one, the deadline is checked outside both locks so a failure cannot leave either held, and the back-off is bounded by the time remaining so the loop cannot overshoot its budget. It is Listing 13.3's idea with the housekeeping made explicit.

✓Cheat sheet & self-check

If you need…UseWhy not the other one
Plain mutual exclusionsynchronizedIntrinsic locks release automatically; explicit locks leak when you forget finally
A cancellable lock waitlockInterruptibly()An intrinsic lock wait ignores interruption — §7.1.6 lists it as non-interruptible blocking
Acquisition inside a time budgettryLock(timeout, unit)synchronized cannot be abandoned once started
Recovery from lock-ordering deadlocktryLock() plus back-offIntrinsic-lock deadlock is fatal; only a restart clears it
Non-block-structured acquire/releaseLockIntrinsic locks must be released in the acquiring block

✅
Do

Write the finally block before the guarded body. Use the timed or interruptible variant when the caller has a deadline or a cancel button. Give back-off loops a random component and a hard deadline. Prefer synchronized unless you can name the feature you need.

🚫
Avoid

Swapping every synchronized for a ReentrantLock "for performance". Fair locks on a hot path. Upgrading a read lock. Returning from inside try without a finally. Holding one lock while waiting for another inside a retry loop.

🧠
The one habit

Before switching to an explicit lock, finish this sentence: "I need ______, which synchronized cannot give me." If the blank is "speed", the answer is no — on Java 6 intrinsic locking is close, and it is the one the JVM is allowed to optimise.

Five questions the chapter leaves you with

  1. Which of my lock acquisitions could hang forever, and which of them could be given a deadline instead?
  2. Does every Lock in this code base have exactly one release path, inside a finally?
  3. Can any of my tasks be cancelled while they are waiting for a lock — and do they notice?
  4. If I turned fairness on tomorrow, what would that do to throughput?
  5. Is my "read-mostly" structure actually read-mostly, or did I assume it?

Notes carried over from the chapter

  1. FindBugs has an "unreleased lock" detector identifying when a Lock is not released on all code paths out of the block in which it was acquired.
  2. Though this particular graph does not show it, the scalability difference between Java 5.0 and Java 6 really does come from improvement in intrinsic locking, rather than from a regression in ReentrantLock.
  3. When the authors started the book, ReentrantLock seemed the last word in lock scalability. Less than a year later, intrinsic locking gives it a good run for its money. Performance is not just a moving target, it can be a fast-moving target.
  4. The polled tryLock always barges, even for fair locks.
  5. The ConcurrentHashMap curve is fairly wiggly between four and eight threads; those variations almost certainly come from measurement noise — hash codes, scheduling, map resizing, garbage collection, or the OS running periodic housekeeping. Real-world performance measurements are full of noise, and the authors made no attempt to clean their graphs artificially.
  6. Under Java 5.0 the lock implementation cannot distinguish between a thread requesting the read lock for the first time and a reentrant lock request, which would make fair read–write locks deadlock-prone.
  7. ReadWriteMap does not implement Map because implementing the view methods such as entrySet and values would be difficult, and the "easy" methods are usually sufficient.

Java Concurrency in Practice · Chapter 14

Chapter 14 — Building Custom Synchronizers

A state-dependent class is one whose operations have state-based preconditions: you cannot take from an empty queue, or read a result that is not finished. Sequentially, such a precondition that fails will never come true — so fail fast. Concurrently, another thread can make it true, so the right answer is usually to wait. This chapter is about the machinery behind that wait: condition predicates, condition queues, and the AbstractQueuedSynchronizer that every blocking class in java.util.concurrent is built on.

📖 pp. 179–194 🧩 6 sections · 16 listings · 1 figure ⏱️ ~30 min read 🏷️ Part IV — Advanced Topics

Chapter in one paragraph

TL;DR — the six things worth remembering

  1. Blocking beats failing, and beats polling. Throwing BufferFullException pushes the state dependence onto every caller; sleeping and re-checking costs CPU or responsiveness. A condition queue makes a thread sleep until exactly the interesting thing happens.
  2. Name the condition predicate. It is the precondition that makes the operation state-dependent (not-full, not-empty, opened-since-n). It appears nowhere in the API, nothing enforces it, and without it every wait is guesswork.
  3. Always while, never if. A wakeup does not mean your predicate is true: the queue may be shared by several predicates, and wait may return spuriously. Test, wait, re-test.
  4. Missed signals are a liveness bug. Notification is not sticky. If a thread waits without first testing the predicate, an event that already happened will never wake it — the toaster rang while you were out.
  5. Prefer notifyAll; use notify only under two conditions. Uniform waiters and one-in, one-out. Most classes satisfy neither, and a single notification then hijacks a signal meant for someone else.
  6. AQS is the one synchronizer underneath. One int of state, a FIFO queue, and tryAcquire/tryRelease. Locks, semaphores, latches, barriers, futures and read–write locks all delegate to it in about twenty lines each.

14.1Managing State Dependence

The easiest way to build a state-dependent class is to build on one that already exists. The rest of this section is what it costs when you cannot.

The class libraries include a number of state-dependent classes — FutureTask, Semaphore, BlockingQueue — with operations having state-based preconditions. You cannot remove an item from an empty queue or retrieve the result of an unfinished task: before those operations can proceed, you must wait until the queue enters the "nonempty" state or the task enters the "completed" state.

In a single-threaded program, a failing precondition will never become true, so classes can simply fail. In a concurrent program, state-based conditions change through the actions of other threads: a pool that was empty a few instructions ago can become nonempty because another thread returned an element. State-dependent methods can sometimes get away with failing, but there is often a better alternative — wait for the precondition to become true. Operations that block until they can proceed are more convenient and less error-prone than those that fail.

The structure of a blocking state-dependent action looks like this — and the locking pattern is unusual, because the lock is released and reacquired in the middle of the operation. The state variables that make up the precondition must be guarded by the object's lock so they can remain constant while it is tested; but if the precondition does not hold, the lock must be released so another thread can change the state — otherwise the precondition can never become true.

BOOK Listing 14.1 · Structure of blocking state-dependent actions 
void blockingAction() throws InterruptedException {
    acquire lock on object state
    while (precondition does not hold) {
        release lock
        wait until precondition might hold
        optionally fail if interrupted or timeout expires
        reacquire lock
    }
    perform action
}

The running example is a bounded buffer, whose put and take each have a precondition. All the implementations below extend BaseBoundedBuffer: a classic array-based circular buffer whose state variables (buf, head, tail, count) are guarded by the buffer's intrinsic lock. It provides synchronized doPut and doTake for subclasses, and hides the underlying state from them.

BOOK Listing 14.2 · Base class for bounded buffer implementations 
@ThreadSafe
public abstract class BaseBoundedBuffer<V> {
    @GuardedBy("this") private final V[] buf;
    @GuardedBy("this") private int tail;
    @GuardedBy("this") private int head;
    @GuardedBy("this") private int count;

    protected BaseBoundedBuffer(int capacity) {
        this.buf = (V[]) new Object[capacity];
    }

    protected synchronized final void doPut(V v) {
        buf[tail] = v;
        if (++tail == buf.length)
            tail = 0;
        ++count;
    }

    protected synchronized final V doTake() {
        V v = buf[head];
        buf[head] = null;
        if (++head == buf.length)
            head = 0;
        --count;
        return v;
    }

    public synchronized final boolean isFull() {
        return count == buf.length;
    }

    public synchronized final boolean isEmpty() {
        return count == 0;
    }
}

14.1.1Example: Propagating Precondition Failure to Callers

GrumpyBoundedBuffer is the crude first attempt. put and take are synchronized to ensure exclusive access, since both employ check-then-act logic.

BOOK Listing 14.3 · Bounded buffer that balks when preconditions are not met 
@ThreadSafe
public class GrumpyBoundedBuffer<V> extends BaseBoundedBuffer<V> {
    public GrumpyBoundedBuffer(int size) { super(size); }

    public synchronized void put(V v) throws BufferFullException {
        if (isFull())
            throw new BufferFullException();
        doPut(v);
    }

    public synchronized V take() throws BufferEmptyException {
        if (isEmpty())
            throw new BufferEmptyException();
        return doTake();
    }
}

Easy to implement, annoying to use. Exceptions are supposed to be for exceptional conditions; "buffer is full" is not exceptional for a bounded buffer any more than "red" is exceptional for a traffic light. The simplification in implementing the buffer is more than made up for by the complication in using it — every caller must be prepared to catch and retry.

BOOK Listing 14.4 · Client logic for calling GrumpyBoundedBuffer 
while (true) {
    try {
        V item = buffer.take();
        // use item
        break;
    } catch (BufferEmptyException e) {
        Thread.sleep(SLEEP_GRANULARITY);
    }
}

Returning an error value instead of throwing is a minor improvement — it does not abuse the exception mechanism — but it does not address the fundamental problem: callers still deal with precondition failures themselves. (Queue offers both options — poll returns null, remove throws — but Queue is not intended for producer–consumer designs; BlockingQueue is the better choice when producers and consumers run concurrently.)

Nor is retrying with a sleep the only option. The caller could retry immediately — busy waiting, or spin waiting — which can consume a lot of CPU if the state does not change for a while. Sleeping instead risks "oversleeping" if the state changes shortly after the sleep begins. The caller is left choosing between the poor CPU usage of spinning and the poor responsiveness of sleeping. (Somewhere between the two is Thread.yield, a hint to the scheduler that now would be a reasonable time to let another thread run.)

🚶

Pushing state dependence back to the caller also makes it nearly impossible to preserve FIFO ordering: by forcing the caller to retry, you lose the information about who arrived first.

14.1.2Example: Crude Blocking by Polling and Sleeping

SleepyBoundedBuffer spares callers the retry logic by encapsulating the same poll-and-sleep mechanism inside put and take — definitely a step in the right direction.

BOOK Listing 14.5 · Bounded buffer using crude blocking 
@ThreadSafe
public class SleepyBoundedBuffer<V> extends BaseBoundedBuffer<V> {
    public SleepyBoundedBuffer(int size) { super(size); }

    public void put(V v) throws InterruptedException {
        while (true) {
            synchronized (this) {
                if (!isFull()) {
                    doPut(v);
                    return;
                }
            }
            Thread.sleep(SLEEP_GRANULARITY);
        }
    }

    public V take() throws InterruptedException {
        while (true) {
            synchronized (this) {
                if (!isEmpty())
                    return doTake();
            }
            Thread.sleep(SLEEP_GRANULARITY);
        }
    }
}

The buffer code must test the appropriate state condition with the buffer lock held, because the variables that represent it are guarded by that lock. If the test fails, the thread sleeps — first releasing the lock so other threads can access the buffer. On waking it reacquires the lock and tries again. Sleeping with the lock held would be a bad idea anywhere; here it would be fatal, because the desired condition can never become true if the lock is not released.

From the caller's perspective this works nicely: the operation proceeds if it can and blocks otherwise, and the caller need not deal with failure and retry. Choosing the sleep granularity is a tradeoff between responsiveness and CPU usage — the smaller the granularity, the more responsive and the more CPU consumed. Figure 14.1 shows the cost of getting it wrong: a delay between the moment buffer space becomes available and the moment the thread wakes and checks again.

SleepyBoundedBuffer also creates a new requirement for the caller — dealing with InterruptedException. When a method blocks waiting for a condition, the polite thing to do is to provide a cancellation mechanism, so like most well-behaved blocking library methods, this buffer supports cancellation through interruption: return early, throw InterruptedException.

14.1.3Condition Queues to the Rescue

Synthesising a blocking operation from polling and sleeping was painful. What we want is a way of suspending a thread that guarantees it is awakened promptly when a condition becomes true. That is exactly what a condition queue does.

🍞

A condition queue is the "toast is ready" bell on your toaster. If you are listening, you are notified promptly and can drop what you are doing. If you are not listening — you went out for the newspaper — you may miss the notification, but on returning to the kitchen you can observe the state of the toaster and either retrieve the toast or start listening again. That observation is the condition predicate, and checking it before you wait is what makes the mechanism work.

A condition queue gives a group of threads — the wait set — a way to wait for a specific condition to become true. Unlike a typical queue whose elements are data items, the elements of a condition queue are the waiting threads.

Just as each object can act as a lock, each object can act as a condition queue, and wait, notify and notifyAll in Object are its API. Intrinsic lock and intrinsic condition queue are related: to call any of the condition queue methods on X you must hold the lock on X. This is because the mechanism for waiting on state-based conditions is necessarily bound to the mechanism for preserving state consistency — you cannot wait for a condition unless you can examine the state, and you cannot release another thread from a wait unless you can modify the state.

Object.wait atomically releases the lock and suspends the current thread, allowing others to acquire the lock and modify the state. Upon waking it reacquires the lock before returning. Intuitively, wait means "I want to sleep, but wake me when something interesting happens", and notification means "something interesting happened".

BOOK Listing 14.6 · Bounded buffer using condition queues 
@ThreadSafe
public class BoundedBuffer<V> extends BaseBoundedBuffer<V> {
    // CONDITION PREDICATE: not-full (!isFull())
    // CONDITION PREDICATE: not-empty (!isEmpty())

    public BoundedBuffer(int size) { super(size); }

    // BLOCKS-UNTIL: not-full
    public synchronized void put(V v) throws InterruptedException {
        while (isFull())
            wait();
        doPut(v);
        notifyAll();
    }

    // BLOCKS-UNTIL: not-empty
    public synchronized V take() throws InterruptedException {
        while (isEmpty())
            wait();
        V v = doTake();
        notifyAll();
        return v;
    }
}

Simpler than the sleeping version, and both more efficient (waking less often when the state does not change) and more responsive (waking promptly when it does). Note what did not change: the semantics are identical to SleepyBoundedBuffer. Condition queues do not let you do anything you cannot do with sleeping and polling; they are an optimisation in three dimensions — CPU efficiency, context-switch overhead and responsiveness.

Almost true: a fair condition queue can guarantee the relative order in which threads are released from the wait set. Intrinsic condition queues, like intrinsic locks, offer no fair queuing; explicit Conditions do.

A production version should also include timed versions of put and take, so blocking operations can time out within a time budget — the timed overload of Object.wait makes that easy.

14.2Using Condition Queues

Condition queues make it easy to build efficient, responsive state-dependent classes — and they are still easy to use incorrectly, because none of the rules are enforced by the compiler.

There are a lot of rules regarding their proper use that are not enforced by the compiler or the platform. This is one of the reasons to build on top of LinkedBlockingQueue, CountDownLatch, Semaphore and FutureTask when you can: if you can get away with it, it is a lot easier.

14.2.1The Condition Predicate

The key to using condition queues correctly is identifying the condition predicates the object may wait for. It is the condition predicate that causes much of the confusion surrounding wait and notify, because it has no instantiation in the API and nothing in either the language specification or the JVM ensures its correct use. It is not mentioned directly in the language spec or the Javadoc at all — but without it, condition waits do not work.

The condition predicate is the precondition that makes an operation state-dependent in the first place. In a bounded buffer, take can proceed only if the buffer is not empty; for take the predicate is "the buffer is not empty". For put it is "the buffer is not full". Condition predicates are expressions built from the state variables of the class: BaseBoundedBuffer tests "not empty" by comparing count to zero and "not full" by comparing it to the buffer size.

Document the predicate

Document the condition predicate(s) associated with a condition queue and the operations that wait on them. There is an important three-way relationship in a condition wait, involving locking, the wait method, and a condition predicate:

  • the predicate involves state variables, and those state variables are guarded by a lock — so before testing the predicate you must hold that lock;
  • the lock object and the condition queue object — the object on which wait and notify are invoked — must be the same object;
  • every call to wait is implicitly associated with a specific predicate, and it must be made while holding that lock.

In BoundedBuffer the buffer state is guarded by the buffer lock and the buffer object is the condition queue. That is why take can test the predicate and then call wait without acquiring anything else — and why, if the predicate is true, it can modify the state in the same atomic operation.

wait releases the lock, blocks the thread, and returns when the timeout expires, the thread is interrupted, or the thread is awakened by a notification. After waking, wait reacquires the lock before returning. A thread waking from wait gets no special priority in reacquiring it — it contends like any other thread entering a synchronized block. That is one of the reasons the predicate may already be false again by the time you look.

14.2.2Waking Up Too Soon

As if the three-way relationship were not complicated enough: the return of wait does not necessarily mean the predicate you were waiting for has become true.

🔔
One queue, many predicates

A single intrinsic condition queue may be used with more than one condition predicate. When you are awakened by notifyAll, that does not mean your predicate is true. It is like having your toaster and coffee maker share a bell: when it rings you still have to look at which device raised it.

🎲
Spurious wakeups

wait is allowed to return "spuriously", not in response to any thread calling notify at all. A toaster with a loose connection: the bell goes off when the toast is ready, and sometimes when it is not.

⏱️
Races after the wakeup

The predicate might have been true when the notifier signalled, and false again by the time you reacquire the lock. Other threads may have acquired the lock and changed the state in between. Or it may not have been true at all since you called wait.

👀
You do not know why

You do not know why another thread called notify; maybe it was because a different predicate on the same queue became true. BoundedBuffer uses one queue for both "not full" and "not empty" — and threads can be waiting for both at the same time, when producers and consumers outnumber the capacity.

For all these reasons, when you wake from wait you must test the predicate again, and go back to waiting (or fail) if it is not yet true. Since you can wake repeatedly without your predicate being true, you must always call wait from within a loop.

BOOK Listing 14.7 · Canonical form for state-dependent methods 
void stateDependentMethod() throws InterruptedException {
    // condition predicate must be guarded by lock
    synchronized(lock) {
        while (!conditionPredicate())
            lock.wait();
        // object is now in desired state
    }
}
📜

The rules for condition waits (Object.wait or Condition.await): always have a condition predicate; always test it before calling wait and again after returning from it; always call wait in a loop; ensure the state variables making up the predicate are guarded by the lock associated with the condition queue; hold that lock when calling wait, notify or notifyAll; and do not release the lock after checking the predicate but before acting on it.

14.2.3Missed Signals

Chapter 10 covered deadlock and livelock. Another form of liveness failure is a missed signal: a thread must wait for a condition that is already true, but fails to check the predicate before waiting. Now it is waiting to be notified of an event that has already happened.

It is like starting the toast, going out for the newspaper, having the bell go off while you are outside, and then sitting down at the kitchen table waiting for the toast bell. You could wait a long time — potentially forever. Unlike the marmalade for your toast, notification is not sticky: if thread A notifies on a condition queue and thread B subsequently waits on it, B does not immediately wake up — another notification is required.

Missed signals are the result of coding errors like the ones the rule list warns against, chiefly failing to test the predicate before calling wait. Structure your waits as in Listing 14.7 and you will not have problems with them.

14.2.4Notification

So far we have described half of a condition wait: waiting. The other half is notification. In a bounded buffer, take blocks if called when the buffer is empty; for it to unblock when the buffer becomes nonempty, every code path that could make the buffer nonempty must perform a notification. In BoundedBuffer there is exactly one such place — after a put. Symmetrically, take notifies after removing an element, in case anyone is waiting on "not full".

📌

Whenever you wait on a condition, make sure that someone will perform a notification whenever the condition predicate becomes true. Finding "someone" is a review exercise: enumerate every method that mutates the state, and check that each one notifies the right queue on the right exit path.

There are two notification methods: notify and notifyAll. To call either you must hold the lock associated with the condition queue. notify causes the JVM to select one waiting thread; notifyAll wakes all of them. Because waiting threads cannot return from wait without reacquiring the lock, the notifying thread should release the lock quickly so they are unblocked as soon as possible.

Because multiple threads could be waiting on the same condition queue for different predicates, using notify instead of notifyAll can be dangerous. Suppose A waits for predicate PA and B waits for PB on the same queue. PB becomes true and C performs a single notify: the JVM wakes one thread of its own choosing. If A is chosen, it wakes, sees PA is still false, and goes back to waiting — while B, which could now make progress, stays asleep. This is not exactly a missed signal; it is more of a hijacked signal, but the problem is the same.

When a single notify is safe

Single notification can be used instead of notifyAll only when both of the following hold:

  • Uniform waiters. Only one condition predicate is associated with the condition queue, and each thread executes the same logic upon returning from wait; and
  • One-in, one-out. A notification on the condition variable enables at most one thread to proceed.

BoundedBuffer meets one-in, one-out but not uniform waiters, because waiting threads may be waiting for either "not full" or "not empty". A starting-gate latch — where a single event releases a set of threads — meets uniform waiters but not one-in, one-out. Most classes meet neither, so the prevailing wisdom is to prefer notifyAll: it may be inefficient, but it is much easier to be sure the class is correct.

That inefficiency is real, though. If ten threads are waiting and notifyAll is called, all ten wake and contend for the lock, and then most or all go straight back to sleep: a lot of context switches and contended acquisitions for each event that enables maybe one thread to proceed. In the worst case, notifyAll results in O(n²) wakeups where n would suffice. This is another place where performance argues one way and safety the other.

Conditional notification

The notification in BoundedBuffer is conservative: it happens on every put and every take. A thread can be released from a wait only if the buffer goes from empty to not empty, or from full to not full — so you could notify only when a put or take effected one of those transitions. That is conditional notification. It can improve performance, but it is tricky to get right and complicates subclassing.

BOOK Listing 14.8 · Using conditional notification in BoundedBuffer.put 
public synchronized void put(V v) throws InterruptedException {
    while (isFull())
        wait();
    boolean wasEmpty = isEmpty();
    doPut(v);
    if (wasEmpty)
        notifyAll();
}

Single notification and conditional notification are optimisations. Follow the principle "first make it right, and then make it fast — if it is not already fast enough": it is easy to introduce strange liveness failures by applying them incorrectly.

14.2.5Example: A Gate Class

The starting-gate latch in TestHarness was constructed with an initial count of one, making it a binary latch: two states, initial and terminal. It prevents threads from passing until it is opened, at which point all can pass. Sometimes the drawback is exactly that such a gate cannot be reclosed.

ThreadGate lets the gate be opened and closed, with an await method that blocks until the gate is open. open uses notifyAll because the semantics fail the one-in, one-out test.

The predicate used by await is more complicated than isOpen. If N threads are waiting when the gate opens, they should all be allowed through — but if the gate is opened and closed in rapid succession, not all would be released if await examined only isOpen: by the time every thread wakes, reacquires the lock and emerges from wait, the gate may have closed again. So every close increments a generation counter, and a thread may pass if the gate is open now or if it has opened since that thread arrived.

BOOK Listing 14.9 · Recloseable gate using wait and notifyAll 
@ThreadSafe
public class ThreadGate {
    // CONDITION-PREDICATE: opened-since(n) (isOpen || generation>n)
    @GuardedBy("this") private boolean isOpen;
    @GuardedBy("this") private int generation;

    public synchronized void close() {
        isOpen = false;
    }

    public synchronized void open() {
        ++generation;
        isOpen = true;
        notifyAll();
    }

    // BLOCKS-UNTIL: opened-since(generation on entry)
    public synchronized void await() throws InterruptedException {
        int arrivalGeneration = generation;
        while (!isOpen && arrivalGeneration == generation)
            wait();
    }
}

Because ThreadGate supports only waiting for the gate to open, it notifies only in open. To support both "wait for open" and "wait for close", it would have to notify in both. This illustrates why state-dependent classes are fragile to maintain: adding a new state-dependent operation may require modifying many code paths that change the object's state, so the appropriate notifications get performed.

14.2.6Subclass Safety Issues

Conditional or single notification introduces constraints that complicate subclassing. If you want to support subclassing at all, you must structure the class so subclasses can add the appropriate notification on behalf of the base class.

A state-dependent class should either fully expose and document its waiting and notification protocols to subclasses, or prevent subclasses from participating in them at all — an extension of "design and document for inheritance, or else prohibit it". At the very least this requires exposing the condition queues and locks and documenting the predicates and synchronization policy; it may also require exposing the state variables. The worst thing a state-dependent class can do is expose its state to subclasses but not document its waiting and notification protocols — like exposing state variables but not documenting the invariants.

One option is to effectively prohibit subclassing, by making the class final or by hiding the condition queues, locks and state variables. Otherwise, if a subclass undermines the way the base class uses notify, it needs to be able to repair the damage. Consider an unbounded blocking stack: pop blocks if empty, push always proceeds — meeting the requirements for single notification. If that class uses single notification and a subclass adds a blocking "pop two consecutive elements" method, there are now two classes of waiters. But if the base class exposes the condition queue and documents its protocols, the subclass can override push to perform notifyAll, restoring safety.

14.2.7Encapsulating Condition Queues

It is generally best to encapsulate the condition queue so it is not accessible outside the class hierarchy that uses it. Otherwise callers may think they understand your protocols and use them inconsistently. You cannot enforce the uniform-waiters requirement for single notification unless the condition queue object is inaccessible to code you do not control: if alien code mistakenly waits on your condition queue, it can subvert your notification protocol and cause a hijacked signal.

Unfortunately this advice conflicts with the most common design pattern for thread-safe classes, in which an object's intrinsic lock guards its state — as BoundedBuffer does, with the buffer object itself as lock and condition queue. It could easily be restructured to use a private lock object and condition queue; the only difference would be that it would no longer support any form of client-side locking.

14.2.8Entry and Exit Protocols

Wellings (2004) characterises the proper use of wait and notify in terms of entry and exit protocols. For each state-dependent operation, and for each operation that modifies state on which another operation has a state dependency, define and document an entry and exit protocol. The entry protocol is the operation's condition predicate; the exit protocol is examining the state variables the operation changed to see whether some other condition predicate may now be true, and if so notifying on the associated queue.

⚙️

AbstractQueuedSynchronizer, on which most of java.util.concurrent is built, exploits the exit-protocol idea directly: rather than letting synchronizers perform their own notification, it requires tryRelease to return a value indicating whether the action may have unblocked one or more waiting threads. Making notification an explicit return value makes it much harder to "forget" to notify on some state transition — the type system nags you about it.

14.3Explicit Condition Objects

Intrinsic locks have exactly one condition queue. That single fact is what forces notifyAll on BoundedBuffer — and Condition is the fix.

Just as Lock generalises intrinsic locks, Condition generalises intrinsic condition queues. Intrinsic condition queues have several drawbacks: each intrinsic lock can have only one associated condition queue, so in classes like BoundedBuffer multiple threads wait on the same queue for different predicates; and the most common locking pattern exposes the condition queue object. Both make it impossible to enforce the uniform-waiters requirement.

A Condition is associated with a single Lock, just as a condition queue is associated with a single intrinsic lock; create one with Lock.newCondition. It offers a richer feature set: multiple wait sets per lock, interruptible and uninterruptible waits, deadline-based waiting, and a choice of fair or non-fair queuing.

BOOK Listing 14.10 · Condition interface 
public interface Condition {
    void await() throws InterruptedException;
    boolean await(long time, TimeUnit unit)
            throws InterruptedException;
    long awaitNanos(long nanosTimeout) throws InterruptedException;
    void awaitUninterruptibly();
    boolean awaitUntil(Date deadline) throws InterruptedException;

    void signal();
    void signalAll();
}

You can have as many Condition objects per Lock as you want. They inherit the fairness setting of their lock: for fair locks, threads are released from await in FIFO order.

⚠️

Hazard warning. The equivalents of wait, notify and notifyAll for Condition are await, signal and signalAll. But Condition extends Object, so it also has wait and notify methods. Use the right versions — await and signal — or you will wait on the monitor of the Condition object itself, which nobody will ever notify.

ConditionBoundedBuffer uses two conditions, notFull and notEmpty, to represent the two predicates explicitly. When take blocks because the buffer is empty it waits on notEmpty; put unblocks it by signalling notEmpty.

BOOK Listing 14.11 · Bounded buffer using explicit condition variables 
@ThreadSafe
public class ConditionBoundedBuffer<T> {
    protected final Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    // CONDITION PREDICATE: notFull (count < items.length)
    private final Condition notFull    = lock.newCondition();
    // CONDITION PREDICATE: notEmpty (count > 0)
    private final Condition notEmpty  = lock.newCondition();
    @GuardedBy("lock")
    private final T[] items = (T[]) new Object[BUFFER_SIZE];
    @GuardedBy("lock") private int tail, head, count;

    // BLOCKS-UNTIL: notFull
    public void put(T x) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (count == items.length)
                notFull.await();
            items[tail] = x;
            if (++tail == items.length)
                tail = 0;
            ++count;
            notEmpty.signal();
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    // BLOCKS-UNTIL: notEmpty
    public T take() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (count == 0)
                notEmpty.await();
            T x = items[head];
            items[head] = null;
            if (++head == items.length)
                head = 0;
            --count;
            notFull.signal();
            return x;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
}

The behaviour is the same as BoundedBuffer, but the use of condition queues is more readable: it is easier to analyse a class that uses multiple Conditions than one that uses a single intrinsic queue with multiple predicates. Separating the predicates into separate wait sets makes it easier to meet the requirements for single notification, and using the more efficient signal instead of signalAll reduces the number of context switches and lock acquisitions triggered by each operation.

The three-way relationship still holds: the variables involved in the predicate must be guarded by the lock, and the lock must be held when testing the predicate and when calling await and signal. (ReentrantLock requires the lock to be held when signalling, but Lock implementations are permitted to construct Conditions that do not have that requirement.)

Choose between explicit Conditions and intrinsic condition queues the same way you choose between ReentrantLock and synchronized: use Condition if you need fair queuing or multiple wait sets per lock, otherwise prefer intrinsic queues. If you already use ReentrantLock for its other features, the choice is already made.

14.4Anatomy of a Synchronizer

ReentrantLock and Semaphore have suspiciously similar interfaces. Neither is built on the other — they share a base class.

Both act as a "gate" allowing only a limited number of threads through at a time: threads arrive and are allowed through (lock or acquire returns), made to wait (it blocks), or turned away (tryLock or tryAcquire returns false). Both allow interruptible, uninterruptible and timed attempts, and both offer fair or non-fair queuing.

Given that commonality you might think one was built on the other — and it is a common exercise to prove a counting semaphore can be implemented with a lock, and vice versa. That works, but it is not what the library does.

BOOK Listing 14.12 · Counting semaphore implemented using Lock 
// Not really how java.util.concurrent.Semaphore is implemented
@ThreadSafe
public class SemaphoreOnLock {
    private final Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    // CONDITION PREDICATE: permitsAvailable (permits > 0)
    private final Condition permitsAvailable = lock.newCondition();
    @GuardedBy("lock") private int permits;

    SemaphoreOnLock(int initialPermits) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            permits = initialPermits;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    // BLOCKS-UNTIL: permitsAvailable
    public void acquire() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (permits <= 0)
                permitsAvailable.await();
            --permits;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    public void release() {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            ++permits;
            permitsAvailable.signal();
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
}

In actuality both are implemented on a common base class, AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS) — as are CountDownLatch, ReentrantReadWriteLock, SynchronousQueue and FutureTask. AQS is a framework for building locks and synchronizers, and a surprisingly broad range of them can be built easily and efficiently with it.

Building on AQS does not just reduce implementation effort; it also avoids paying for multiple points of contention, as you do when you construct one synchronizer on top of another. In SemaphoreOnLock, acquiring a permit has two places it might block: at the lock guarding the semaphore state, and again if no permit is available. AQS-built synchronizers have only one point at which they might block, reducing context-switch overhead and improving throughput.

14.5AbstractQueuedSynchronizer

One int of state, one FIFO queue of waiters, and two methods to override. Everything else is bookkeeping.

Most developers will never use AQS directly; the standard synchronizers cover a fairly wide range of situations. But seeing how they work clarifies a lot about blocking in Java.

The basic operations are variants of acquire and release. Acquisition is the state-dependent operation and can always block. With a lock or semaphore it means "acquire the lock or a permit"; with CountDownLatch it means "wait until the latch has reached its terminal state"; with FutureTask, "wait until the task has completed". Release is not blocking — it may allow blocked threads to proceed.

AQS manages a single integer of state, manipulated through the protected getState, setState and compareAndSetState methods. That integer can represent anything: ReentrantLock uses it as the hold count, Semaphore as the permits remaining, FutureTask as the task status. Synchronizers may keep additional state themselves — ReentrantLock tracks the owning thread so it can distinguish reentrant from contended acquisition.

BOOK Listing 14.13 · Canonical forms for acquisition and release in AQS 
boolean acquire() throws InterruptedException {
    while (state does not permit acquire) {
        if (blocking acquisition requested) {
            enqueue current thread if not already queued
            block current thread
        }
        else
            return failure
    }
    possibly update synchronization state
    dequeue thread if it was queued
    return success
}

void release() {
    update synchronization state
    if (new state may permit a blocked thread to acquire)
        unblock one or more queued threads
}

Acquisition has two parts. First the synchronizer decides whether the current state permits acquisition — that decision is the synchronizer's semantics: acquiring a lock succeeds if it is unheld, acquiring a latch succeeds if the latch is terminal. Second, acquisition may update the state: a lock goes from unheld to held, a semaphore's permit count drops. Acquiring a latch, notably, does not change its state, since one thread acquiring it does not affect whether others can.

A synchronizer supporting exclusive acquisition implements tryAcquire, tryRelease and isHeldExclusively; one supporting shared acquisition implements tryAcquireShared and tryReleaseShared. AQS's acquire, acquireShared, release and releaseShared call those try forms to decide whether the operation can proceed. For tryAcquireShared, a negative return means failure, zero means exclusive acquisition and a positive value means non-exclusive acquisition. tryRelease and tryReleaseShared should return true if the release may have unblocked a waiting thread — the exit protocol, expressed as a return value.

14.5.1A Simple Latch

OneShotLatch is a binary latch implemented with AQS: two public methods, await and signal, corresponding to acquire and release. Initially closed; any thread calling await blocks until the latch opens. Once opened, waiting threads are released and subsequent arrivals pass straight through.

BOOK Listing 14.14 · Binary latch using AbstractQueuedSynchronizer 
@ThreadSafe
public class OneShotLatch {
    private final Sync sync = new Sync();

    public void signal() { sync.releaseShared(0); }

    public void await() throws InterruptedException {
        sync.acquireSharedInterruptibly(0);
    }

    private class Sync extends AbstractQueuedSynchronizer {
        protected int tryAcquireShared(int ignored) {
            // Succeed if latch is open (state == 1), else fail
            return (getState() == 1) ? 1 : -1;
        }

        protected boolean tryReleaseShared(int ignored) {
            setState(1);  // Latch is now open
            return true;  // Other threads may now be able to acquire

        }
    }
}

The AQS state holds the latch state: closed (zero) or open (one). await calls acquireSharedInterruptibly, which consults tryAcquireShared. If the latch was already open it returns success and the thread passes; otherwise it returns failure, and acquireSharedInterruptibly interprets that as "enqueue this thread". signal calls releaseShared, which consults tryReleaseShared — that sets the state to open and returns true, telling AQS the synchronizer is fully released, so every waiting thread re-attempts acquisition and now succeeds.

🪄

OneShotLatch is a fully functional, usable, performant synchronizer in about twenty lines of code. It lacks extras — timed acquisition, state inspection — but AQS provides timed acquisition variants and inspection utilities for free. Note the delegation: OneShotLatch could have extended AQS, but that would expose a large public API and undermine its two-method interface. No synchronizer in java.util.concurrent extends AQS directly; they all delegate to private inner subclasses.

14.6AQS in java.util.concurrent

Five synchronizers, one base class, five different meanings for the same integer.

ClassWhat the AQS state meansWhich try methods
ReentrantLockThe lock hold count; a separate owner field identifies the owning threadtryAcquire, tryRelease, isHeldExclusively
SemaphorePermits currently availabletryAcquireShared, tryReleaseShared
CountDownLatchThe current count; reaching zero is the terminal statetryAcquireShared, tryReleaseShared
FutureTaskTask status — running, completed or cancelled — plus result/exception fieldstryAcquireShared, tryReleaseShared
ReentrantReadWriteLock16 bits of write-lock count plus 16 bits of read-lock countexclusive for writes, shared for reads

14.6.1ReentrantLock

ReentrantLock supports only exclusive acquisition, so it implements tryAcquire, tryRelease and isHeldExclusively. It uses the state as the hold count and maintains an owner variable holding the owning thread's identity, modified only when the current thread has just acquired the lock or is just about to release it. tryRelease checks owner before allowing an unlock; tryAcquire uses it to tell a reentrant acquisition from a contended one.

BOOK Listing 14.15 · tryAcquire implementation from non-fair ReentrantLock 
protected boolean tryAcquire(int ignored) {
    final Thread current = Thread.currentThread();
    int c = getState();
    if (c == 0) {
        if (compareAndSetState(0, 1)) {
            owner = current;
            return true;
        }
    } else if (current == owner) {
        setState(c+1);
        return true;
    }
    return false;
}

If the lock is unheld, attempt to update the state atomically with compareAndSetState — the state may have changed since it was read a few instructions ago, so the CAS both sets it and confirms it has not moved. If the lock is already held, either increment the count (reentrant) or fail (contended).

Because the protected state-manipulation methods have the memory semantics of a volatile read or write, and ReentrantLock is careful to read owner only after calling getState and to write it only before calling setState, it can piggyback on the memory semantics of the synchronization state and avoid further synchronization (see §16.1.4).

14.6.2Semaphore and CountDownLatch

Semaphore uses the state as the count of available permits. tryAcquireShared computes the number remaining and fails if there are not enough; otherwise it tries to reduce the count atomically, and if that succeeds the acquire succeeded. The return value also encodes whether other shared acquisitions might now succeed — in which case other waiting threads are unblocked too.

BOOK Listing 14.16 · tryAcquireShared and tryReleaseShared from Semaphore 
protected int tryAcquireShared(int acquires) {
    while (true) {
        int available = getState();
        int remaining = available - acquires;
        if (remaining < 0
                || compareAndSetState(available, remaining))
            return remaining;
    }
}

protected boolean tryReleaseShared(int releases) {
    while (true) {
        int p = getState();
        if (compareAndSetState(p, p + releases))
            return true;
    }
}

The loop terminates on one of two things: not enough permits, or a successful CAS. Any individual CAS may fail due to contention with another thread, causing a retry, but one of those two termination criteria becomes true within a reasonable number of retries. tryReleaseShared increments the count and retries until the update succeeds, returning whether other threads might have been unblocked.

CountDownLatch works the same way, with the state as the current count: countDown calls release, decrementing and unblocking waiters when the count reaches zero; await calls acquire, returning immediately at zero and blocking otherwise.

14.6.3FutureTask

At first glance FutureTask does not even look like a synchronizer. But Future.get has semantics very close to a latch: if some event (completion or cancellation of the task) has occurred, threads can proceed; otherwise they are queued until it does.

FutureTask uses the AQS state for task status — running, completed or cancelled — and keeps additional fields for the result of the computation or the exception it threw, plus a reference to the thread running it (while running), so a cancelled task can be interrupted.

14.6.4ReentrantReadWriteLock

The ReadWriteLock interface suggests two locks, but in the AQS-based implementation a single subclass manages both: 16 bits of the state for the write-lock count, the other 16 for the read-lock count. Read operations use shared acquire and release; write operations use exclusive acquire and release.

AQS maintains a queue of waiting threads, tracking whether each requested exclusive or shared access. In ReentrantReadWriteLock, when the lock becomes available: if the thread at the head of the queue wanted write access it gets it; if the head wanted read access, all queued threads up to the first writer get it.

That mechanism does not permit a reader-preference or writer-preference policy. For that, the AQS wait queue would have to be something other than FIFO, or two queues would be needed. Such strict ordering is rarely needed in practice: if the non-fair version does not offer acceptable liveness, the fair version usually provides satisfactory ordering and guarantees non-starvation of readers and writers.

Summary of the chapter

If you need to implement a state-dependent class — one whose methods must block if a state-based precondition does not hold — the best strategy is usually to build on an existing library class such as Semaphore, BlockingQueue or CountDownLatch. Sometimes the library does not provide a sufficient foundation; in those cases you can build your own synchronizers using intrinsic condition queues, explicit Condition objects, or AbstractQueuedSynchronizer. Intrinsic condition queues are tightly bound to intrinsic locking, since the mechanism for managing state dependence is necessarily tied to the mechanism for ensuring state consistency. Similarly, explicit Conditions are tightly bound to explicit Locks, and offer an extended feature set: multiple wait sets per lock, interruptible or uninterruptible waits, fair or non-fair queuing, and deadline-based waiting.

A consumer wants to take from an empty buffer. A producer will put an item at tick 4. Run the same scenario under four protocols and watch when the consumer gets its item — and how much CPU it burns getting there.
