The fourth protocol is the chapter's central bug in miniature. The producer's notifyAll at tick 4 happens before the consumer calls wait — or the consumer checks nothing and simply waits after the state has already changed. Notification is not sticky, so the consumer sleeps forever. No exception, no timeout, no log line: just a thread that never comes back. This is why "test the predicate before you wait" is rule one, and why the entry protocol has to be documented.

§Patterns worth stealing

The sixteen listings above are the book's. These two are the shapes worth keeping: a state-dependent base class that makes the predicate and the notification impossible to forget, and a hand-rolled synchronizer with timed acquisition.

1Make the predicate part of the class

PATTERN A guarded state machine where wait and notify come in pairs 
/**
 * Every blocking method names its predicate in a method, and every mutator
 * ends in exactly one call to a single exit-protocol helper.
 */
public final class BoundedQueue<T> {
    private final Object[] items;
    private final Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition notFull  = lock.newCondition();
    private int head, tail, count;

    public BoundedQueue(int capacity) { items = new Object[capacity]; }

    /* the exit protocol: whoever changed the state says so, once */
    private void changed() {
        notEmpty.signal();   // someone may now be able to take
        notFull.signal();    // someone may now be able to put
    }

    public T take(long timeout, TimeUnit unit) throws InterruptedException {
        long nanos = unit.toNanos(timeout);
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (count == 0)                       // predicate, in a loop
                if (nanos <= 0)
                    return null;                     // timed out, not deadlocked
                else
                    nanos = notEmpty.awaitNanos(nanos);
            @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") T x = (T) items[head];
            items[head] = null;                      // do not retain
            if (++head == items.length) head = 0;
            --count;
            changed();
            return x;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    public boolean put(T x, long timeout, TimeUnit unit) throws InterruptedException {
        long nanos = unit.toNanos(timeout);
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (count == items.length)
                if (nanos <= 0)
                    return false;
                else
                    nanos = notFull.awaitNanos(nanos);
            items[tail] = x;
            if (++tail == items.length) tail = 0;
            ++count;
            changed();
            return true;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
}

Three habits make this maintainable. The predicates are two one-line expressions that read like the documentation. The notification lives in one method, so a new mutator cannot forget it — and because the two Conditions are separate, signal is safe here in a way it would not be with a single intrinsic queue. And awaitNanos returns the remaining time, so the deadline survives spurious wakeups and multiple loop iterations.

2A synchronizer you can time out

PATTERN Counting semaphore on AQS: state, tryAcquireShared, tryReleaseShared 
/**
 * The whole of a counting semaphore, AQS-style: one int of state, two
 * try methods, and the base class does the queueing, parking and timing.
 */
public final class CountingSemaphore {
    private final Sync sync;

    public CountingSemaphore(int permits) {
        if (permits < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative permits");
        sync = new Sync(permits);
    }

    public void acquire() throws InterruptedException { sync.acquireSharedInterruptibly(1); }
    public boolean tryAcquire(long t, TimeUnit u) throws InterruptedException {
        return sync.tryAcquireSharedNanos(1, u.toNanos(t));
    }
    public void release() { sync.releaseShared(1); }
    public int availablePermits() { return sync.getPermits(); }

    private static final class Sync extends AbstractQueuedSynchronizer {
        Sync(int permits) { setState(permits); }
        int getPermits() { return getState(); }

        /* negative = failed; zero = acquired, do not propagate;
           positive = acquired and others may proceed too */
        @Override protected int tryAcquireShared(int acquires) {
            for (;;) {
                int available = getState();
                int remaining = available - acquires;
                if (remaining < 0 || compareAndSetState(available, remaining))
                    return remaining;
            }
        }

        @Override protected boolean tryReleaseShared(int releases) {
            for (;;) {
                int current = getState();
                int next = current + releases;
                if (next < current) throw new IllegalStateException("overflow");
                if (compareAndSetState(current, next))
                    return true;          // may have unblocked a waiter
            }
        }
    }
}

Note what is absent: no queue, no park/unpark, no interrupt handling, no timeout arithmetic. AQS gives all of that because the subclass only has to answer "does this state permit acquisition, and what is the new state?" — which is exactly the entry/exit protocol of §14.2.8 turned into two methods with meaningful return values.

✓Cheat sheet & self-check

SymptomLikely causeFix
A thread waits forever though the condition is trueMissed signal: no predicate test before wait, and the notification already happenedTest the predicate first, always inside a while
One waiter wakes, the eligible one does notnotify on a queue serving two predicates — a hijacked signalUse notifyAll, or split into two Conditions
Waiter wakes for no reasonSpurious wakeup, or the state changed again before it reacquired the lockThe loop is not optional — re-test after every return from wait
Everything blocks, nothing progressesWaiting with the lock held, so the state can never changeRelease before sleeping; that is precisely what wait/await do atomically
IllegalMonitorStateExceptionCalling wait/notify without holding the lock, or Condition.wait by mistakeHold the lock; and use await/signal, never wait/notify, on a Condition
Throughput collapses with many waitersnotifyAll waking everyone for one slotSeparate wait sets via Condition, then signal
Latency spikes of exactly the poll intervalSleep-based polling granularityReal notification, or a much smaller granularity with a CPU budget
Subclass breaks the notificationsNew state-dependent method, base class used single notificationExpose and document the protocol, or make the class final
Callers wrap everything in try/catch and retryPrecondition failure propagated instead of blockingEncapsulate the wait; use BlockingQueue when you can
A timed wait returns immediately every timeawait(nanos) called in a loop with the original timeout, not the remaining oneUse the value returned by awaitNanos as the new budget
✅
Do

Write the predicate down and name it in a comment. Wait in a while. Notify after every state change that could unblock anyone. Prefer library synchronizers; when you must roll your own, prefer a private lock and private condition queues.

🚫
Avoid

if around a wait. Notification inside a block that changes nothing. notify without checking uniform waiters and one-in, one-out. Exposing your condition queue to subclasses without documenting the protocol. Sleeping while holding a lock.

🧠
The one habit

For every wait, find the code that will notify it, and prove that code runs after the state changed. For every notify, name the predicate it satisfies. If either answer needs a paragraph instead of a sentence, use a library class.

Five questions the chapter leaves you with

  1. What is the condition predicate for each of my blocking methods — and could a reviewer read it from the code?
  2. Which of my condition queues serve more than one predicate, and am I calling notifyAll there?
  3. Does every state-changing path reach a notification, including the exception paths?
  4. Could I have built this on Semaphore, BlockingQueue or CountDownLatch instead?
  5. If I published my condition queue, what would a subclass have to do to break my protocol?

Notes carried over from the chapter

  1. Pushing the state dependence back to the caller also makes it nearly impossible to preserve FIFO ordering; by forcing the caller to retry, you lose the information about who arrived first.
  2. Queue offers both options — poll returns null if empty, remove throws — but Queue is not intended for producer–consumer designs. BlockingQueue is the better choice.
  3. We will spare you the details of Snow White's other five bounded buffer implementations, especially SneezyBoundedBuffer.
  4. It is usually a bad idea for a thread to sleep or otherwise block with a lock held, but here it is even worse: the desired condition can never become true if the lock is not released.
  5. Not quite true: a fair condition queue can guarantee the relative order in which threads are released from the wait set. Intrinsic condition queues offer no fair queuing; explicit Conditions do.
  6. ConditionBoundedBuffer in §14.3 is even better: it is more efficient because it can use single notification instead of notifyAll.
  7. The shared-bell situation describes Tim's kitchen pretty well: so many devices beep that when you hear one you have to inspect the toaster, the microwave, the coffee maker and several others to determine the cause.
  8. To push the breakfast analogy way too far, a spurious wakeup is a toaster with a loose connection that rings when the toast is ready and also sometimes when it is not.
  9. It is actually possible for threads to be waiting for both "not full" and "not empty" at the same time — this happens when the number of producers/consumers exceeds the buffer capacity.
  10. In order to emerge from this wait, someone else would have to make toast, but that will only make matters worse: when the bell rings, you will then have a disagreement about toast ownership.
  11. Java 6 replaces the AQS-based SynchronousQueue with a (more scalable) non-blocking version.
  12. ReentrantLock requires that the lock be held when calling signal or signalAll, but Lock implementations are permitted to construct Conditions that do not have this requirement.
  13. Because the protected state-manipulation methods have the memory semantics of a volatile read or write, and ReentrantLock is careful about ordering those accesses around the owner field, it can piggyback on the memory semantics of the synchronization state and avoid further synchronization — see §16.1.4.
  14. The JDK source is the best reference; it is also available with fewer licensing restrictions from the concurrency-interest pages at gee.cs.oswego.edu.
  15. This mechanism does not permit a reader-preference or writer-preference policy, as some read–write lock implementations do. For that, the AQS wait queue would need to be something other than FIFO, or two queues would be needed.

Summary of Java Concurrency in Practice, Chapter 14 (Building Custom Synchronizers), pp. 179–194. All code listings are the book's, with annotations added; Figure 14.1 is reproduced from the book PDF for study purposes.

Java Concurrency in Practice · Chapter 15

Chapter 15 — Atomic Variables and Non-blocking Synchronization

Locks are pessimistic: assume interference, take exclusive control, and if you cannot, get suspended. Modern processors offer a second way — compare-and-swap, which assumes nothing, tries the update, and merely reports whether somebody beat you to it. That single instruction is the source of most of the scalability in java.util.concurrent, and the foundation of a whole class of algorithms that cannot deadlock because nothing ever waits.

📖 pp. 195–206 🧩 4 sections · 8 listings · 5 figures ⏱️ ~26 min read 🏷️ Part IV — Advanced Topics

Chapter in one paragraph

TL;DR — the six things worth remembering

  1. Locking is pessimistic; CAS is optimistic. Locking asks permission; CAS asks forgiveness — "I think V should be A; if it is, put B there, otherwise tell me I was wrong." It never blocks the loser.
  2. Atomic variables are "better volatiles". Same visibility as volatile, plus atomic read-modify-write. Not a replacement for invariants spanning two variables — for that you need an immutable holder in an AtomicReference.
  3. Atomics win at realistic contention; locks win at absurd contention. A lock reacts to contention by suspending threads, which reduces wasted CPU. A CAS loop reacts by retrying immediately, which at extreme contention just makes more contention — and at normal contention is exactly right.
  4. True scalability means eliminating contention, not managing it. The third curve in every figure is a ThreadLocal: four times the throughput of either contended option.
  5. Non-blocking means one thread's failure cannot stop another. Lock-free adds that at every step some thread makes progress. CAS-only algorithms, built correctly, get both — plus immunity to deadlock and priority inversion.
  6. The hard part is the surrounding algorithm, not the CAS. Which is why you should use ConcurrentLinkedQueue rather than write a Michael–Scott queue, and why the ABA problem bites algorithms that recycle nodes.

15.1Disadvantages of Locking

Locking is correct, well understood, and — for fine-grained operations under contention — a heavyweight hammer.

A consistent locking protocol guarantees that whichever thread holds the lock guarding a set of variables has exclusive access to them, and that its changes are visible to threads that subsequently acquire the lock. Modern JVMs optimise uncontended acquisition fairly effectively. But if multiple threads request the lock at the same time, the JVM enlists the operating system: some unfortunate thread is suspended and later resumed, and on resumption may have to wait for other threads to finish their scheduling quanta before it actually runs. Suspending and resuming a thread has a lot of overhead and generally entails a lengthy interruption. For lock-based classes with fine-grained operations — the synchronized collections, where most methods are only a few instructions — the ratio of scheduling overhead to useful work can be very high when the lock is frequently contended.

(A smart JVM need not suspend a thread on contention: it can use profiling data to choose adaptively between suspension and spin locking, based on how long the lock was held during previous acquisitions.)

volatile is lighter, because it involves no context switches or thread scheduling. But it cannot construct atomic compound actions: it is unusable when one variable depends on another, or when a variable's new value depends on its old value. That rules out counters and mutexes — the everyday tools.

🔢

++i looks atomic and is three operations: fetch the current value, add one, write it back. To avoid losing an update the entire read-modify-write must be atomic. The only way we have seen so far is locking, as in Counter. Counter is thread-safe and performs fine with little or no contention — but under contention performance suffers from context-switch overhead and scheduling delays. When locks are held so briefly, being put to sleep is a harsh penalty for asking for the lock at the wrong moment.

⏸️
A waiting thread can do nothing else

While blocked on a lock the thread is unavailable for any other work — it is not even free to check whether it still wants the lock.

🐢
A delayed holder delays everyone

If the holder is descheduled, page-faults, or blocks on I/O, no thread needing that lock can progress.

🔀
Priority inversion

A high-priority thread blocked behind a low-priority holder is effectively demoted to that holder's priority. It should have had precedence; it waits anyway.

💀
A permanently blocked holder stops everything

Infinite loop, deadlock, livelock — any liveness failure in the holder becomes a liveness failure for every thread that will ever need the lock.

Even ignoring these hazards, locking is simply a heavyweight mechanism for fine-grained operations. What we want is something like volatile, but with atomic updates as well. Modern processors offer exactly that.

15.2Hardware Support for Concurrency

"It is easier to obtain forgiveness than permission" — where easier means more efficient.

Exclusive locking is pessimistic: it assumes the worst (if you do not lock your door, gremlins will come in and rearrange your stuff) and does not proceed until it can guarantee no interference. For fine-grained operations the alternative is optimistic: proceed with the update, hopeful that it completes without interference, and rely on collision detection to discover that somebody else got there first — in which case the operation fails and can be retried.

Multiprocessor processors provide special instructions for this. Early ones had atomic test-and-set, fetch-and-increment or swap, enough to build mutexes and from those more sophisticated objects. Today nearly every processor has some form of atomic read-modify-write: compare-and-swap, or load-linked/store-conditional. Operating systems and JVMs have always used them to implement locks; until Java 5.0 they were not available to Java classes.

15.2.1Compare and Swap

CAS has three operands: a memory location V, the expected old value A, and the new value B. It atomically updates V to B only if V currently matches A; otherwise it does nothing. Either way it returns the value currently in V. (The compareAndSet variant returns whether it succeeded instead.) In other words: "I think V should have the value A; if it does, put B there, otherwise don't change it but tell me I was wrong."

CAS is optimistic — it proceeds in hope of success and can detect failure if another thread updated the variable since it was last examined. PowerPC and friends get the same functionality from a pair of instructions (load-linked / store-conditional).

BOOK Listing 15.1 · Simulated CAS operation 
@ThreadSafe
public class SimulatedCAS {
    @GuardedBy("this") private int value;

    public synchronized int get() { return value; }

    public synchronized int compareAndSwap(int expectedValue,
                                           int newValue) {
        int oldValue = value;
        if (oldValue == expectedValue)
            value = newValue;
        return oldValue;
    }

    public synchronized boolean compareAndSet(int expectedValue,
                                              int newValue) {
        return (expectedValue
                == compareAndSwap(expectedValue, newValue));
    }
}

That listing illustrates the semantics, not the implementation or the performance — the real thing is one instruction, not three synchronized methods.

The typical pattern is: read A from V, derive B from A, then CAS V from A to B so long as nobody changed V in the meantime. When several threads attempt this simultaneously, one wins and the rest lose — but the losers are not punished with suspension. They are told they did not win this time and may try again. Because a thread that loses a CAS is not blocked, it can retry, take some other recovery action, or do nothing at all. That flexibility eliminates most of the liveness hazards of locking, though in unusual cases it can introduce livelock (§10.3.3).

Doing nothing may be a perfectly sensible response to a failed CAS: in some non-blocking algorithms — such as the linked queue below — a failed CAS means someone else already did the work you were planning to do.

15.2.2A Non-blocking Counter

CasCounter implements a thread-safe counter using CAS, in the canonical form: fetch the old value, transform it, CAS the new value in, retry immediately on failure. Retrying is usually the right strategy, though under extreme contention it may be worth waiting or backing off first, to avoid livelock.

BOOK Listing 15.2 · Non-blocking counter using CAS 
@ThreadSafe
public class CasCounter {
    private SimulatedCAS value;

    public int getValue() {
        return value.get();
    }

    public int increment() {
        int v;
        do {
            v = value.get();
        }
        while (v != value.compareAndSwap(v, v + 1));
        return v + 1;
    }
}
⚡

At first glance the CAS counter looks worse: more operations, more complicated control flow, and a mysterious atomic instruction. In reality CAS-based counters significantly outperform lock-based ones with even a little contention — and often with none. The uncontended lock fast path typically costs at least one CAS plus lock housekeeping, so the best case for a lock is worse than the normal case for CAS. And since the CAS almost always succeeds, the hardware predicts the branch in the while loop almost perfectly.

The syntax for locking is compact; the work the JVM and OS do is not. Locking traverses a complicated code path in the JVM and may involve OS-level locking, thread suspension and context switches. In the best case it requires at least one CAS anyway — so using a lock moves the CAS out of sight without saving any execution cost. A CAS written in your own code involves no JVM code, no system calls and no scheduling. What looks like a longer code path at the application level is a much shorter one once JVM and OS activity are counted.

The primary disadvantage of CAS is that it forces the caller to deal with contention — retry, back off, or give up — whereas a lock deals with it automatically by blocking. (The bigger disadvantage, the book's footnote says, is the difficulty of constructing the surrounding algorithms correctly.) CAS cost varies widely: a handful of clock cycles on a single CPU, and roughly 10 to 150 cycles uncontended on multiprocessors at the time of writing. A useful rule of thumb: the uncontended lock fast path costs about twice a CAS.

15.2.3CAS Support in the JVM

Before Java 5.0 there was no way to get the processor to do a CAS short of writing native code. Java 5.0 added low-level support exposing CAS on int, long and object references; the JVM compiles them into the most efficient means the hardware provides, inlining the appropriate instruction where one exists, and falling back to a spin lock where it does not. That support is used by the AtomicXXX classes in java.util.concurrent.atomic, which in turn are used — directly or indirectly — to implement most of java.util.concurrent.

15.3Atomic Variable Classes

Twelve classes, four families, one job: narrow the scope of contention to a single variable — which is as fine-grained as contention gets.

Atomic variables are finer-grained and lighter-weight than locks, and critical for high-performance concurrent code on multiprocessors. They limit the scope of contention to a single variable. The fast path for updating one is no slower than the fast path for acquiring a lock, and usually faster; the slow path is definitely faster, because it does not involve suspending and rescheduling threads. With atomics, threads are more likely to proceed without delay and have an easier time recovering if they do hit contention.

They generalise volatile to support atomic conditional read-modify-write. AtomicInteger provides get and set with the memory semantics of volatile reads and writes of an int, an atomic compareAndSet (which, if successful, has the memory effects of both a volatile read and a volatile write), and — for convenience — atomic add, increment and decrement. It resembles an extended Counter, but scales far better because it can exploit hardware support directly.

FamilyClassesWhat it gives you
ScalarsAtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean, AtomicReferenceCAS on one value; the Integer and Long versions also do arithmetic. For other primitive types, cast short/byte through int, and use floatToIntBits/doubleToLongBits for floating point.
Field updatersAtomicIntegerFieldUpdater, AtomicLongFieldUpdater, AtomicReferenceFieldUpdaterA reflection-based view of an existing volatile field, so CAS can be applied without changing the field's type. §15.4.3.
ArraysAtomicIntegerArray, AtomicLongArray, AtomicReferenceArrayAtomic element updates — notably, a volatile array gives volatile semantics only to the array reference, never to its elements.
CompoundAtomicStampedReference, AtomicMarkableReferenceAtomic update of a reference paired with a version number or a mark bit. §15.4.4.

While the atomic scalars extend Number, they do not — and cannot — extend the primitive wrapper classes: Integer and Long are immutable, while the atomic classes are mutable. They also do not redefine hashCode or equals; each instance is distinct, and like most mutable objects they are poor keys for hash-based collections.

15.3.1Atomics as "Better Volatiles"

§3.4.2 used a volatile reference to an immutable object to update several state variables atomically. That example relied on check-then-act, but the race was harmless because occasionally losing an update did not matter. In most other situations such a check-then-act is not harmless. NumberRange could not be implemented safely with a volatile reference to an immutable holder for the bounds, nor with two atomic integers holding them: because the invariant constrains both numbers and they cannot be updated simultaneously while preserving it, any such implementation has unsafe check-then-act sequences.

Combine the two techniques — an immutable value object, and an atomic reference to it — and the race closes: CasNumberRange stores an IntPair in an AtomicReference and uses compareAndSet to update either bound without NumberRange's race.

BOOK Listing 15.3 · Preserving multivariable invariants using CAS 
public class CasNumberRange {
    @Immutable
    private static class IntPair {
        final int lower;  // Invariant: lower <= upper
        final int upper;
        ...
    }
    private final AtomicReference<IntPair> values =
        new AtomicReference<IntPair>(new IntPair(0, 0));

    public int getLower() { return values.get().lower; }
    public int getUpper() { return values.get().upper; }

    public void setLower(int i) {
        while (true) {
            IntPair oldv = values.get();
            if (i > oldv.upper)
                throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                   "Can't set lower to " + i + " > upper");
            IntPair newv = new IntPair(i, oldv.upper);
            if (values.compareAndSet(oldv, newv))
                return;
        }
    }
    // similarly for setUpper
}
🔁

Read the failure path as the design: a failed CAS does not throw, it re-reads and retries — and the invariant check happens inside the loop, against freshly read state. If the check were hoisted outside the loop, the exception could be raised against a stale pair. That is the whole difference between this and NumberRange.

15.3.2Performance Comparison: Locks Versus Atomic Variables

To show the scalability difference the book built a benchmark around a pseudorandom number generator: the next "random" number is a deterministic function of the previous one, so a PRNG must remember the previous number as part of its state — one shared variable, updated on every call, which is the ideal shape for this comparison. The test driver repeatedly generates a number (touching shared state) and then performs a number of "busy-work" iterations on strictly thread-local data.

BOOK Listing 15.4 · Random number generator using ReentrantLock 
@ThreadSafe
public class ReentrantLockPseudoRandom extends PseudoRandom {
    private final Lock lock = new ReentrantLock(false);
    private int seed;

    ReentrantLockPseudoRandom(int seed) {
        this.seed = seed;
    }

    public int nextInt(int n) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            int s = seed;
            seed = calculateNext(s);
            int remainder = s % n;
            return remainder > 0 ? remainder : remainder + n;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
}
BOOK Listing 15.5 · Random number generator using AtomicInteger 
@ThreadSafe
public class AtomicPseudoRandom extends PseudoRandom {
    private AtomicInteger seed;

    AtomicPseudoRandom(int seed) {
        this.seed = new AtomicInteger(seed);
    }

    public int nextInt(int n) {
        while (true) {
            int s = seed.get();
            int nextSeed = calculateNext(s);
            if (seed.compareAndSet(s, nextSeed)) {
                int remainder = s % n;
                return remainder > 0 ? remainder : remainder + n;
            }
        }
    }
}

The two figures show throughput with low and moderate simulated work per iteration. With little thread-local computation the lock or atomic variable experiences heavy contention; with more, less — because each thread touches it less often.

So at high contention locking tends to outperform atomics, but at more realistic contention levels atomics outperform locks. A lock reacts to contention by suspending threads, reducing CPU usage and synchronization traffic on the shared memory bus — much as blocking producers in a producer–consumer design reduce the load on consumers and let them catch up. With atomics, contention management is pushed back to the calling class: AtomicPseudoRandom reacts to contention by retrying immediately, which is usually right, but in a high-contention environment just creates more contention.

🚦

The book's analogy for the same trade-off elsewhere: traffic lights give better throughput for heavy traffic, rotaries for light traffic; Ethernet's contention scheme performs better at low traffic, token passing better at heavy traffic. Every contention scheme has a load at which it is the wrong choice.

Before condemning the atomic version, note that Figure 15.1's contention level is unrealistically high: no real program does nothing but contend for a lock or an atomic variable. In practice atomics tend to scale better than locks because they deal more effectively with typical contention. (They also win on single-CPU systems, where a CAS always succeeds unless a thread is preempted mid read-modify-write.) With low to moderate contention atomics offer better scalability; with high contention locks offer better contention avoidance.

Both figures include a third curve: a PseudoRandom that keeps its state in a ThreadLocal. That changes the class's behaviour — each thread gets its own private sequence instead of all threads sharing one — but it illustrates the more important point: it is often cheaper not to share state at all. We can improve scalability by dealing more effectively with contention, but true scalability is achieved only by eliminating contention entirely.

15.4Non-blocking Algorithms

A lock-based algorithm fails when a thread holding a lock fails. A non-blocking algorithm is defined precisely so that cannot happen.

Lock-based algorithms are at risk for a number of liveness failures: if a thread holding a lock is delayed by blocking I/O, a page fault or anything else, no thread may make progress. The definitions matter here:

🛡️
Non-blocking

Failure or suspension of any thread cannot cause failure or suspension of another thread. No thread is ever prevented from proceeding by another thread's misfortune.

🚀
Lock-free

At each step, some thread can make progress. Not the same as non-blocking: it is a stronger, system-level progress guarantee.

✅
CAS-only, built correctly

Algorithms that use CAS exclusively for coordination are both non-blocking and lock-free: an uncontended CAS always succeeds, and when threads contend one always wins, so progress always happens.

⚠️
Still not hazard-free

Immune to deadlock and priority inversion — but repeated retries can still cause starvation or livelock. They remove blocking failures, not fairness ones.

We have already seen one non-blocking algorithm: CasCounter. Good non-blocking algorithms are known for stacks, queues, priority queues and hash tables — though designing new ones is a task best left to experts.

15.4.1A Non-blocking Stack

The key to constructing non-blocking algorithms is limiting atomic changes to a single variable while keeping the data structure consistent. In linked collections you can often express state transitions as changes to individual links, each represented by an AtomicReference that must be updated atomically.

Stacks are the simplest linked structure: each element refers to one other, and is referred to by one reference. ConcurrentStack is a linked list of Nodes rooted at top. push prepares a new node whose next field refers to the current top, then CASes it into place. If the same node is still on top, the CAS succeeds; if the top has changed, the CAS fails, push recomputes against the current state and tries again. Either way the stack is consistent after the CAS.

BOOK Listing 15.6 · Non-blocking stack using Treiber's algorithm (Treiber, 1986) 
@ThreadSafe
public class ConcurrentStack <E> {
    AtomicReference<Node<E>> top = new AtomicReference<Node<E>>();

    public void push(E item) {
        Node<E> newHead = new Node<E>(item);
        Node<E> oldHead;
        do {
            oldHead = top.get();
            newHead.next = oldHead;
        } while (!top.compareAndSet(oldHead, newHead));
    }

    public E pop() {
        Node<E> oldHead;
        Node<E> newHead;
        do {
            oldHead = top.get();
            if (oldHead == null)
                return null;
            newHead = oldHead.next;
        } while (!top.compareAndSet(oldHead, newHead));
        return oldHead.item;
    }

    private static class Node <E> {
        public final E item;
        public Node<E> next;

        public Node(E item) {
            this.item = item;
        }
    }
}

CasCounter and ConcurrentStack show the defining characteristic of all non-blocking algorithms: some work is done speculatively and may have to be redone. Building the node assumes the next reference will still be correct when the node is installed; the code is prepared to rebuild it otherwise.

The thread safety comes from the same place locking's does — compareAndSet provides both atomicity and visibility. A changing thread uses compareAndSet, which has the memory effects of a volatile write; a reading thread calls get on the same AtomicReference, which has the memory effects of a volatile read. So changes made by one thread are safely published to any other that examines the list, and the list is modified by a CAS that either updates the top atomically or fails on detected interference.

15.4.2A Non-blocking Linked List

A linked queue is harder than a stack because it needs fast access to both ends. It keeps separate head and tail pointers, and two references point at the tail node: the next of the current last element, and tail itself. A successful insertion must update both atomically — and at first glance that is impossible with atomic variables: two separate CASes, and if the first succeeds while the second fails the queue is inconsistent; even if both succeed, another thread may look in between.

The Michael–Scott algorithm (used by ConcurrentLinkedQueue) requires two tricks. First, keep the structure in a consistent state at every intermediate point, so that a thread arriving mid-update can tell an update is in progress and knows not to apply its own. Second — so that a thread failing mid-update does not block everyone else — make sure enough information is already in the structure for the arriving thread to finish the other thread's update for it. If B helps A, B can proceed without waiting; when A resumes it finds the job already done.

As in many queue algorithms, an empty queue consists of a "sentinel" or "dummy" node, with head and tail both initialised to it. The tail pointer always refers to the sentinel (if empty), the last element, or — if an operation is mid-update — the second-to-last element.

Insertion updates two pointers: first the next of the current last element, linking the new node to the end of the list; then tail, swinging it round to the new last element. Between those two operations the queue is in the intermediate state.

The key observation enabling both tricks: in the quiescent state tail.next is null; in the intermediate state it is non-null. So any thread can tell the queue's state just by looking at tail.next, and if the queue is intermediate it can be restored to quiescent by advancing tail one node — finishing the operation for whichever thread is mid-insertion.

BOOK Listing 15.7 · Insertion in the Michael-Scott non-blocking queue algorithm 
@ThreadSafe
public class LinkedQueue <E> {
    private static class Node <E> {
        final E item;
        final AtomicReference<Node<E>> next;

        public Node(E item, Node<E> next) {
            this.item = item;
            this.next = new AtomicReference<Node<E>>(next);
        }
    }

    private final Node<E> dummy = new Node<E>(null, null);
    private final AtomicReference<Node<E>> head
            = new AtomicReference<Node<E>>(dummy);
    private final AtomicReference<Node<E>> tail
            = new AtomicReference<Node<E>>(dummy);

    public boolean put(E item) {
        Node<E> newNode = new Node<E>(item, null);
        while (true) {
            Node<E> curTail = tail.get();
            Node<E> tailNext = curTail.next.get();
            if (curTail == tail.get()) {
                if (tailNext != null) {

                    // Queue in intermediate state, advance tail
                    tail.compareAndSet(curTail, tailNext);

                } else {
                    // In quiescent state, try inserting new node
                    if (curTail.next.compareAndSet(null, newNode)) {

                        // Insertion succeeded, try advancing tail
                        tail.compareAndSet(curTail, newNode);

                        return true;
                   }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

put first checks whether the queue is intermediate before trying to insert (step A). If it is, some thread is between its steps C and D — so rather than wait, the current thread helps by advancing the tail (step B), then repeats the check in case another thread has started inserting, until it finds the quiescent state.

The CAS at step C could fail if two threads insert simultaneously; no harm is done, nothing has changed, and the thread reloads tail and retries. Once C succeeds the insertion is considered to have taken effect — the second CAS (step D) is cleanup, which either the inserting thread or any other can perform. If D fails, the inserting thread returns anyway rather than retrying, because no retry is needed: another thread has already finished the job at its own step B. That works because no thread links a new node without first checking whether tail.next is non-null and advancing the tail until it is not.

15.4.3Atomic Field Updaters

The real ConcurrentLinkedQueue is slightly different: instead of wrapping each Node's link in an AtomicReference, it uses an ordinary volatile field and updates it through the reflection-based AtomicReferenceFieldUpdater.

BOOK Listing 15.8 · Using atomic field updaters in ConcurrentLinkedQueue 
private class Node<E> {
    private final E item;
    private volatile Node<E> next;

    public Node(E item) {
        this.item = item;
    }
}

private static AtomicReferenceFieldUpdater<Node, Node> nextUpdater
        = AtomicReferenceFieldUpdater.newUpdater(
                Node.class, Node.class, "next");

The field updater classes (Integer, Long and Reference versions) are a reflection-based "view" of an existing volatile field, letting CAS apply to fields you already have. They have no constructors; you call the newUpdater factory with the class and field name. They are not tied to an instance: one updater can update the target field on any instance of the target class.

🔓

Their atomicity guarantees are weaker: you cannot prevent the underlying field from being modified directly. compareAndSet and the arithmetic methods guarantee atomicity only with respect to other threads that also go through the updater. In ConcurrentLinkedQueue the approach is used purely for performance — for frequently allocated, short-lived nodes, avoiding an AtomicReference per node is enough to reduce insertion cost. In nearly all situations ordinary atomic variables do just fine, and only a few cases need field updaters. (They are also useful when you need atomic updates while preserving the serialized form of an existing class.)

15.4.4The ABA Problem

ABA is an anomaly of naive CAS use in algorithms where nodes can be recycled — primarily in environments without garbage collection. A CAS effectively asks "is the value of V still A?", and proceeds if so. In most situations, including every example in this chapter, that is entirely sufficient. But sometimes what you really want to ask is "has the value of V changed since I last observed it to be A?" — and for some algorithms, going A → B → A still counts as a change that requires a retry.

Why it shows up in memory-managed code rarely, and in hand-managed code often

ABA arises in algorithms that do their own memory management for link nodes. There, the fact that the head of a list still refers to a previously observed node is not enough to conclude that the contents of the list have not changed: the node may have been popped, reused, and pushed back with different contents.

If you cannot avoid ABA by letting the garbage collector manage link nodes for you, the fix is simple: instead of updating a reference, update a pair — a reference and a version number. Even if the value goes A → B → A, the version numbers differ.

AtomicStampedReference atomically updates an object-reference-plus-integer pair, giving "versioned" references immune to ABA (in practice — theoretically the counter can wrap). AtomicMarkableReference updates a reference-plus-boolean pair, which some algorithms use to let a node remain in a list while marked as deleted.

Many processors provide a double-wide CAS (CAS2 or CASX) that operates on a pointer-integer pair, which would make this reasonably efficient; as of Java 6, AtomicStampedReference does not use double-wide CAS even where it is available. (Double-wide CAS is not DCAS, which operates on two unrelated memory locations; as of the book's writing, no current processor implements DCAS.)

Summary of the chapter

Non-blocking algorithms maintain thread safety by using low-level concurrency primitives such as compare-and-swap instead of locks. Those primitives are exposed through the atomic variable classes, which can also be used as "better volatile variables" providing atomic update operations for integers and object references. Non-blocking algorithms are difficult to design and implement, but can offer better scalability under typical conditions and greater resistance to liveness failures. Many of the advances in concurrent performance from one JVM version to the next come from the use of non-blocking algorithms, both within the JVM and in the platform libraries.

The last row is the punchline of Figures 15.1 and 15.2 as well. CAS and mutexes are two ways of managing contention; the third curve in each of those graphs — ThreadLocal, at roughly four times the throughput — is what happens when you stop having contention. "True scalability is achieved only by eliminating contention entirely."

§Patterns worth stealing

The eight listings above are the book's. These two are the shapes worth keeping: a retry loop written properly, and a versioned reference that is immune to ABA.

1The CAS retry loop, done properly

PATTERN Read — compute — CAS, with a bounded spin and a fallback 
/**
 * The canonical optimistic loop: snapshot, compute, CAS, repeat.
 * Note what each piece is for -- this is where non-blocking code goes wrong.
 */
public final class Optimistic {
    private Optimistic() { }

    public interface Update<T> { T apply(T current); }

    /**
     * Returns the value after the update. Spins are bounded so that a
     * pathological contention pattern cannot produce unbounded livelock.
     */
    public static <T> T update(AtomicReference<T> ref, Update<T> fn,
                              int maxAttempts) {
        for (int attempt = 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++) {
            T current = ref.get();          // volatile read; must be INSIDE the loop
            T next = fn.apply(current);     // pure: may be discarded and recomputed
            if (ref.compareAndSet(current, next))
                return next;                // committed: has volatile-write semantics
            /* failed: somebody else won. Pausing is optional, but at high
               contention an immediate retry is what turns a race into a storm. */
            if (attempt > 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted())
                break;                      // stay responsive to cancellation
            Thread.onSpinWait();            // hint: we are spinning, not blocking
        }
        throw new IllegalStateException("could not commit after " + maxAttempts);
    }

    /* counters: do not write this, use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() */
    public static int incrementBounded(AtomicInteger counter, int maxAttempts) {
        for (int attempt = 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++) {
            int current = counter.get();
            if (current == Integer.MAX_VALUE)
                throw new ArithmeticException("overflow");
            if (counter.compareAndSet(current, current + 1))
                return current + 1;
        }
        throw new IllegalStateException("contended counter gave up");
    }
}

Three details separate this from a broken version: the read happens inside the loop, so a retry always computes against fresh state; the update function must be pure, because its result can be thrown away at any moment; and the loop is bounded — the book's footnote is right that retries are theoretically unbounded, and there are production systems where an unbounded spin under contention is a availability bug rather than a theoretical one.

2A versioned reference that cannot be fooled

PATTERN AtomicStampedReference for ABA-prone state, plus a comparison helper 
/**
 * A single-slot register whose CAS also checks a version, so A -> B -> A
 * is detected as a change. Useful when slots are recycled by hand.
 */
public final class VersionedSlot<T> {
    private final AtomicStampedReference<T> ref;

    public VersionedSlot(T initial) {
        ref = new AtomicStampedReference<>(initial, 0);
    }

    public T get() { return ref.getReference(); }
    public int version() { return ref.getStamp(); }

    /**
     * Replace the value only if it is still `expected` with the expected stamp.
     * Returns false if either the reference or the version has moved on --
     * which is the whole point: A -> B -> A fails here, where plain CAS
     * would have wrongly succeeded.
     */
    public boolean replace(T expected, int expectedStamp, T next) {
        int[] stampHolder = new int[1];
        T current = ref.get(stampHolder);          // atomic snapshot of both
        if (current != expected || stampHolder[0] != expectedStamp)
            return false;
        return ref.compareAndSet(expected, next, expectedStamp, expectedStamp + 1);
    }

    /**
     * Compare-and-set on the reference alone, bumping the version. Convenient
     * for idempotent updates where the caller cannot track stamps.
     */
    public boolean set(T next) {
        int[] stampHolder = new int[1];
        for (;;) {
            T current = ref.get(stampHolder);
            int stamp = stampHolder[0];
            if (ref.compareAndSet(current, next, stamp, stamp + 1))
                return true;                       // version always advances
        }
    }

    /* the trap this avoids */
    static <T> boolean naive(AtomicReference<T> r, T a, T b) {
        // returns true even if r went a -> other -> a in the meantime
        return r.compareAndSet(a, b);
    }
}

get(int[] stampHolder) is the awkward-looking part, and it is the point: it reads the reference and the stamp in one atomic operation. Reading them with two separate calls would reintroduce exactly the race the class exists to prevent. In garbage-collected Java you will rarely need this — node recycling is the usual source of ABA — but the technique is worth recognising when you see a stamp field in someone else's lock-free code.

TermMeaning as used hereWhere it goes

✓Cheat sheet & self-check

If you need…UseWhy
A counter or sequence generatorAtomicInteger/AtomicLongAtomic arithmetic with no suspension; a lock adds housekeeping around the same CAS

✅
Do

Read the value inside the retry loop. Keep the update function pure. Bound the spin, or back off, under possible contention. Use immutable value objects for multi-field invariants. Prefer the library's non-blocking collections to your own.

🚫
Avoid

Hoisting the get() out of the loop — the classic lost-update bug. Two atomics pretending to be one invariant. Unbounded spin loops. Field updaters without documenting the weaker guarantee. Hand-rolling a lock-free queue because the lock "felt slow".

🧠
The one habit

Before choosing a mechanism, ask how often the threads actually collide. None: eliminate the sharing. Occasional: an atomic. Heavy and sustained: a lock. The figures in this chapter are one picture of that decision — and the top curve in both is the one where nobody collides.

Five questions the chapter leaves you with

  1. Which of my shared variables are volatile today but really need an atomic read-modify-write?
  2. Do I have two atomics that are supposed to hold an invariant together?
  3. What is my retry loop's bound — and what does the caller see if it is hit?
  4. How contended is my hot variable, in the terms of Figures 15.1 and 15.2 — and did I measure, or assume?
  5. Could this state simply be thread-local?

Notes carried over from the chapter

  1. A smart JVM need not suspend a thread when it contends for a lock; it could use profiling data to decide adaptively between suspension and spin locking, based on how long the lock was held during previous acquisitions.
  2. It is theoretically possible, though wholly impractical, to use the semantics of volatile to construct mutexes and other synchronizers (Raynal, 1986).
  3. Doing nothing may be a perfectly sensible response to a failed CAS: in some non-blocking algorithms, such as the linked queue algorithm in §15.4.2, a failed CAS means someone else already did the work you were planning to do.
  4. Theoretically a CAS loop could retry arbitrarily many times if other threads keep winning the race; in practice this sort of starvation rarely happens.
  5. Actually the biggest disadvantage of CAS is the difficulty of constructing the surrounding algorithms correctly.
  6. The same holds in other domains: traffic lights provide better throughput for high traffic but rotaries for low traffic; Ethernet's contention scheme performs better at low traffic, token passing better with heavy traffic.
  7. For a full account of the correctness of the Michael–Scott algorithm, see Michael and Scott (1996) or Herlihy and Shavit (2006).
  8. Immune in practice, anyway; theoretically the counter could wrap.
  9. Many processors provide a double-wide CAS (CAS2 or CASX) operating on a pointer-integer pair, which would make this reasonably efficient; as of Java 6, AtomicStampedReference does not use it even on platforms that support it. Double-wide CAS differs from DCAS, which operates on two unrelated memory locations — and as of this writing no processor implements DCAS.
