Java Concurrency in Practice · Chapter 16

Chapter 16 — The Java Memory Model

Everything in this book rests on one question, asked at the level of a single variable: when is a write made by one thread guaranteed to be visible to another? The answer is the JMM — a partial ordering called happens-before. This chapter pulls back the curtain: why reordering exists, what the eight rules are, how FutureTask rides on an ordering it did not create, and why the double-checked locking idiom was broken for years.

📖 pp. 207–215 🧩 3 sections · 8 listings · 2 figures ⏱️ ~24 min read 🏷️ Part IV — Advanced Topics

Chapter in one paragraph

TL;DR — the six things worth remembering

  1. A memory model answers one question: "under what conditions does a thread that reads aVariable see the value 3?" Without synchronization the answer may be "later", "never", or "a value that was never written there".
  2. Reordering is not a bug, it is the optimisation. Compilers, JITs and processors all reorder freely, and the JLS only demands as-if-serial semantics within a thread. That latitude is where much of the last twenty years of performance came from.
  3. happens-before is the whole contract. If A happens-before B, B sees A's results. If there is no happens-before edge, the JVM may reorder freely — and a program with no data races is guaranteed sequential consistency.
  4. Eight rules generate every edge you will ever use: program order, monitor lock, volatile variable, thread start, thread termination, interruption, finalizer, and transitivity.
  5. Publication safety is an edge, not a habit. Unsafe publication lets a thread see a non-null reference to a half-constructed object; safe publication is just a guaranteed happens-before from the publisher to the consumer.
  6. Immutable objects get a free pass. Initialization safety freezes the final fields at constructor exit, so a properly constructed immutable object is safe to share however it is published — even through a data race.

16.1What is a Memory Model, and Why Would I Want One?

One thread assigns aVariable = 3. When, exactly, does another thread see 3?

That sounds like a dumb question. In the absence of synchronization there are several reasons a thread might not immediately — or ever — see the result of an operation in another thread:

🛠️
Compilers reorder

The compiler may emit instructions in a different order than the source suggests, or keep a variable in a register instead of memory.

🔀
Processors run in parallel

Hardware may execute independent instructions out of order, or while an earlier one is still in flight.

🗄️
Caches commit out of order

Two writes may reach main memory in the opposite order from the one in which they were issued.

👻
Caches are private

A value sitting in another processor's local cache simply may not be visible to you at all.

Together these can stop a thread from seeing the most up-to-date value, and can make memory actions in other threads appear to happen out of order — if you do not use adequate synchronization.

In a single-threaded environment all of these tricks are invisible: the Java Language Specification requires the JVM to maintain within-thread as-if-serial semantics. As long as the program has the same result as if it were executed in program order in a strictly sequential environment, all these games are permissible. And that is a good thing, because these rearrangements are responsible for much of the improvement in computing performance in recent years — pipelined superscalar execution, dynamic instruction scheduling, speculative execution, sophisticated multilevel caches, and compilers with global register allocation.

In a multithreaded environment the illusion of sequentiality cannot be maintained without significant cost. Threads mostly do their own thing, so excessive inter-thread coordination would only slow the application for no benefit. It is only when threads share data that coordination is needed — and the JVM relies on the program to say when that is, by using synchronization.

The JMM specifies the minimal guarantees the JVM must make about when writes become visible to other threads. It balances predictability and ease of development against the reality of implementing high-performance JVMs on many processor architectures. Some of it may be disturbing at first if you are not familiar with the tricks modern processors and compilers use.

16.1.1Platform Memory Models

In a shared-memory multiprocessor each processor has its own cache, periodically reconciled with main memory. Architectures provide varying degrees of cache coherence; some offer only minimal guarantees, allowing different processors to see different values for the same location at virtually any time. The operating system, compiler and runtime — and sometimes the program — must make up the difference between what the hardware provides and what thread safety requires.

Keeping every processor informed about every other processor is expensive, and most of the time the information is not needed, so processors relax their coherence guarantees. An architecture's memory model says what guarantees programs can expect, and names the special instructions — memory barriers or fences — that buy the extra coordination when data is shared. Java shields you from the differences: the JVM inserts the barriers at the appropriate places.

🚫

One convenient mental model is sequential consistency: a single global order of operations, where every read sees the last write to that variable by any processor. It is happy, unrealistic, and false — no modern multiprocessor offers sequential consistency, and neither does the JMM. The von Neumann model is only a vague approximation of how modern multiprocessors behave. Developers assume it constantly, and that assumption is the source of most of the surprises in this chapter.

The bottom line: modern shared-memory multiprocessors and compilers can do surprising things when data is shared across threads, unless you have told them not to through memory barriers. Fortunately Java programs need not place barriers; they need only identify when shared state is accessed, by using synchronization properly.

16.1.2Reordering

Chapter 2 used interaction diagrams to show "unlucky timing" — the scheduler interleaving operations so as to produce wrong results. It gets worse: the JMM can permit actions to appear to execute in different orders from the perspective of different threads. All the reasons operations might be delayed or appear out of order are grouped under reordering.

PossibleReordering shows how hard it is to reason about even the simplest concurrent program without correct synchronization. It is easy to see how it could print (1,0), (0,1) or (1,1): A could run to completion first, B could, or they could interleave. But it can also print (0,0) — the actions in each thread have no dataflow dependence on each other, so they can be executed out of order. (Even if they run in order, the timing by which caches flush can make A's assignments appear reversed to B.)

BOOK Listing 16.1 · Insufficiently Synchronized Program that can have Surprising Results. Don't Do this. 
public class PossibleReordering {
    static int x = 0, y = 0;
    static int a = 0, b = 0;

    public static void main(String[] args)
            throws InterruptedException {
        Thread one = new Thread(new Runnable() {
            public void run() {
                a = 1;
                x = b;
            }
        });
        Thread other = new Thread(new Runnable() {
            public void run() {
                b = 1;
                y = a;
            }
        });
        one.start(); other.start();
        one.join();   other.join();
        System.out.println("( "+ x + "," + y + ")");
    }
}

PossibleReordering is a trivial program and it is still surprisingly tricky to enumerate its possible results. Rather than reason about ordering in the absence of synchronization — which is prohibitively difficult — it is much easier to ensure the program uses synchronization appropriately. Synchronization inhibits the compiler, runtime and hardware from reordering memory operations in ways that would violate the JMM's visibility guarantees.

On most popular processor architectures the memory model is strong enough that a volatile read costs about the same as a non-volatile read.

16.1.3The Java Memory Model in 500 Words or Less

The JMM is specified in terms of actions: reads and writes of variables, lock and unlock of monitors, and starting and joining with threads. It defines a partial ordering called happens-before over all actions in the program. To guarantee that the thread executing action B can see the results of action A — whether or not A and B occur in different threads — there must be a happens-before relationship between A and B. In the absence of a happens-before ordering, the JVM is free to reorder the two as it pleases.

Two definitions that do all the work

Data race. A variable is read by more than one thread, and written by at least one thread, but the reads and writes are not ordered by happens-before.

Correctly synchronized. A program with no data races. Correctly synchronized programs exhibit sequential consistency: all actions appear to happen in a fixed, global order.

And here are all the rules. Every happens-before edge you will ever rely on comes from one of them:

#RuleGives you the edgeIn practice
1Program orderEach action in a thread happens-before every later action in that thread.Within a thread, everything is ordered — this is what makes the other rules composable.
2Monitor lockAn unlock on a monitor happens-before every subsequent lock on that same monitor.The whole basis of synchronized: exit publishes, entry acquires.
3Volatile variableA write to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of that same field.A volatile write is a cheap one-way publication point. Atomic variables share these semantics.
4Thread startA call to Thread.start happens-before every action in the started thread.Anything set up before start() is visible to the new thread.
5Thread terminationAny action in a thread happens-before another thread detects it has terminated.join() returning, or isAlive() returning false, publishes everything the thread did.
6Interruptioninterrupt happens-before the interrupted thread detects the interrupt.InterruptedException, isInterrupted, interrupted.
7FinalizerThe end of a constructor happens-before the start of that object's finalizer.Rarely relevant now, but it is in the model.
8TransitivityIf A happens-before B and B happens-before C, then A happens-before C.The rule that lets you chain a lock or volatile write to everything around it.

Even though actions are only partially ordered, the synchronization actions — lock acquisition and release, reads and writes of volatile variables — are totally ordered. That is what makes it sensible to speak of a "subsequent" lock acquisition or volatile read.

Figure 16.2 shows the relation when two threads synchronize on a common lock. All actions within A are ordered by program order, as are those within B. Because A releases M and B subsequently acquires M, everything A did before the release is ordered before everything B does after the acquisition. When two threads synchronize on different locks, we can say nothing about ordering between them: there is no happens-before relation at all.

🔗

The subtlety worth staring at in Figure 16.2: y = 1 happens before A takes the lock, yet B sees it after taking the lock. Nothing had to be done to y specially — it rode along on the lock's edge, by program order plus the monitor rule plus transitivity. That is the same mechanism §16.1.4 turns into a deliberate technique.

16.1.4Piggybacking on Synchronization

Because happens-before is so strong, you can sometimes piggyback on the visibility properties of an existing synchronization: combine the program order rule with one of the other rules (usually monitor lock or volatile variable) to order accesses to a variable that is not otherwise guarded. The technique is very sensitive to the order in which statements occur, and therefore fragile — an advanced trick to be reserved for squeezing the last drop of performance out of the most performance-critical classes, like ReentrantLock.

FutureTask illustrates it. AQS maintains an integer of synchronizer state, which FutureTask uses to store the task state: running, completed or cancelled. But FutureTask also keeps additional variables, such as the result of the computation. When one thread calls set to save the result and another calls get to retrieve it, the two had better be ordered by happens-before. The reference to the result could be made volatile, but it is possible to exploit existing synchronization at lower cost.

FutureTask is carefully crafted so that a successful call to tryReleaseShared always happens-before a subsequent call to tryAcquireShared: tryReleaseShared always writes to a volatile variable that is read by tryAcquireShared. Since innerSet writes result before calling releaseShared (which calls tryReleaseShared), and innerGet reads result after calling acquireShared (which calls tryAcquireShared), program order plus the volatile rule ensure the write of result in innerSet happens-before the read of result in innerGet.

BOOK Listing 16.2 · Inner Class of FutureTask Illustrating Synchronization Piggybacking 
// Inner class of FutureTask
private final class Sync extends AbstractQueuedSynchronizer {
    private static final int RUNNING = 1, RAN = 2, CANCELLED = 4;
    private V result;
    private Exception exception;

    void innerSet(V v) {
        while (true) {
            int s = getState();
            if (ranOrCancelled(s))
                return;
            if (compareAndSetState(s, RAN))
                break;
        }
        result = v;
        releaseShared(0);
        done();
    }

    V innerGet() throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
        acquireSharedInterruptibly(0);
        if (getState() == CANCELLED)
            throw new CancellationException();
        if (exception != null)
            throw new ExecutionException(exception);
        return result;
    }
}

We call this piggybacking because it uses an existing happens-before ordering, created for some other reason, to ensure visibility of X — rather than creating an ordering specifically for publishing X. It is fragile and should not be undertaken casually. But in some cases it is perfectly reasonable, such as when a class commits to a happens-before ordering between methods as part of its specification. Safe publication using a BlockingQueue is exactly that: putting an object and subsequently taking it constitutes safe publication because the implementation guarantees the enqueue happens-before the dequeue.

Happens-before orderings the class library promises you

  • Placing an item in a thread-safe collection happens-before another thread retrieves that item;
  • Counting down on a CountDownLatch happens-before a thread returns from await on that latch;
  • Releasing a permit to a Semaphore happens-before acquiring a permit from that same semaphore;
  • Actions taken by the task represented by a Future happen-before another thread successfully returns from Future.get;
  • Submitting a Runnable or Callable to an Executor happens-before the task begins execution;
  • A thread arriving at a CyclicBarrier or Exchanger happens-before the other threads are released from that same barrier or exchange point — and with a barrier action, arriving happens-before the action, which happens-before the release.

16.2Publication

Chapter 3's publication rules are not style advice. They are the JMM, viewed from a higher altitude.

The safe-publication techniques described in Chapter 3 derive their safety from guarantees provided by the JMM; the risks of improper publication are consequences of the absence of a happens-before ordering between publishing a shared object and accessing it from another thread.

16.2.1Unsafe Publication

The possibility of reordering in the absence of happens-before explains why publishing an object without adequate synchronization can allow another thread to see a partially constructed object (§3.5). Initializing a new object involves writing its fields; publishing a reference involves writing another variable — the reference. If publishing does not happen-before the consuming thread loading that reference, then the write of the reference can be reordered (from the consumer's perspective) with the writes to the fields. The consumer can then see an up-to-date reference and out-of-date state.

Unsafe publication can result from incorrect lazy initialization. At first glance the only problem with UnsafeLazyInitialization looks like the check-then-act race from §2.2.2 — and you might be willing to overlook that, plus the inefficiency of creating the Resource more than once, if all instances are interchangeable. Unfortunately it is still not safe even then, because another thread could observe a partially constructed Resource.

BOOK Listing 16.3 · Unsafe Lazy Initialization. Don't Do this. 
@NotThreadSafe
public class UnsafeLazyInitialization {
    private static Resource resource;

    public static Resource getInstance() {
        if (resource == null)
            resource = new Resource();  // unsafe publication
        return resource;
    }
}

Suppose thread A is first to invoke getInstance: it sees null, instantiates a Resource, and sets resource to reference it. When B later calls getInstance it might see the non-null value and use the already-constructed object. This looks harmless, but there is no happens-before ordering between A's write of resource and B's read of it. A data race has been used to publish the object, so B is not guaranteed to see the correct state.

The constructor changes the fields of the freshly allocated Resource from their default values (written by the Object constructor) to their initial values. Since neither thread used synchronization, B could see A's actions in a different order than A performed them — so even though A initialized the Resource before setting the reference, B could see the write to resource as occurring before the writes to the fields. B could thus see a partially constructed Resource, in an invalid state, whose state may unexpectedly change later.

🧨

With the exception of immutable objects, it is not safe to use an object initialized by another thread unless publication happens-before the consuming thread uses it. This is the single sentence the rest of §16.2 unpacks.

16.2.2Safe Publication

The safe-publication idioms from Chapter 3 ensure the published object is visible because they ensure the publication happens-before the consuming thread loads the reference. If A places X on a BlockingQueue (and no thread subsequently modifies it) and B retrieves it, B is guaranteed to see X as A left it — the implementations have enough internal synchronization that the put happens-before the take. Similarly, a shared variable guarded by a lock, or a shared volatile variable, orders reads and writes by happens-before.

This is actually a stronger promise than safe publication alone. When X is safely published from A to B, safe publication guarantees visibility of the state of X — but not of the state of other variables A may have touched. If A putting X on a queue happens-before B fetching X, then not only does B see X as A left it, B sees everything A did before the handoff. That is the "piggyback" from §16.1.4, and it is why handing an object to an executor carries your setup work with it.

The JMM guarantees B sees a value at least as up to date as the value A wrote; subsequent writes may or may not be visible.

Why then focus so heavily on @GuardedBy and safe publication when the JMM already gives us the more powerful happens-before? Because thinking in terms of handing off object ownership fits better into most program designs than thinking about the visibility of individual memory writes. Happens-before operates at the level of individual memory accesses — it is a sort of "concurrency assembly language". Safe publication operates at a level closer to your program's design.

16.2.3Safe Initialization Idioms

It sometimes makes sense to defer initializing objects that are expensive to construct, but we have seen how misuse of lazy initialization leads to trouble. UnsafeLazyInitialization can be fixed by making getInstance synchronized. Because the code path is short (a test and a predicted branch), if getInstance is not called frequently by many threads there is little enough contention that this performs adequately.

BOOK Listing 16.4 · Thread-safe Lazy Initialization 
@ThreadSafe
public class SafeLazyInitialization {
    private static Resource resource;

    public synchronized static Resource getInstance() {
        if (resource == null)
            resource = new Resource();
        return resource;
    }
}

Static fields with initializers — or fields initialized in a static initialization block — get additional thread-safety guarantees. Static initializers run at class initialization time, after loading but before the class is used by any thread. Because the JVM acquires a lock during initialization [JLS 12.4.2] and every thread acquires that lock at least once to ensure the class is loaded, memory writes made during static initialization are automatically visible to all threads. Statically initialized objects therefore need no explicit synchronization, either during construction or when referenced.

That applies only to the as-constructed state: if the object is mutable, readers and writers still need synchronization to make subsequent modifications visible and to avoid corruption.

BOOK Listing 16.5 · Eager Initialization 
@ThreadSafe
public class EagerInitialization {
    private static Resource resource  = new Resource();

    public static Resource getResource() { return resource; }
}

Eager initialization eliminates the synchronization cost paid on every call to getInstance in SafeLazyInitialization. It can be combined with the JVM's lazy class loading to get lazy initialization with no synchronization on the common path: the lazy initialization holder class idiom [EJ Item 48] uses a class whose only purpose is to initialize the Resource. The JVM defers initializing ResourceHolder until it is actually used [JLS 12.4.1], and because the Resource is initialized by a static initializer, no additional synchronization is needed. The first call to getResource by any thread causes ResourceHolder to be loaded and initialized, at which point the Resource is created through the static initializer.

BOOK Listing 16.6 · Lazy Initialization Holder Class Idiom 
@ThreadSafe
public class ResourceFactory {
     private static class ResourceHolder {
         public static Resource resource = new Resource();
     }

     public static Resource getResource() {
         return  ResourceHolder.resource ;
     }
}
🏆

Of the four idioms, the holder class is the one to reach for by default: lazy, thread-safe, and free of synchronization on the hot path — and it needs no explanation of happens-before to justify it. Eager initialization is second, and is simpler still when you do not mind the cost at startup. The next section covers the one that looks cleverest and does not work.

16.2.4Double-checked Locking

No book on concurrency would be complete without the infamous double-checked locking (DCL) anti-pattern. In very early JVMs, synchronization — even uncontended — had a significant cost, so many clever (or clever-looking) tricks were invented to reduce its impact: some good, some bad, some ugly. DCL falls into "ugly".

At the time, lazy initialization was common, to avoid unnecessary expensive work or shorten startup. A properly written lazy initialization method requires synchronization. But synchronization was slow and — more importantly — not completely understood: the exclusion aspects were well enough understood, the visibility aspects were not.

DCL purported to offer the best of both worlds: lazy initialization without paying the synchronization penalty on the common path. It first checked whether initialization was needed without synchronizing, and if the reference was not null, used it. Otherwise it synchronized and checked again, ensuring only one thread actually initialized the shared Resource. The common path — fetching a reference to an already constructed object — used no synchronization. And that is precisely where the problem is: it is possible for a thread to see a partially constructed Resource.

BOOK Listing 16.7 · Double-checked-locking Anti-pattern. Don't Do this. 
@NotThreadSafe
public class DoubleCheckedLocking {
    private static Resource resource;

    public static Resource getInstance() {
        if (resource == null) {
            synchronized (DoubleCheckedLocking.class) {
                if (resource == null)
                    resource = new Resource();
            }
        }
        return resource;
    }
}
⚠️

The real problem with DCL is the assumption that the worst thing that can happen when reading a shared reference without synchronization is seeing a stale value — in which case the idiom compensates by trying again under the lock. But the worst case is considerably worse: you can see a current value of the reference and stale values for the object's state, which means the object can be observed in an invalid or incorrect state. Retrying under the lock does not help, because the outer test already said "initialized".

Subsequent changes in the JMM (Java 5.0 and later) have made DCL work if resource is made volatile, and the performance impact of that is small, since volatile reads are usually only slightly more expensive than non-volatile reads. Nevertheless this is an idiom whose utility has largely passed: the forces that motivated it — slow uncontended synchronization, slow JVM startup — are gone, which makes it less effective as an optimization. The lazy initialization holder idiom offers the same benefits and is easier to understand.

16.3Initialization Safety

The one place where publishing through a data race is safe: when the object is immutable and properly constructed.

The guarantee of initialization safety allows properly constructed immutable objects to be safely shared across threads without synchronization, regardless of how they are published — even if published through a data race. (Which means UnsafeLazyInitialization is actually safe if Resource is immutable.)

Without initialization safety, supposedly immutable objects like String could appear to change their value if synchronization were not used by both publishing and consuming threads. The security architecture relies on the immutability of String; a lack of initialization safety could create vulnerabilities that let malicious code bypass security checks.

Initialization safety guarantees that, for properly constructed objects, all threads see the correct values of final fields set by the constructor, regardless of how the object is published. Furthermore, any variables reachable through a final field of a properly constructed object — the elements of a final array, the contents of a HashMap referenced by a final field — are also guaranteed visible to other threads.

The freeze

For objects with final fields, initialization safety prohibits reordering any part of construction with the initial load of a reference to that object. All writes to final fields made by the constructor — as well as to variables reachable through those fields — become "frozen" when the constructor completes, and any thread that obtains a reference to the object is guaranteed to see a value at least as up to date as the frozen value. Writes that initialize variables reachable through final fields are not reordered with operations following the post-construction freeze.

Initialization safety means SafeStates could be safely published even through unsafe lazy initialization, or by stashing a reference to it in a public static field with no synchronization — even though it uses no synchronization itself and relies on a non-thread-safe HashSet.

BOOK Listing 16.8 · Initialization Safety for Immutable Objects 
@ThreadSafe
public class SafeStates {
    private  final  Map<String, String> states;

    public SafeStates() {
        states = new HashMap<String, String>();
        states.put("alaska", "AK");
        states.put("alabama", "AL");
        ...
        states.put("wyoming", "WY");
    }

    public String getAbbreviation(String s) {
        return states.get(s);
    }
}

But a number of small changes to SafeStates would take away its thread safety:

🔓
states not final

Without the final there is no freeze, so initialization safety has nothing to guarantee about that field.

✏️
Contents modified after construction

If any method other than the constructor modified the map, initialization safety would not be strong enough for unsynchronized access.

🧩
Other non-final fields

Other threads might still see incorrect values for those fields — the guarantee covers only what is reachable through finals.

🏃
this escapes during construction

Letting the object escape invalidates the initialization-safety guarantee entirely: the freeze happens at constructor exit.

Initialization safety makes visibility guarantees only for the values reachable through final fields as of the time the constructor finishes. For values reachable through non-final fields, or values that may change after construction, you must use synchronization to ensure visibility.

Summary of the chapter

The Java Memory Model specifies when the actions of one thread on memory are guaranteed to be visible to another. The specifics involve ensuring that operations are ordered by a partial ordering called happens-before, which is specified at the level of individual memory and synchronization operations. In the absence of sufficient synchronization, some very strange things can happen when threads access shared data. However, the higher-level rules offered in Chapters 2 and 3 — such as @GuardedBy and safe publication — can be used to ensure thread safety without resorting to the low-level details of happens-before.

▶Interactive: which outcomes are legal?

PossibleReordering can print four different pairs — and (0,0) is the one that should not be possible and is. Step through the outcomes under each synchronization discipline and watch the set shrink as happens-before edges are added.

Step through: with no synchronization, all four outcomes are allowed — including the one where both threads read 0.
DisciplineEdge that existsOutcomes allowedWhat it costs

🎯

The row that matters is the first: (0,0) requires each thread to read the other's variable before writing its own, which is a reordering of two independent writes. Nothing in the JMM forbids it when there is no happens-before edge — and once you have seen it, "just add synchronization" stops looking like boilerplate and starts looking like the only thing standing between you and an object that is visible before it is built.

§Patterns worth stealing

Two listings: every lazy-initialization idiom in one file, annotated with the edge each one relies on, and a fixed PossibleReordering you can actually run.

1The four initialization idioms, with their happens-before edges

PATTERN Unsafe, synchronized, holder-idiom and fixed double-checked locking side by side 
public final class Lazy {
    private Lazy() { }

    static final class Resource {
        final String name;
        Resource(String name) { this.name = name; }
    }

    /* 1. UNSAFE. No happens-before edge between the write of `resource`
       and any thread that reads it, so a consumer can see a non-null
       reference to a half-built Resource. A data race, full stop. */
    static class Unsafe {
        private static Resource resource;
        static Resource get() {
            if (resource == null)
                resource = new Resource("unsafe");
            return resource;
        }
    }

    /* 2. SYNCHRONIZED. The monitor rule supplies the edge: unlock on
       Lazy.class happens-before the next lock, and program order carries
       the constructor's writes along with it. Correct, and the cost is
       one lock acquisition per call. */
    static class Synchronized {
        private static Resource resource;
        static synchronized Resource get() {
            if (resource == null)
                resource = new Resource("synchronized");
            return resource;
        }
    }

    /* 3. HOLDER IDIOM. The JVM's class-initialization lock does the work
       once; after that, reads are plain reads of a static final that was
       frozen at class init. No synchronization on the common path. */
    static class Holder {
        private static class ResourceHolder {
            static final Resource RESOURCE = new Resource("holder");
        }
        static Resource get() { return ResourceHolder.RESOURCE; }
    }

    /* 4. DOUBLE-CHECKED LOCKING, FIXED. Only correct because `resource`
       is volatile: the volatile rule orders the constructor's writes
       before the publication read. Without volatile this is Listing 16.7
       and it is broken -- the outer test can succeed on a reference whose
       fields are not yet visible. */
    static class FixedDcl {
        private static volatile Resource resource;
        static Resource get() {
            Resource r = resource;          // one volatile read, then use it
            if (r == null) {
                synchronized (FixedDcl.class) {
                    r = resource;
                    if (r == null) {
                        r = new Resource("dcl");
                        resource = r;       // volatile write publishes it
                    }
                }
            }
            return r;
        }
    }
}

Note the one-line change between idiom 4 and the anti-pattern in Listing 16.7: volatile. That single keyword is the difference between "no ordering" and "the volatile rule applies", and it is exactly the sort of change that is invisible in code review. If you remember nothing else from this chapter: a reference read without synchronization tells you nothing about the state of the object it points at.

2A runnable PossibleReordering, and its fix

PATTERN ReorderingDemo: demonstrable data race, then the same thing with an edge 
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;

/**
 * Runs PossibleReordering many times and tallies the outcomes it observes.
 * The unsynchronized variant will -- rarely, on real hardware -- report
 * (0,0); the synchronized variant never can, because the two threads are
 * ordered by the monitor rule.
 */
public class ReorderingDemo {

    /* the book's program, kept honest: no volatile, no locks */
    static class UnsafePair {
        int x = 0, y = 0, a = 0, b = 0;

        void run() throws InterruptedException {
            Thread one = new Thread(() -> { a = 1; x = b; });
            Thread other = new Thread(() -> { b = 1; y = a; });
            one.start(); other.start();
            one.join(); other.join();
        }
        String result() { return "(" + x + "," + y + ")"; }
    }

    /* same program, one shared lock: the unlock->lock edge means at least
       one thread must see the other's write, so (0,0) is impossible */
    static class SafePair {
        int x = 0, y = 0, a = 0, b = 0;
        private final Object lock = new Object();

        void run() throws InterruptedException {
            Thread one = new Thread(() -> {
                synchronized (lock) { a = 1; x = b; }
            });
            Thread other = new Thread(() -> {
                synchronized (lock) { b = 1; y = a; }
            });
            one.start(); other.start();
            one.join(); other.join();
        }
        String result() { return "(" + x + "," + y + ")"; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int drafts = 20_000;
        java.util.Map<String, Integer> unsafe = new java.util.TreeMap<>();
        java.util.Map<String, Integer> safe = new java.util.TreeMap<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < drafts; i++) {
            UnsafePair u = new UnsafePair();
            u.run();
            unsafe.merge(u.result(), 1, Integer::sum);

            SafePair s = new SafePair();
            s.run();
            safe.merge(s.result(), 1, Integer::sum);
        }
        System.out.println("unsynchronized: " + unsafe);
        System.out.println("synchronized:   " + safe);
        /* Do not "fix" a flaky test by re-running it. If UnsafePair ever
           prints (0,0) -- or a reader sees a half-built object -- the
           program has a data race, and more runs only change the odds. */
    }
}

Two things to notice. First, the loop is not a fix for anything — it is a demonstration that the outcome set is genuinely larger without synchronization, and that the probability is small enough that a single green run tells you nothing (Chapter 12's point, arriving here from the other direction). Second, the fixed version does not make the result correct in any business sense — (0,1) and (1,0) are still possible — it only forbids the outcome that involves seeing a thread's work out of order.

§Vocabulary introduced in Chapter 16

TermMeaning as used hereWhere it goes
Memory modelThe rules that say when a write by one thread becomes visible to a read in another.Ch. 16.1
As-if-serialThe JLS guarantee within a thread: any reordering is fine as long as the thread's own result is unchanged.Ch. 16.1
Sequential consistencyOne global order of all operations, each read seeing the last write. No modern multiprocessor offers it, and neither does the JMM.Ch. 16.1.1
Memory barrier / fenceThe special instruction an architecture requires to buy extra ordering guarantees. Java inserts them for you.Ch. 16.1.1
Cache coherenceThe degree to which processors agree about the contents of a location. Weaker coherence, more performance, more surprises.Ch. 16.1.1
ReorderingThe umbrella term for compilers, JITs and processors moving actions around, or making them appear to happen out of order.Ch. 16.1.2
ActionThe unit the JMM orders: a variable read or write, a monitor lock or unlock, a thread start or join.Ch. 16.1.3
happens-beforeThe partial ordering that guarantees visibility: if A happens-before B, B sees A's effects.Ch. 16.1.3
Partial orderingA relation that is antisymmetric, reflexive and transitive but not total: some pairs are simply unordered.Ch. 16.1.3
Data raceA variable read by more than one thread and written by at least one, with the accesses unordered by happens-before.Ch. 16.1.3
Correctly synchronizedA program with no data races — and therefore with sequential-consistency semantics.Ch. 16.1.3
Program order ruleWithin a thread, earlier actions happen-before later ones.Ch. 16.1.3
Monitor lock ruleAn unlock happens-before every subsequent lock of the same monitor.Ch. 16.1.3
Volatile variable ruleA write to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of it.Ch. 16.1.3
PiggybackingUsing an existing happens-before edge, created for another purpose, to publish a variable that is not otherwise guarded.Ch. 16.1.4
Unsafe publicationPublishing a reference without an edge, so consumers may see a partially constructed object.Ch. 16.2.1
Partially constructed objectA visible reference whose fields are still defaults or otherwise not what the constructor wrote.Ch. 16.2.1
Safe publicationAny idiom that establishes happens-before from publisher to consumer: a lock, a volatile, a concurrent collection, a static initializer.Ch. 16.2.2
Lazy initialization holder idiomLazy construction via a nested class's static initializer — lazy, thread-safe, and synchronization-free on the hot path.Ch. 16.2.3
Double-checked lockingThe anti-pattern that tests a reference outside the lock. Broken unless the reference is volatile.Ch. 16.2.4
Initialization safetyThe guarantee that properly constructed objects show correct final field values to all threads, however published.Ch. 16.3
FreezeThe moment a constructor completes, after which writes to final fields (and what they reach) cannot be reordered.Ch. 16.3

✓Cheat sheet & self-check

I want…The edge I needUse
A field written before a thread starts to be visible to itthread start ruleSet it up before calling start()
Everything a thread did to be visible after it finishesthread termination rulejoin(), or Future.get, or a latch
A group of fields changed together to be seen togethermonitor lock ruleMutate them inside synchronized; read them inside synchronized
One flag or reference published without exclusionvolatile variable rulevolatile — and remember it publishes everything you wrote before it
An object handed from one thread to anotherwhatever the queue/latch/executor promisesBlockingQueue, Executor, CountDownLatch, Future
A lazily created singletonclass-initialization lockLazy initialization holder idiom (Listing 16.6)
An immutable object shared freelyinitialization safetyAll fields final, no escape during construction, no mutation after
CAS-style updates with visibilityvolatile variable ruleAtomic variables — same memory semantics as volatile
Reordering to stop at a chosen pointa barrier, inserted for youAny of the above; you never place barriers by hand in Java
To reason about a concurrent program—Don't reason about interleavings. Establish an edge and reason about the edge
✅
Do

Ask "what is the happens-before edge?" before asking "is this fast?". Make fields final and classes immutable where you can. Use the holder idiom for lazy singletons. Prefer safe publication through library types whose contract states the edge.

🚫
Avoid

Reading a shared reference outside synchronization and then trusting its fields. Double-checked locking without volatile. Letting this escape a constructor. Assuming sequential consistency. Piggybacking on an edge nobody documented.

🧠
The one habit

When you see a shared mutable field, name the edge that makes it visible. If you cannot name it, you have a data race — and no amount of testing will tell you so reliably.

Five questions the chapter leaves you with

  1. For every field my threads share, which happens-before edge publishes it?
  2. Did I read a reference outside synchronization and then use the object's state?
  3. Is there a lazy-initialization path here that does not use the holder idiom, and why?
  4. Which of my classes claim to be immutable but have a non-final field, or let this escape?
  5. Am I relying on piggybacking that the class's specification never promised?

Notes carried over from the chapter

  1. On most popular processor architectures the memory model is strong enough that the performance cost of a volatile read is in line with that of a non-volatile read.
  2. A partial ordering is a relation on a set that is antisymmetric, reflexive and transitive, but for any two elements x and y it need not be the case that x ≤ y or y ≤ x. We use partial orderings every day to express preferences: we may prefer sushi to cheeseburgers and Mozart to Mahler, but we do not necessarily have a clear preference between cheeseburgers and Mozart.
  3. Locks and unlocks on explicit Lock objects have the same memory semantics as intrinsic locks.
  4. Reads and writes of atomic variables have the same memory semantics as volatile variables.
  5. The JMM guarantees that B sees a value at least as up to date as the value A wrote; subsequent writes may or may not be visible.
  6. This applies only to objects reachable only through final fields of the object under construction.

Java Concurrency in Practice · Appendix A

Appendix A — Annotations for Concurrency

Every class in this book has carried a promise in its annotation header — @ThreadSafe, @Immutable, @GuardedBy("lock"). This appendix is the contract behind those three words: what each annotation asserts, who it is for, how to write a lock expression that a reviewer can check, and how a static analysis tool can turn the whole thing into a build failure. It is three pages, and it is the part of the book most likely to outlive the book.

📖 p. 216 🧩 2 sections · 3 listings ⏱️ ~14 min read 🏷️ Part IV — Appendix A

Appendix in one paragraph

TL;DR — the five things worth remembering

  1. Three class-level annotations carry the public promise: @Immutable (which implies @ThreadSafe), @ThreadSafe, and @NotThreadSafe. The default, unannotated case is "presume not thread-safe".
  2. They serve three audiences, not one. Users learn whether they need a lock; maintainers learn whether the guarantee must be preserved; and static analysis tools can check that an @Immutable class actually is immutable.
  3. @GuardedBy(lock) documents the synchronization policy — which state variable is protected by which lock. It is the one annotation that pays for itself in code review.
  4. The lock argument has exactly five legal shapes: "this", "fieldName", "ClassName.fieldName", "methodName()", "ClassName.class".
  5. The bug it prevents is specific: a class that guards its state correctly today, then gains a field nobody guards, or a method that forgets to take the lock. Documenting the mapping is what makes those omissions visible.

A.1Class Annotations

Three annotations, one question: does this class need a lock before I use it?

This book has used annotations such as @GuardedBy and @ThreadSafe to show how thread-safety promises and synchronization policies can be documented. This appendix documents those annotations; their source code can be downloaded from the book's website. (There are, of course, additional thread-safety promises and implementation details that should be documented but that are not captured by this minimal set.)

Three class-level annotations describe a class's intended thread-safety promises: @Immutable, @ThreadSafe and @NotThreadSafe. @Immutable means, of course, that the class is immutable — and implies @ThreadSafe. @NotThreadSafe is optional: if a class is not annotated as thread-safe it should be presumed not to be thread-safe, but if you want to make that extra clear, use @NotThreadSafe.

AnnotationAssertsImpliesWhen to use it
@ImmutableThe state cannot change after construction; it is safe to share without synchronization and to publish however you like.@ThreadSafe — immutability is the strongest form of thread safety.Final fields throughout, this never escapes construction, no mutators, and any reachable mutable object is neither mutated nor exposed.
@ThreadSafeThe class is safe for concurrent use — it has a synchronization policy and it can be relied on.Nothing.Any class whose contract is a thread-safety guarantee, whether it achieves that with locks, atomics or confinement.
@NotThreadSafeNo such guarantee exists; callers must confine or externalize the locking.Nothing.Optional — but useful when the absence of an annotation might be read as an oversight rather than a decision.
🧾

The important asymmetry is in the default: a class with no annotation should be presumed not thread-safe. That is a deliberately pessimistic default, and it is the right one — it means the absence of a promise is never read as a promise, and it makes every @ThreadSafe in a codebase a real claim rather than decoration.

These annotations are relatively unintrusive and are beneficial to both users and maintainers. Users can see immediately whether a class is thread-safe; maintainers can see immediately whether the thread-safety guarantees must be preserved. Annotations are also useful to a third constituency: tools. Static code analysis tools may be able to verify that the code complies with the contract the annotation indicates — such as verifying that a class annotated @Immutable actually is immutable.

Why a tool can check this at all

Each annotation is a claim narrow enough to be decidable. "Every field is final" is a checkable property; "this class is thread-safe" is not — which is exactly why the book states the strategy explicitly, field by field, in the second annotation rather than expecting a tool to infer it. The class-level annotations are documentation with a machine-readable edge; @GuardedBy is the part that makes the claim specific enough to verify.

A.2Field and Method Annotations

The class annotations are public documentation. Everything else is for maintainers — and this is the part they actually need.

The class-level annotations above are part of the public documentation for the class. Other aspects of a class's thread-safety strategy are entirely for maintainers and are not part of its public documentation.

Classes that use locking should document which state variables are guarded with which locks, and which locks are used to guard those variables. A common source of inadvertent non-thread-safety is when a thread-safe class consistently uses locking to guard its state, but is later modified to add either new state variables that are not adequately guarded by locking, or new methods that do not use locking properly to guard the existing state variables. Documenting which variables are guarded by which locks can help prevent both types of omissions.

@GuardedBy(lock) documents that a field or method should be accessed only with a specific lock held. The lock argument identifies the lock that should be held when accessing the annotated field or method. There are exactly five possible shapes for that argument:

FormMeansTypical use
@GuardedBy("this")The intrinsic lock of the containing object — the object of which the method or field is a member.The ordinary synchronized instance method or synchronized (this) block.
@GuardedBy("fieldName")The lock associated with the object referenced by the named field — an intrinsic lock for fields that do not refer to a Lock, or an explicit Lock for fields that do.Private lock objects: private final Object lock = new Object(); or private final Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();.
@GuardedBy("ClassName.fieldName")Like the previous form, but the lock object lives in a static field of another class.A shared, well-known lock — for example a lock in a registry or a class-level monitor.
@GuardedBy("methodName()")The lock object returned by calling the named method.Classes that expose their lock via an accessor, so the exact object is available to callers and tools.
@GuardedBy("ClassName.class")The class literal object for the named class.Static state guarded by the class-level monitor: synchronized (Foo.class).

Using @GuardedBy to identify each state variable that needs locking, and which lock guards it, can assist in maintenance and code reviews, and can help automated analysis tools spot potential thread-safety errors.

BOOK Listing A.1 · The three class-level annotations in context 
/*
 * The class-level annotation is the PUBLIC promise. Note the default:
 * an unannotated class should be presumed NOT thread-safe, so every
 * @ThreadSafe in a codebase is a claim someone had to make on purpose.
 */

@Immutable
public final class Point {
    private final int x;
    private final int y;

    public Point(int x, int y) {
        this.x = x;
        this.y = y;
    }

    public int getX() { return x; }
    public int getY() { return y; }
    // @Immutable implies @ThreadSafe: no lock needed to share a Point.
}

@ThreadSafe
public class Counter {
    @GuardedBy("this") private long value;      // the strategy, stated

    public synchronized long get() { return value; }
    public synchronized long increment() { return ++value; }
}

@NotThreadSafe
public class StringList {                        // optional, but explicit
    private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<String>();
    public void add(String s) { items.add(s); }  // caller must lock
    public int size() { return items.size(); }
}
BOOK Listing A.2 · All five @GuardedBy lock expressions 
public class GuardedByForms {

    /* (1) "this" -- the intrinsic lock of the containing object */
    @GuardedBy("this") private int instanceState;

    public synchronized void bump() { instanceState++; }


    /* (2) "fieldName" -- a private lock object, either kind */
    private final Object intrinsicLock = new Object();
    @GuardedBy("intrinsicLock") private int guardedByObject;

    private final Lock explicitLock = new ReentrantLock();
    @GuardedBy("explicitLock") private int guardedByLock;

    public void setGuardedByObject(int v) {
        synchronized (intrinsicLock) { guardedByObject = v; }
    }

    public void setGuardedByLock(int v) {
        explicitLock.lock();                    // same semantics as intrinsic
        try { guardedByLock = v; } finally { explicitLock.unlock(); }
    }


    /* (3) "ClassName.fieldName" -- a lock held in another class's
       static field, e.g. a shared registry lock */
    @GuardedBy("Registry.LOCK") private int guardedElsewhere;

    public void setGuardedElsewhere(int v) {
        synchronized (Registry.LOCK) { guardedElsewhere = v; }
    }


    /* (4) "methodName()" -- the lock is returned by an accessor, so
       callers and tools can name the exact object */
    private final Object myLock = new Object();
    Object lock() { return myLock; }

    @GuardedBy("lock()") private int guardedByAccessor;

    public void setGuardedByAccessor(int v) {
        synchronized (lock()) { guardedByAccessor = v; }
    }


    /* (5) "ClassName.class" -- the class literal, for static state */
    @GuardedBy("GuardedByForms.class") private static int staticState;

    public static void bumpStatic() {
        synchronized (GuardedByForms.class) { staticState++; }
    }
}
🧨

An annotation is not enforcement. @GuardedBy documents a rule the compiler will not check; a caller that ignores it compiled fine. What it buys you is that the omission is now visible — to a reviewer, to a maintainer adding a sixth field, and to a tool that knows the convention. Every unguarded field in a class that uses @GuardedBy elsewhere is a question someone will ask.

🎯

The fourth row is the one to remember. A wrong @GuardedBy is not a harmless typo — it tells the next maintainer, and the next analysis run, that a field is protected by a lock that does not protect it. The annotation has to be checked as carefully as the code it describes, which is precisely what the third row makes possible: once the policy exists, not matching it becomes a detectable error.

§Patterns worth stealing

Two listings: the annotation set as declarations you can drop into a package, and a class whose policy survives the change that usually breaks one.

1The annotations themselves

PATTERN The five declarations, with retention and target 
package net.jcip.annotations;

import java.lang.annotation.Documented;
import java.lang.annotation.ElementType;
import java.lang.annotation.Retention;
import java.lang.annotation.RetentionPolicy;
import java.lang.annotation.Target;

/*
 * These are the declarations behind the annotations used throughout the
 * book (the source is downloadable from the book's site). Two details
 * matter in practice: RUNTIME retention, so analysis tools and reflection
 * can see them at all, and TYPE-only targeting for the class-level three,
 * so a @ThreadSafe on a method is a compile error rather than a silent
 * misunderstanding.
 */

/** The class is immutable and therefore thread-safe. Implies @ThreadSafe. */
@Documented
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Immutable { }

/** The class can be used safely from multiple threads. */
@Documented
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface ThreadSafe { }

/** The class is not safe for concurrent use; callers must lock or confine. */
@Documented
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface NotThreadSafe { }

/**
 * The field or method must be accessed only while holding `value`.
 * Legal forms: "this", "fieldName", "ClassName.fieldName",
 * "methodName()", "ClassName.class".
 */
@Documented
@Target({ ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.METHOD })
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface GuardedBy {
    String value();
}

Retention is the detail that decides whether any of this is checkable. SOURCE retention would make these pure comments; RUNTIME makes them visible to an analysis tool or a test that reflects over the class, which is what turns a documented policy into a gate.

2A policy that survives the next commit

PATTERN DocumentedPolicy: every field accounted for, including the new one 
/**
 * The synchronization policy, stated once:
 *   - all mutable instance state is guarded by `lock`
 *   - `staticCount` is guarded by the class literal
 *   - `owner` is final and immutable, so it needs no lock at all
 * A field added later that is neither final nor annotated is the bug this
 * class is shaped to make obvious.
 */
@ThreadSafe
public class DocumentedPolicy {
    private final Object lock = new Object();

    @GuardedBy("lock") private int value;
    @GuardedBy("lock") private int cache;
    @GuardedBy("DocumentedPolicy.class") private static int staticCount;

    private final String owner;          // final + immutable: no lock required

    public DocumentedPolicy(String owner) { this.owner = owner; }

    public int get() {
        synchronized (lock) { return value; }
    }

    public void set(int v) {
        synchronized (lock) {
            value = v;
            cache = v * 2;               // both fields, one lock, one critical section
        }
    }

    public String owner() { return owner; }   // safe: immutable state only

    public static void bump() {
        synchronized (DocumentedPolicy.class) { staticCount++; }
    }

    /* The maintainer's checklist for this class:
     *   1. new mutable field?  -> add @GuardedBy, and use that lock
     *   2. new method touching `value` or `cache`?  -> take `lock`
     *   3. tempted to lock `this`?  -> do not; callers hold that monitor
     */
}

This is the whole appendix in one class: a stated policy, one annotation per mutable field, a comment explaining why the immutable field needs nothing, and a checklist for the change that usually breaks thread safety. Note the deliberate use of a private lock rather than @GuardedBy("this") — exposing the monitor lets clients hold it, which is exactly the escape route §4.2 warned about.

§Vocabulary introduced in Appendix A

TermMeaning as used hereWhere it goes
@ImmutableClass-level promise that the object's state cannot change after construction. Implies thread safety.Ch. A.1
@ThreadSafeClass-level promise that concurrent use is safe. The claim, not the technique.Ch. A.1
@NotThreadSafeExplicit statement that no guarantee exists. Optional, because unsafe is already the default.Ch. A.1
@GuardedByField- or method-level statement of which lock must be held when accessing it.Ch. A.2
Synchronization policyThe mapping from state variables to the locks that guard them, plus the rules for using both.Ch. A.2
Lock expressionThe string argument to @GuardedBy; one of five documented shapes.Ch. A.2
Intrinsic lock ("this")The monitor of the containing object, named by @GuardedBy("this") and acquired by a synchronized instance method.Ch. A.2
Private lock objectA lock held in a private field, named by @GuardedBy("fieldName"); preferred over "this" because clients cannot acquire it.Ch. A.2
Class literal lockThe lock named by @GuardedBy("ClassName.class"), used for static state.Ch. A.2
OmissionThe failure mode annotations exist to prevent: a new field with no lock, or a new method that forgets one.Ch. A.2
Static analysisA tool that verifies code against the contract an annotation states — the third audience for these annotations.Ch. A.1
Retention (RUNTIME)Why the annotations survive into the class file: so tools and tests can read them.Pattern 1

✓Cheat sheet & self-check

State I am documentingAnnotationNote
An immutable class@ImmutableFinal fields, no escape, no mutation — the strongest claim you can make
A thread-safe class with a lock@ThreadSafe + @GuardedBy per fieldThe class promise plus the per-field strategy
A class that needs external locking@NotThreadSafeOptional, but it stops "unannotated" from reading as "probably fine"
Instance state behind a private lock@GuardedBy("lock")Preferred to "this"; clients cannot hold your private lock
State behind an explicit Lock@GuardedBy("fieldName")Same form whether the field is an object monitor or a Lock
Static state@GuardedBy("ClassName.class")Pair it with synchronized (ClassName.class)
A lock borrowed from another class@GuardedBy("ClassName.fieldName")Use only when the shared lock is genuinely part of the design
A lock exposed through an accessor@GuardedBy("methodName()")Lets callers and tools name the exact object
An immutable field inside a mutable classnothingfinal plus immutability needs no lock — say so in a comment
A field you are not sure aboutnothing — yetAn unguarded field is a question, not a decision; resolve it before merging
✅
Do

Annotate every class whose thread safety you have actually reasoned about. State the policy once in a class comment, then @GuardedBy every mutable field. Use a private lock object. Prefer @Immutable when you can earn it.

🚫
Avoid

@ThreadSafe copied onto a class nobody has verified. @GuardedBy("this") on state that is also reachable through a client-held monitor. A named lock that does not match the code. Treating the annotations as enforcement.

🧠
The one habit

When you add a field, add its annotation in the same commit. The annotation is the only artifact that makes the next omission somebody else's visible mistake instead of your invisible one.

Five questions the appendix leaves you with

  1. Which of my classes have a thread-safety guarantee that is not written down anywhere?
  2. For every mutable field, can I name the lock in one of the five legal forms?
  3. Am I using "this" where a private lock object would be safer?
  4. Would an analysis tool reading my annotations be checking real rules, or checking nothing?
  5. If someone added a field tomorrow, what in this class would make them stop and think?

Notes carried over from the appendix

  1. These annotations were intended to be used in conjunction with a static analysis tool, or simply as a consistent documentation convention; the source code for them is available from the book's website.
  2. @Immutable implies @ThreadSafe: an immutable object needs no synchronization to be shared safely, which is why Chapter 3 treats immutability as the strongest form of thread safety.
  3. An unannotated class should be presumed not to be thread-safe; @NotThreadSafe exists to make that explicit where the absence of an annotation might otherwise be read as an oversight.
  4. The five legal forms of the @GuardedBy lock argument are "this", "fieldName", "ClassName.fieldName", "methodName()" and "ClassName.class".
  5. For fields that do not refer to a Lock, the named lock is the intrinsic lock of the referenced object; for fields that refer to a Lock, it is that Lock.
  6. The failure mode the appendix names: a thread-safe class that later gains state variables not adequately guarded, or methods that do not use locking properly to guard the existing state.

Summary of Java Concurrency in Practice, Appendix A (Annotations for Concurrency), p. 216. The annotation declarations in Pattern 1 follow the net.jcip.annotations package distributed with the book; the example classes are the annotations applied as the appendix describes.
